books.title: More Valuable Than Gold
books.art_why: Real rainforest, animals, miners, gold, and conservation projects exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: The Amazon Rainforest Region.
pages.brief: A book-opening page with an Amazon rainforest theme, arranged as a quiet contents view with no characters or action; rows of section markers suggest the topics of rainforest, threats, gold, mining, protection, and glossary in a calm educational layout.

pages.text: The tangled trees of the Amazon rainforest are home to millions of species of animals and plants. The Amazon Rainforest Imagine walking through a beautiful forest with giant trees, vines, and large, colorful flowers. Strange sounds made by birds, monkeys, and other wild animals fill the air. Big, brightly colored snakes, frogs, and insects crawl along the branches. The temperature is high, but raindrops sprinkle through leaves overhead.
pages.brief: A lush Amazon rainforest scene with giant trees, hanging vines, and large colorful flowers. Birds, monkeys, and other wild animals make sounds in the tangled branches; big bright snakes, frogs, and insects crawl along leaves while raindrops fall through the canopy.

pages.text: Threats to the Rainforest The Amazon River flows for about 4,000 miles (6,437 km) from the Andes Mountains to the Atlantic Ocean. In the river valley, constant warm temperatures and large amounts of rain allow for amazing biodiversity in the rainforest. The Amazon rainforest is so vast that it seems as though nothing could harm it. However, people destroy huge areas of the rainforest every year through deforestation. Deforestation happens for many reasons. Loggers cut down trees to make paper and wood products, such as furniture. Ranchers clear land for cattle. Farmers use land to grow soybeans, corn, and other crops. 2000 2006 These satellite photos show the effects of logging in one section of the Amazon rainforest from 2000 to 2006.
pages.brief: The Amazon River winds from the Andes Mountains toward the Atlantic Ocean through a warm, rainy rainforest. In the same forest, loggers cut trees, ranchers clear land for cattle, and farmers plant crops; two satellite views of one section show logging changes between 2000 and 2006.

pages.text: A scientist holds a young Hyacinth Macaw. These endangered birds are native to the Amazon rainforest. Tens of thousands of plant species, billions of insects, and many fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals live in the Amazon region. The forest’s destruction has wiped out thousands of plant and animal species. Scientists might have been able to study these extinct plants and animals to learn things that could help people. The Amazon rainforest is also home to hundreds of Indigenous communities, like the Yanomami and Munduruku (moon-doo-roo- KOO) peoples. Mining, logging, ranching, and farming operations overtake Indigenous lands and bring violence, disease, and destruction of Indigenous cultures and knowledge.
pages.brief: A scientist carefully holds a young Hyacinth Macaw in the Amazon rainforest. Dense plants and many animals fill the habitat around them. The page also recalls that hundreds of Indigenous communities, including the Yanomami and Munduruku peoples, live in the rainforest.

pages.text: Do You Know? Plants store large amounts of carbon, which they use to make energy. When humans burn the rainforest, large amounts of carbon dioxide are released into the air. Scientists think that in the future, the deforestation of the Amazon rainforest will produce more carbon dioxide than it removes. The deforestation of the Amazon rainforest adds to global climate change as well. Rainforest plants remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere for photosynthesis, the process by which they make their own food. With fewer plants, more carbon dioxide stays in the atmosphere. Large amounts of carbon dioxide trap heat in Earth’s atmosphere and contribute to global warming. Though not the greatest causes of deforestation, gold prospecting and mining cause long-term damage. They also affect more than just the areas around the mines. The high price of gold fuels demand, which means the destruction will continue for years to come.
pages.brief: Plants in the Amazon rainforest take in carbon dioxide and store carbon as they make food. When people burn the forest, carbon dioxide rises into the air. Gold prospecting and mining also cause long-term damage beyond the mine areas.

pages.text: Why Gold? Gold is very valuable and difficult to find in nature. Large amounts of it exist underground in the Amazon Valley. People mainly use gold to make jewelry. However, many computers, cell phones, and televisions contain gold wires. Gold on the outside of spacecraft keeps the Sun’s heat from damaging equipment. With so many uses for gold—and more expected—the price and global demand of this rare metal is often high. Gold Price per Ounce, 2000 to 2022 To meet the high demand, many companies based in countries like Canada, the United Kingdom, and Australia offer miners more money than they can earn doing more environmentally- friendly jobs. Because deforestation contributes to high poverty levels, many families are forced to choose jobs like mining for gold.
pages.brief: Gold jewelry, computer wires, cell phones, televisions, and spacecraft equipment show many uses for the rare metal. Underground gold lies in the Amazon Valley, while a rising price chart suggests high demand that pushes some poor families toward mining jobs.

pages.text: Illegal miners in Peru search for gold in a protected part of the rainforest. Gold Mining in the Amazon The methods used in gold prospecting and mining are harmful to people as well as the rainforest. Many of the gold mines are small, illegal operations located in parts of the forest protected by governments. Many South American governments do not have enough money or officers to protect the land, which means these mines wipe out more and more of the forest every year.
pages.brief: Illegal miners search for gold in a protected part of the Peruvian rainforest. Their small mining operation sits inside forest land meant to be guarded, while governments lack enough money and officers to stop the mines from spreading each year.

pages.text: To get the buried gold, prospectors cut down or burn all the trees. They then dig a deep pit with machines or blast out a pit with dynamite. The pit may be as deep as 50 feet (15 m). Miners blast away the walls of the pit with powerful water cannons. This process loosens the ore, which contains the gold, from the walls. The loosened, muddy mixture is sucked up into dump trucks that empty the mud into containers. The water cannons that miners use have enough power to lift a person off the ground.
pages.brief: Prospectors cut down or burn trees, then dig or blast a deep pit in the rainforest. Powerful water cannons break loose the muddy ore from the pit walls, and dump trucks suck up and carry the mixture away; the water jets are strong enough to lift a person.

pages.text: A miner pours the mercury and gold mixture into a tub to be processed. Handling mercury is extremely dangerous. (Inset) After processing tons of soil, a miner shows how much gold he has found in one day. Workers mix the mud with mercury, a toxic metal, sometimes using their bare hands or feet. The mercury separates the gold from the ore. Some smaller mines use copper pans or sheets to separate the gold and mercury mixture from the mud. Others use sluices, in which a filter captures the heavier gold and mercury mixture as the watery mud runs down. The mercury is removed from the gold, often by burning it away. The gold can then be sold.
pages.brief: A miner pours a mercury and gold mixture into a tub for processing. Nearby, workers mix muddy ore with toxic mercury, sometimes with bare hands or feet, and a small inset view shows the tiny amount of gold one miner found after processing tons of soil.

As larger fish eat smaller fish, the amount of mercury in the bodies of the larger fish increases until they become poisonous. When people or other animals drink contaminated water or eat contaminated plants or fish, they become poisoned by the large amounts of mercury. pages.brief: Mercury from mining spreads through forest soil, crops, rivers, and fish. Small fish carry mercury; larger fish eat them and become poisonous. People and animals that drink contaminated water or eat contaminated plants and fish grow sick, and miners who breathe fumes or touch mercury with bare skin also suffer.

pages.text: Illegal miners clear away the rainforest to make their camps. Protecting the Rainforest Many people are working to protect and preserve the rainforest. This is difficult work. Gold mining, logging, ranching, and other harmful activities are profitable and widespread throughout the Amazon region. Some governments in the Amazon region are spending more money to enforce laws and close down illegal mines. However, as long as poor people have few jobs and little money, they may want or need to mine gold. The best solution to the problem of rainforest destruction may be for governments to improve economic opportunities. For example, the government of Brazil has programs to improve the education and job skills of people who can’t otherwise afford schooling or training. This allows them to get other jobs besides those that harm the rainforest.
pages.brief: Illegal miners clear away rainforest to make their camps. In response, people work to protect and preserve the forest: governments try to enforce laws and close illegal mines, while Brazil’s programmes improve education and job skills so people can find jobs that do not harm the rainforest.

pages.text: Governments are not alone in protecting the rainforest. They have help from conservation organizations. These groups work with government agencies, businesses, and other organizations to study and conserve natural places. Continued efforts by both governments and conservation organizations are necessary to stop illegal mining and protect the rainforest. The destruction of the Amazon affects the entire world. Are the jewelry and other things we make from gold really worth damaging the health of the planet and its inhabitants? A farmer checks on a young tree as part of a reforestation project in Brazil.
pages.brief: A farmer checks on a young tree in a reforestation project in Brazil. Conservation organizations work with government agencies, businesses, and other groups to study and conserve natural places, while continued efforts by governments and conservation groups are needed to stop illegal mining and protect the rainforest.

pages.brief: A huge Burmese python lies coiled in Florida marsh grass, its patterned body thick and long; a tiny hatchling slithers nearby. The adult snake shows the size the species can reach, while the hatchling is ready to begin eating and growing in the warm wetland.

pages.text: Introduction Slogging through ankle-deep water in the Florida Everglades, the scientists approach their target. Suddenly, one of the team pounces and grabs the tail of a huge snake. Another researcher lunges and grabs the snake behind its head. Others quickly join the wrestling match between humans and this 16-foot (4.9 m), 150-pound (68 kg) Burmese python. The python finally tires, and they haul it back to the lab for study. The scientists win this time. A bigger battle is underway, though, because Burmese pythons aren’t even supposed to be in Florida. These large snakes are native to the jungles and marshy grasslands of India and other parts of South Asia. What are they doing in Florida?
pages.brief: Scientists wade through ankle-deep water in the Florida Everglades and wrestle a 16-foot, 150-pound Burmese python. One grabs its tail, another grips behind its head, and the team struggles with the huge snake before hauling it back to a lab for study.

pages.text: No one knows for sure how Burmese pythons got into the Everglades ecosystem. The first invaders may have escaped from Florida pet shops, or maybe some pet owners released their pythons when they grew too big to care for. Once the snakes got loose, they thrived in the heat and humidity, hiding in the tangled underbrush and gobbling up other animals. The invasion of the pythons was underway. Pythons as Pets Burmese pythons have become trendy pets among some snake fans. They are cheap to buy and are believed to be easy to control. Some owners can be careless about their pets, though. They may be unaware of how fast and how huge pythons grow. In a couple of years, a 2-foot (.6 m) snake can grow to 12 feet (3.7 m). Also, snakes are escape artists that will squeeze their way out of cages or aquariums that are not carefully locked. Now and then, large pet pythons have attacked and even killed people. In 2012, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service banned bringing new Burmese pythons into the United States. Owners must also insert a microchip into pet pythons to make them easier A man holds his pet to trace. Burmese python.
pages.brief: A man holds his large pet Burmese python, its thick body draped across his arms. Nearby, a smaller python rests inside a securely locked enclosure. The scene shows how a pet can grow huge and why careless owners, escape-prone snakes, and rules about microchips matter.

pages.text: Threats by the Thousands The first Burmese python was reported in the Everglades in 1979. Another sixteen years passed before the next one was found. Since 2000, though, python reports have grown more and more common. When a nest of python eggs was discovered, it confirmed what wildlife biologists feared: Burmese pythons were breeding in the wild. Pythons reproduce more than fifty eggs a year, and within three years of hatching, young pythons themselves are ready to breed. The result in the Everglades has been a population explosion as, year after year, more pythons lay eggs and more pythons survive. Python Removals in and Around Everglades National Park An increasing python population was probably only one factor that led to the dramatic rise in captures.
pages.brief: Wildlife biologists kneel beside a nest of white python eggs hidden in Everglades brush, confirming the snakes are breeding in the wild. An adult Burmese python coils nearby. The nest suggests how more than fifty eggs a year can lead to a population explosion and many more captured snakes.

pages.text: An Everglades Nightmare The Everglades—nicknamed the River of Grass—is one of the most unusual ecosystems in North America. A region of wetlands in southern Florida, it consists mainly of marshes, swamps, and grasslands. Few hills and fewer buildings rise on the broad, flat landscape, but it is rich with plant and animal life and is an important home for many native insects, fish, mammals, and other animals. The American alligator is perhaps the most familiar Everglades native. This leathery reptile can grow up to 16 feet (4.9 m) long and is a fierce predator. Rarer is the Florida panther—only a few dozen of these big cats still roam in the wild. The Everglades is also home to many smaller mammals and is a paradise for birds, including the bald eagle, great egret, roseate spoonbill, and many other wading birds. With jaguars and pumas gone from Florida, the only big cat left there is the panther. Its population is tiny.
pages.brief: A broad, flat Everglades wetland stretches out with marshes, swamps, and grasslands. An American alligator rests near the water, a Florida panther stands among the grass, and wading birds such as a great egret and roseate spoonbill gather nearby, showing the rich native animal life.

pages.text: Burmese pythons will gulp down any animal they can catch. In fact, they have been called “eating machines.” In the Everglades, researchers discovered a python that had killed and swallowed an 80-pound (36 kg) deer. In another case, they found a dead python with a 6-foot (1.8 m) alligator in its mouth. The two animals had killed each other in a life-or-death struggle. Worried that pythons might wipe out some of Florida’s native animals, one research team set out to discover whether this might be the case. In areas with large numbers of these snakes, the researchers studied the populations of small mammals, such as marsh rabbits, raccoons, bobcats, and opossums. They looked at animal counts along roadways from 1996–1997, before pythons became common, and then examined the same data for more recent years. What the team found was shocking: The populations of all these mammals had crashed. There were no signs of marsh rabbits or foxes at all. Yet where pythons were rare or absent, populations were unchanged. Many scientists think pythons are responsible—either they ate all these animals or wiped out the smaller animals that are food for bobcats, foxes, and other predators.
pages.brief: A Burmese python with a swollen belly lies in Everglades grass after swallowing an 80-pound deer, while another dead python holds a 6-foot alligator in its mouth. Nearby, researchers study small mammals along roadways, finding marsh rabbits, raccoons, bobcats, and opossums have crashed where pythons are common.

pages.text: Vanishing Mammals Scientists compared mammal numbers in Everglades National Park before 2000 with numbers from 2003–2011. With the rise of pythons, native mammal numbers have crashed. Bobcat 87.5% decline Opossum 98.9% decline Raccoon 99.3% decline Marsh rabbit 100% decline Red fox 100% decline.
pages.brief: In an Everglades scene, a bobcat, opossum, raccoon, marsh rabbit, and red fox stand sparsely among the grass, while a Burmese python coils nearby. The animals appear few and scattered, reflecting the sharp decline in native mammal numbers after pythons became common in the park.

pages.text: Threatened and Threatening Even as they threaten native animals that are endangered in the United States (eating the Florida panther’s prey, for instance, or simply eating wood storks), Burmese pythons are endangered in South Asia. Their numbers have been shrinking there because of the destruction of their habitat. Also, they are hunted for their skins and meat, as well as captured and sold as exotic pets. The number of nesting wood storks has risen since it was listed as an endangered species in 1984. Habitat protection has helped; pythons may not. Pythons also eat birds in the Everglades. In one study, researchers found that birds make up 25 percent of a python’s diet. The feathers and bones of rare and endangered species, such as the wood stork, have been found in pythons’ bellies. How do scientists know what the pythons are eating? In most cases, they do a necropsy, slicing open dead pythons and studying the dead animals they find in their stomachs. The remains have mostly been of mammals, but birds that live in or near water are also at risk of being eaten.
pages.brief: A researcher slices open a dead Burmese python and studies feathers and bones from birds found in its stomach. A wood stork stands in a nearby wetland. The scene shows pythons eating rare native birds, even as the snakes are endangered in South Asia and hunted for their skins and meat.

pages.text: Part of why native animals may be so helpless against pythons is because these snakes are newcomers. Native species have evolved Burmese pythons together, adapting to live at the top of the one another in order to Everglades food chain. coexist. For 16 million years, no snakes in Florida have been big enough to prey on many of these animals. The natives may not know how to protect themselves or their young from this invasive predator. What’s more, the ecosystem lacks any way to keep the invader in check. Burmese pythons live at the top of the Everglades food chain. Alligators will eat them if they can, but once a python gets big enough, it will even attack alligators. Skip Snow, a biologist at Everglades National Park, pulls a bird from a python’s stomach.
pages.brief: Biologist Skip Snow kneels beside a dead Burmese python in Everglades grass and pulls a bird from its stomach. An alligator rests nearby. The scene shows the python at the top of the food chain, while native animals that evolved without such a large snake may not know how to protect themselves.

pages.text: Fighting Back Finding pythons in the Everglades is tough. The landscape makes it easy for pythons to hide—and hard for humans to find them. Burmese pythons may hide in the grass and brush, and they can stay underwater for up to thirty minutes. Still, Florida workers and volunteers are taking action to try to bring pythons under control. At Everglades National Park, they track down and capture the snakes when possible— almost 2,000 in recent years. Hunters are also allowed to capture the snakes or kill them for their skins and meat. Unfortunately, hunters sometimes mistakenly kill small native snakes, thinking they are baby pythons. One way researchers track pythons is by using radio transmitters. They insert the device into a live snake and release it, and that snake might lead them to other pythons. A researcher inserts a radio tag into a live Burmese python.
pages.brief: A researcher inserts a radio transmitter into a live Burmese python in the Everglades, then will release it to lead the team to other pythons. Nearby, workers and volunteers search tall grass and shallow water; hunters may also capture or kill snakes, sometimes mistaking small native snakes for baby pythons.

pages.text: New laws have been put in place to prevent pet pythons from joining those in the wild. Still, most experts believe it is already too late to stop the python takeover of Florida. Wildlife biologists today fear that Burmese pythons may invade other parts of the country. They can swim to new territory and survive in most places where winters don’t get too cold. Many southern states could be at risk, from South Carolina all the way to California. Scientists continue to investigate the role that pythons play in the changing Everglades ecosystem. Until they learn more, they are careful about putting all the blame on pythons. Still, what we learn about these snake invaders in Florida may keep them from making their way across the country. A Burmese python curls up in the grass at Everglades National Park in Florida.
pages.brief: A Burmese python curls tightly in tall grass at Everglades National Park in Florida, its patterned body looped in the flat wetland. The snake could swim to new territory and survive in southern places where winters are not too cold, while scientists continue studying its role in the changing ecosystem.

pages.text: Pakistan and the Swat Valley.
pages.brief: A clean, orderly contents layout presents the book’s sections in sequence: introduction, Malala’s world, Malala’s work, the attack, a global voice, and a glossary. The simple arrangement suggests the structure of the story without showing people or a scene.

pages.text: Malala studies in Pakistan before the events that made her famous. Introduction Can you imagine living in a country where some children aren’t allowed to attend school? Where a child’s highest hope is to be able to get an education, and that hope is denied? This is the world in which a brave girl named Malala grew up. Malala’s Name Malala was named for a courageous poet and warrior woman who lived in Afghanistan long ago. She led Afghan fighters to victory in a battle against invading British soldiers in 1880.
pages.brief: A young Malala is shown studying in Pakistan before the events that made her famous. In a historical imagining, a courageous Afghan poet and warrior woman leads Afghan fighters to victory against invading British soldiers in 1880.

pages.text: Malala’s mother, Tor Pekai, is a homemaker who follows Muslim traditions by living a private life out of view of others. Malala says that she admires her mother but knows that her own path in life is different. The Swat District is an area of northern Pakistan with high mountains and lush green valleys. Many people consider the region beautiful, and it used to attract tourists. However, not many people visit the area anymore because of the Taliban, a political group based in Pakistan and Afghanistan. The Taliban follow an extreme and fundamentalist version of the Islamic religion that is very different from the version followed by most Muslims. As part of their beliefs, the Taliban severely limit the rights of women. Most residents of areas controlled by the Taliban are forced to follow strict religious rules. For example, music, movies, and television are not allowed. The rules for women and girls are especially strict. Women and girls may not work outside the home, attend school, or wear makeup or bright clothing. They are not permitted to laugh out loud. After a certain age, girls cannot be outside the home without a male relative. The Taliban use violence, including acts of terrorism, to enforce their laws.
pages.brief: Tor Pekai, Malala’s mother, is shown as a homemaker inside a private home, following Muslim traditions, while Malala watches with admiration but sees her own path as different. Beyond them rise the Swat District’s high mountains and lush green valleys, beautiful but with few tourists because of the Taliban.

pages.text: Malala’s family is deeply religious—but their religious practices didn’t align with the Taliban’s. When asked about her religion, Malala is quick to point out that the Islamic religion does not oppose education for girls. In her words, “Islam says that it is not only each child’s right to get [an] education, rather it is their duty and responsibility.” The Taliban started trying to take control of the Swat Valley in 2007. Pakistan’s government and army were unable to stop them. The Taliban attacked police officers and blew up religious and government buildings. Their many acts of violence included destroying girls’ schools in the area. By the end of 2008, the Taliban had blown up roughly 400 schools in Swat and over 1,500 schools in total. The Taliban announced that as of January 15, 2009, girls would no longer be allowed to attend school in the areas under their control. Local people the rubble of a girls’ high school in the Swat Valley in 2009.
pages.brief: Malala stands with her family in a religious setting, calm as she explains that Islam supports education for girls. In another part of the Swat Valley, local people stand amid the rubble of a bombed girls’ high school in 2009, with broken walls and debris around them.

pages.text: Throughout this period, Malala’s father kept his schools open, even though it was dangerous. Over half of Malala’s classmates were pulled out of school because their parents feared the Taliban. Malala stopped wearing her school uniform to avoid being targeted. Why Is Education Important? Education is much more than learning how to read and write. Education provides people with the tools they need to care for themselves and their families and to be active in their communities. Think about the following questions: • How can education affect the kind of job a person might have? • How might an education help people care for their families better? Consider things like food, medical care, educational opportunities for children, and other goods and services. • How might education and the prevention of child labor be connected? • How does education help make a community healthier? • How might education about certain issues affect the choices that people make when they vote? • How does education promote peace in communities and countries? • How might science education affect people’s attitudes about the environment? • How else does education make a difference in people’s lives?
pages.brief: Malala’s father keeps his school open despite danger. Many classmates have been pulled out by fearful parents, leaving fewer students. Malala stands with the remaining pupils, not wearing her school uniform to avoid being targeted, while her father watches over the school.

Malala started blogging on the Internet for the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) in 2009 at age eleven. She blogged about her dreams for her life and about what it was like to live under the rule of the Taliban. She used a pseudonym, or fake name, to hide her identity and keep from being targeted for her writing. After her blog was translated into English, people around the world read it. They were shocked about the situation in Swat and the Taliban’s efforts to prevent girls from attending school. Although Malala hoped to keep her identity private, her secret got out in December 2009.

pages.text: As Malala continued to speak out about education as a basic human right, her fame grew. She gave many interviews on television and in print. In 2010, the New York Times made a movie about her life. In 2011, Desmond Tutu, a world- famous activist and religious leader from South Africa, nominated Malala for the International Children’s Peace Prize. That same Pakistan’s National Youth Peace Prize. In her own country and around the world, she was a voice of hope and Malala’s courageous stand for the rights of girls made her famous around the world. empowerment. As Malala spoke out more and more, she and her father were both seen as threats to the Taliban’s goals. When she was fourteen, her family learned that the Taliban had called for her to die. Malala was afraid for her father’s safety since he was an anti-Taliban activist. However, neither she nor her family thought at first that she was in danger because she was a child.
pages.brief: Malala gives many television and print interviews as her fame grows, becoming a voice of hope and empowerment for girls’ rights. A film about her life and awards for peace are suggested. At home, she and her father look worried after learning the Taliban called for her to die.

pages.text: Malala suffered terrible wounds as a result of being attacked by the Taliban in 2012. She recovered from the attack in a hospital in England. The Attack Malala paid careful attention to her family’s safety as well as her own. She locked doors and avoided walking home from school. Instead, she took the bus. On October 9, 2012, she rode the bus home from school with several friends. A man got on the bus and asked which girl was Malala. Even though no one answered with words, her friends looked at her, so the man knew. He pulled out a gun and fired three shots, one of which struck Malala and injured her very badly. Two other girls were hit, too, though neither one had serious injuries.
pages.brief: On October 9, 2012, Malala rides the bus home from school with several friends. A man steps onto the bus and asks which girl is Malala; her friends’ silent glances reveal her. He pulls out a gun and fires, striking Malala and two other girls.

Malala was then transferred to a hospital in Birmingham, England. Many people made sure she received the best possible care. She and her family stayed in the United Kingdom, and she graduated from high school in 2017. Malala wasn’t happy to be away from the Swat Valley or her friends. pages.text: Malala is introduced at the United Nations headquarters in New York City on July 12, 2013, before making her first speech following her attack. (Left) Malala’s book A Global Voice In July 2013, Malala gave a speech at the United Nations, less than one year after the attack. She called for children around the world to be permitted to get an education. Later that year, Malala received Europe’s top human rights award for her dedication to freedom of thought and human rights. She has met with President Obama, Queen Elizabeth II, and other world figures. Focus on Girls’ Education In 2012, United Nations Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon asked governments, organizations, businesses, religious leaders, and other people and groups around the globe to support education for girls. That same year, the United Nations and Pakistan established the Malala Fund for Girls’ Education. President Zardari of Pakistan donated the first $10 million.
pages.brief: Malala is introduced at the United Nations headquarters in New York City on July 12, 2013, before giving her first speech after the attack. She speaks to an audience, calling for education for children worldwide, and her book is nearby. Leaders later establish the Malala Fund for Girls’ Education.

pages.text: In October 2014, Malala was chosen to receive the Nobel Peace Prize. At age seventeen, she was the youngest person ever given that honor. Malala said the award made her feel “more powerful and courageous.” She dedicated her award to “all those children who are voiceless,” saying, “My message to children around the world is [to] stand up for your rights.” The Taliban tried to silence Malala, but instead they made her voice carry even more loudly. She continues to support every child’s right to an education and refuses to be silenced by fear. Malala’s goal is to someday be Pakistan’s prime minister. Her father became a Special Advisor on Global Education for the United Nations. Malala and her father continue to work together, guided by their vision of a peaceful world and an education for every child. Malala meets U.S. President Barack Obama, First Lady Michelle Obama, and Malia Obama at the White House on October 11, 2013.
pages.brief: In October 2014, Malala receives the Nobel Peace Prize, the youngest person ever given that honor at age seventeen. In another scene, she meets U.S. President Barack Obama, First Lady Michelle Obama, and Malia Obama at the White House on October 11, 2013. Her father works beside her as a UN education advisor.

pages.brief: A village street in Egypt with several buildings painted in bright, colorful patterns. The houses stand close together under warm sunlight, and the scene focuses on the painted walls and simple village setting. The colorful paint gives the village a lively look.

pages.text: Egypt MEDITERRANEAN SEA Israel Alexandria Cairo Jordan Giza Pyramids Saudi Arabia Libya Egypt Gulf of Suez Luxor Aswan High Dam Aswan RED SEA EUROPE ASIA Sudan AFRICA Where Is It? The Arab Republic of Egypt is in the northeastern corner of the continent of Africa. A small part of the country, the Sinai (SEYE-neye) Peninsula, is located in Asia. The Sinai Peninsula shares its border with Israel and Palestine. To the north of Egypt is the Mediterranean (MEH-duh-tuh-RAY-nee-uhn) Sea, and to the east of much of the country is the Red Sea. The country has 2,450 kilometers (1,522 mi.) of coastline. Sudan is to the south of Egypt, and to the west is Libya.
pages.brief: A map-like view of northeastern Africa and the Middle East, with Egypt in the corner of Africa and the Sinai Peninsula in Asia. The Mediterranean Sea lies north, the Red Sea east, Sudan south, and Libya west, with Israel and Palestine nearby.

pages.text: People More than 106 million people live in Egypt. Many of Egypt’s cities and towns are located along the Nile, which runs through the eastern part of the country. Because the rest of the country is mainly desert, a large majority of Egyptians live near the Nile. People use ground water for cooking, washing, and drinking, and they use Egyptian farmers use hoses river water for irrigating to pump water into canals crops. to irrigate their crops. Many farmers grow cotton for Egypt’s large textile industry in the fertile land along the banks of the Nile. Farmers also grow wheat, rice, corn, beans, fruits, and vegetables. They dig canals that channel the river water to their crops for irrigation. In Egypt’s cities, many people work in service industries, and tourism is an important part of the country’s economy. In addition, people work in factories to produce textiles and process food.
pages.brief: Egyptian farmers working fertile land beside the Nile, using hoses and canals to bring river water to their crops. Cotton, wheat, rice, corn, beans, fruits, and vegetables grow there. In cities, people work in service industries, tourism, and factories producing textiles and processed food.

pages.text: Most people in Egypt speak some form of Arabic. Most Egyptians are descended from people who originally lived in the Arabian Peninsula in Asia. Other Egyptians are of African descent, and many of these groups have their own languages as well. About 90 percent of Egyptians are Muslim, meaning they follow the religion of Islam. Nearly 10 percent are Christian. Christianity was the dominant religion in Egypt before Islam spread to the region around 640. Many Egyptians in cities wear Muslims attend a lecture at a mosque in Cairo. and many Egyptians also wear long-sleeved tunics called galabayas (gal-ah-BAY-ahs). Men often wear white, blue, or gray ones, while unmarried women usually wear bright colors. In addition, Muslim women typically wear a veil, called a hijab (hih-JAHB), that covers their heads.
pages.brief: A group of Muslims seated at a lecture inside a mosque in Cairo. Some wear long-sleeved tunics called galabayas, and Muslim women wear veils called hijabs that cover their heads, while the gathering listens in a spacious mosque interior.

pages.text: Egypt’s Landforms MEDITERRANEAN SEA Libyan Sinai Plateau Cairo Qattara Peninsula Depression Sinai Desert Mount Egypt Catherine Sahara Desert Nile River Gulf of E a s te r n D e s e r t Suez RED SEA We s te r n D e s e r t Lake Nasser Land Most of Egypt is covered with deserts. The large Western Desert covers two-thirds of the country, the Eastern Desert lies next to the Red Sea, and the smaller Sinai Desert covers the Sinai Peninsula. All these deserts are part of the Sahara. Each desert has its own unique characteristics. The Western Desert looks like an endless sea of sand dunes with many sharp rocks. The Eastern Desert has wadis (WAH-deez), or dry beds of seasonal rivers that fill up with water only after a heavy rain. The Eastern Desert also includes rugged mountains in the east. The Sinai Desert has tall mountains and deep canyons. In all three deserts, green oases can be found.
pages.brief: A wide desert landscape across Egypt, with the large Western Desert showing sand dunes and sharp rocks, the Eastern Desert with dry wadis and rugged mountains, and the smaller Sinai Desert with tall mountains and deep canyons. Green oases appear among the sands.

pages.text: Lake Nasser Sinai Mountains Western Desert The fertile Nile River Valley is the border between the Western and Eastern Deserts. The Nile is one of the longest rivers in the world, flowing from south to north and ending at the Mediterranean Sea. Near its mouth, the river spreads out into the triangle-shaped Nile Delta. This well-irrigated land holds some of the most fertile soil in Egypt. The Nile Delta stretches about 160 kilometers (100 mi.) between Cairo and the Mediterranean Sea. In the south of Egypt, the Nile forms the world’s largest artificial lake, Lake Nasser. The lake was created in the 1960s when the Aswan Dam was built. Some historical sites were originally located on the land flooded to create Lake Nasser but were moved and reconstructed on safer ground nearby.
pages.brief: The Nile River flowing from south to north through Egypt, spreading into the triangle-shaped Nile Delta near the Mediterranean Sea. In the south, Lake Nasser stretches wide behind the Aswan Dam, with the Sinai Mountains and Western Desert visible nearby.

pages.text: Hatshepsut The temple of Hatshepsut (haht-SHEP-soot) is located across the Nile from the present-day city of Luxor, near the site of the ancient Egyptian city of Thebes. Hatshepsut is one of the few known female Egyptian pharaohs. She reigned from around 1473 to 1458 bce. Ancient images show her wearing a false beard and traditional male clothing. History Thousands of years ago, one of the world’s first civilizations developed along the banks of the Nile in Egypt. The seasonal flooding of the river provided rich land for the ancient Egyptians, and they were among the first people in the world to grow crops and use a plow. For about three thousand years, thirty different dynasties of pharaohs ruled ancient Egypt. Some ancient Egyptians believed the pharaohs were living gods, and they built huge stone monuments and tombs for them. The ancient Egyptians were also polytheistic, which means they believed in many gods. The pharaohs led the building of elaborate stone temples to honor different Egyptian gods. Between about 2700 and 1000 bce, Egypt was one of the greatest civilizations in the world.
pages.brief: The temple of Hatshepsut across the Nile from Luxor, near ancient Thebes. Ancient Egyptians farm the fertile flooded banks of the Nile, build stone monuments and tombs for pharaohs, and honor many gods in elaborate temples. Hatshepsut is shown wearing a false beard and traditional male clothing.

pages.text: Over the centuries, several outside forces have conquered or occupied Egypt. In 332 bce, the emperor Alexander the Great invaded Egypt and made it part of the Greek Empire. Egypt was under Greek rule for about three hundred years. Alexander founded the city of Alexandria, which still sits on the northern coast and is the country’s main seaport. After centuries of Roman and Persian control, in 640 ce, a Muslim army from the Arabian Peninsula conquered Egypt. Muslim dynasties, including the Fatimids, Mamluks, and Ottomans, ruled Egypt until the 1700s. In 1798, France attempted to invade Egypt, motivating the British to become involved in Egypt’s government—the British did not want France to gain control of Egypt. The Ottoman Empire regained control of Egypt through the next century, but British and French influence remained. During World War I (1914–1918), Britain made Egypt a British protectorate, or a country that is protected and controlled by another country. In 1922 Egypt won its independence from the British.
pages.brief: A panoramic historical illustration showing waves of outside rulers reaching Egypt across the centuries: Greek soldiers with Alexander, the seaport of Alexandria, Muslim dynasties, and later British and French influence, ending with Egypt gaining independence in 1922.

pages.text: Landmarks Every year, millions of people visit Egypt to see its ancient landmarks. One of the most famous landmarks is the Valley of the Kings in southern Egypt. Some of Egypt’s most famous pharaohs were buried here in more than sixty tombs, along with countless treasures. Tomb robbers stole many of these treasures long ago. However, the tomb of Tutankhamun (toot-an-KAH-muhn) still had its treasures when it was discovered in 1922. Many of these amazing treasures are displayed in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo. The temples at Abu Simbel, along the banks of Lake Nasser, are another popular tourist site. Two of the temples were built by Ramses II, pharaoh of Egypt from 1279 to 1213 bce. Four giant stone statues of Ramses II sit at the entrance to the Great Temple, which temple at Abu Simbel was carved out of a cliff. Inside this temple, three hallways extend into the cliff and include more statues and painted scenes. The hallways lead to a shrine at the temple’s center dedicated to some of the Egyptian gods.
pages.brief: The Valley of the Kings in southern Egypt, with more than sixty tombs and treasures, including Tutankhamun's tomb. Nearby, the Great Temple at Abu Simbel stands carved into a cliff beside Lake Nasser, with four giant stone statues of Ramses II at its entrance.

pages.text: Camels are particularly well suited to Egypt’s desert conditions because they can survive on very little water. Animals People in Egypt’s rural areas raise many animals, such as sheep, goats, donkeys, and water buffalo. Some people also raise and use camels for work. Some wild animals live in the harsh conditions of the deserts. One desert animal is the fennec, a small fox with large ears. The fennec spends most of its day underground in a burrow and comes out at night to find food. Many snakes, lizards, and scorpions also live in the deserts. The ibex (EYE-beks), a sturdy wild goat, is another animal that can survive in the deserts’ difficult conditions. The Nile and its valley are also home to many kinds of animals. Hundreds of different types of fish swim in the Nile’s waters, and crocodiles can be found in the southern part of the river.
pages.brief: Camels, sheep, goats, donkeys, and water buffalo in Egypt's rural areas. In the desert, a fennec fox with large ears rests in a burrow by day, while snakes, lizards, scorpions, and an ibex survive the harsh conditions. Fish and crocodiles swim in the Nile.

pages.text: Riding in a felucca, or small sailing boat, on the Nile is a popular tourist activity in Egypt. Conclusion Egypt is an amazing country filled with history. Both animals and people live in its rugged deserts. Cutting a path through the desert, the Nile River provides life-giving water and fertile land for crops. Throughout history, the various civilizations that found a home in Egypt shaped its people and culture and produced knowledge that benefited the world. Egypt’s many historical sites hold secrets and treasures that should be important to everyone.
pages.brief: A felucca, a small sailing boat, glides along the Nile River with tourists aboard. The river cuts through rugged desert, bringing life-giving water and fertile land for crops, while Egypt's long history and many civilizations shape the people and culture around it.

books.title: The Last Great Race
books.art_why: The Iditarod, sled dogs, mushers, and Alaskan settings all exist in the real world today, so real photographs are possible.

pages.text: A musher and sled-dog team in the wilderness Introduction It is hard to imagine anyone wanting to travel almost 2,000 kilometers (1,242 mi) across the Alaskan wilderness in the dead of winter. It is even harder to imagine someone doing it behind a sled pulled by a team of dogs. Yet every year since 1973, dozens of people have participated in what is known as “The Last Great Race on Earth.” The race, better known as the Iditarod, starts in Anchorage, Alaska, on the first Saturday in March. It is without a doubt one of the most grueling sporting events ever held.
pages.brief: A musher travels with a sled-dog team in the Alaskan wilderness as the dogs pull the sled through winter terrain. The scene introduces the Iditarod race, which starts in Anchorage on the first Saturday in March.

pages.text: However, as technology and modes of transportation improved, the Iditarod Trail was used less and less. That meant there was less need for Alaskan sled dogs. Several people living in Alaska began to consider ways to preserve the skill of dogsledding. They wanted to help save the Alaskan sled dogs. Do You Know? Some people mistakenly give the serum run of 1925 credit for being the inspiration behind the Iditarod. The serum run happened after a terrible disease called diphtheria struck the town of Nome, Alaska. The disease could only be treated with an injection of serum. A fierce storm prevented transport of the serum from Anchorage to rural Nome by other means. So, dogsledding teams rushed the serum to the town, saving many lives. Although the events were amazing, they were not the origin of the Iditarod. Balto, lead dog of one of the sled teams that took serum to Nome.
pages.brief: Balto, a lead sled dog, stands with a dogsled team after carrying serum to Nome during the 1925 serum run. The scene shows the dogsledding effort that saved lives when a fierce storm blocked other transport to the town.

pages.text: History The practice of dogsledding was created from a mix of Native and Russian skills. It was the main mode of transport in rural Alaska for centuries. But by 1967, dogs were being replaced by snowmobiles, cars, and trucks. Two Alaskans, Dorothy Page Redington Sr., wanted to do would help save old tradition. Dorothy, an Alaska history buff, and Joe, a dog breeder and Alaskan museum named after Dorothy Page to hold a sled- dog race along the Iditarod Trail, a route that saw more and more use during the Alaskan gold rush. The trail got its name from Native Alaskans, who called the surrounding hunting area Haiditarod, or “The Distant Place.” The route of the first race was about 90 kilometers (56 mi) and took only two days to complete.
pages.brief: Dorothy Page, an Alaska history buff, and Joe Redington Sr., a dog breeder, stand with sled dogs in rural Alaska. They work to save dogsledding as snowmobiles, cars, and trucks replace dog teams along the Iditarod Trail.

pages.text: In order to attract mushers, Joe and Dorothy raised $25,000 in prize money. This was to get 58 mushers to enter. But the next year, the race was the mild winter led to a lack of snow Joe Redington Sr. and a lack of interest. Another race was held in 1969, but organizers could only raise enough money for a $1,000 prize, and only 12 mushers entered. But the lack of interest did not discourage Joe Redington Sr. He was determined to make the race longer and more challenging. In 1973, he extended the route to around 1,800 kilometers (1,100 mi). It now stretched from Anchorage to Nome and was the longest sled-dog race in the world. Joe managed to increase the prize money to about $50,000. In 1973, 35 mushers entered the first official Iditarod. It took the winner 20 days to complete the race, and the last-place finisher reached Nome 12 days later.
pages.brief: Joe Redington Sr. stands with sled dogs as he plans a longer, more challenging Iditarod race from Anchorage to Nome. In 1973, 35 mushers enter the first official Iditarod, and the winner takes 20 days to finish.

pages.text: The Route The trail taken by the mushers carrying serum in 1925 covers only about half of today’s northern Iditarod race trail. The current trail uses two routes, the northern and the southern, which split off for about 500 kilometers (300 mi) in the middle of the race. On even-numbered years, mushers take the northern route, and on odd- numbered years, they take the southern route. The official opening of the race is a bustling ceremony in Anchorage. The dogs make a ceremonial run to Eagle River. Then the dogs are trucked to the official start in Wasilla. This way, the dogs are on the dangerous city streets of Anchorage, and they do not have to cross Cook Inlet. The busy start in Anchorage.
pages.brief: A busy race start in Anchorage, Alaska, shows sled-dog teams and people gathered on city streets. The dogs make a ceremonial run to Eagle River before they are trucked to the official start in Wasilla.

pages.text: The Iditarod Trail.
pages.brief: A wide scene showing the Iditarod Trail as the central subject, with no people, dogs, sleds, or buildings visible. The view focuses only on the trail itself alone, with nothing else added to the scene.

pages.text: Legendary musher Susan Butcher, who set a record four wins in five years, and her sled dogs. Not every team starts at the same time. Instead, teams take off at two-minute intervals to prevent teams from running into each other. The differences in time are erased at the required 24-hour stop, where officials hold the teams back for a few extra minutes. Since the race takes over a week to complete, there are 26 checkpoints along the route where mushers and dogs can rest. Before the race begins, mushers send dog food and other supplies to the checkpoints so they will not have to carry them on the trail. The average distance between checkpoints is 74 kilometers (46 mi)—longer than the entire 1967 race—and the greatest distance between checkpoints is 150 kilometers (93 mi).
pages.brief: Susan Butcher, a legendary musher, stands with her sled dogs on the trail. She set a record with four wins in five years, while teams start at two-minute intervals and rest at checkpoints along the route.

pages.text: Off they go! The dogs can keep a steady speed of about 19 kilometers per hour (12 mph) for about 4 to 6 hours before they get tired. This is usually long enough to get from one checkpoint to the next. But the dogs also rest on the trail, so the mushers don’t always stop at every checkpoint. In order to keep the teams on course through the trackless wilderness, the trail is marked with orange stakes and reflective tape. Additional markers are set up in the mountains and along the coast. Each year, volunteers set out about 12,000 stakes. Getting lost could cost a musher their life, so it is important that the trail be well marked.
pages.brief: A dog team runs at a steady pace through the trackless wilderness, with orange stakes and reflective tape marking the trail. The dogs can keep going for four to six hours before they tire and rest on the trail.

pages.text: The Iditarod Trail is filled with some of the most beautiful scenery in the world. It crosses the Alaska Mountain Range at a gap known as Rainy Pass, though during the Iditarod, it is more likely to be a snowy pass. The trail also follows the Yukon River Valley and travels along the coast of the Bering Sea before reaching Nome. Along the way, it passes through thick forests and over frozen tundra. The teams must cross frozen streams and rivers, which can be deadly if the ice is too thin. Wild as moose have to attack and kill dogs. And racers driving snow. Rainy Pass, the highest elevation on the race.
pages.brief: A sled-dog team crosses Rainy Pass in the Alaska Mountain Range, the highest elevation on the race, through snowy scenery. The trail also passes forests, frozen tundra, frozen streams and rivers, and the coast of the Bering Sea.

pages.text: The trail ends in the small city of Nome. During the winter, the sun rises for only a few hours a day, and the race is a welcome celebration for the residents. Citizens of Nome line the streets to watch the finishers come in. While 55 to 75 mushers usually start, every year several drop out because of sickness, injury, or simple exhaustion. Today, winners of the Iditarod usually complete the race in 10 to 12 days. A record time of 8 days, 18 hours, and 46 minutes was set in 2011 by Inupiat Jewish racer John Baker. There can be a full week between the times when the first and last mushers cross the finish line. Do You Know? During the early days of dogsledding, a red lantern was hung outside a check- point to help the musher find shelter. The lantern remained lit until the musher arrived. Today, a red lantern is hung over the finish line of the Iditarod. The lantern is lit at the start of the race, and the last musher to cross the line puts it out.
pages.brief: Citizens of Nome line the streets to watch mushers and sled-dog teams finish the Iditarod under the winter sky. A red lantern hangs over the finish line, and the last musher to cross puts it out.

pages.text: The Mushers Mushers come from all walks of life. They include professional athletes, tradespeople, authors, doctors, teachers, and lawyers. Since 1974, people of all genders have competed in the Iditarod. Two women have won the race. One of them, Susan Butcher, has won four times. While many are Alaskans, mushers come from all around the world. They come from many of the 50 states and from countries such as Canada, Russia, Norway, Japan, New Zealand, Great Britain, and Italy. To enter the Iditarod, a musher must be at least 18 years old. They must have competed in a previous Iditarod or two qualifying races of at least 805 kilometers (500 mi) in the previous two years. Sled-dog racing is a Do You Know? solo sport, and all mushers Since 1986, the compete in the Iditarod Iditabike Race has been held alongside the alone. They have no crews Iditarod Trail. pages.brief: Mushers from many walks of life—professional athletes, tradespeople, authors, doctors, teachers, and lawyers—stand with their sled dogs during the race. Each musher competes alone, feeding and caring for the dogs even before feeding themselves.

pages.text: Unfortunately, the costs of competing in the race have risen over the years. Feeding and caring for the dogs, and sled equipment, are all expensive. This has led to difficulties for Indigenous Alaskan mushers who live in smaller rural communities to enter. In 2018, less than 10 out of the 67 mushers in the competition were Indigenous Alaskan. Still, mushers like Ketil Reitan and Peter Kaiser are trying to keep the activity alive. So what would cause someone to brave temperatures as low as −51° Celsius (−60° F), strong winds, blowing snow, wild animals, and treacherous ice, all on very little sleep? The winner’s prize of $50,000 or more may be an incentive, but most do it for the challenge, for the love of the sport, and the love of their dogs. Most participants are thrilled simply to finish the race. Musher Ketil Reitan and his sled-dog team.
pages.brief: Ketil Reitan and his sled-dog team travel through harsh winter conditions with strong winds, blowing snow, and treacherous ice. The scene shows the challenge that draws mushers to the Iditarod for the love of the sport and their dogs.

pages.text: The Dogs The Iditarod is really about the dogs. The dogs who run the race, called huskies, have been specially bred to pull sleds the way collies have been bred to herd sheep. The sturdy, tough huskies can pull a sled carrying supplies and the musher, a total weight of 136 to 182 kilograms (300–400 lbs). This may seem like a lot, but huskies love to pull. Huskies have also been bred to withstand extreme cold. They have two layers of fur. The outer layer, made of thick hairs, protects the dog from wind and water. The inner layer is a lot like a sheep’s wool. It serves to insulate the body from cold temperatures and keep body heat from escaping. Some people even use husky hair to make warm hats and gloves. Huskies can’t hide their enthusiasm.
pages.brief: A sturdy husky stands in the cold, showing its thick double coat of fur. Huskies are bred to pull sleds carrying supplies and a musher, and they love to pull, with an outer coat for wind and water and an inner coat for warmth.

pages.text: The dogs do not lose heat by sweating through their skin as humans do. Instead, they pant, and they sweat through their feet. These adaptations allow huskies to run comfortably at temperatures below −51° Celsius (−60° F). Do You Know? Often, sled dogs on the Iditarod wear “booties” on their feet. The booties keep the dogs’ paws dry and prevent cuts from the sharp ice and rocks on the trail. A dog team can go through as many as 1,000 booties during an Iditarod. This can get pretty expensive, since the booties cost about fifty cents each.
pages.brief: A husky wears protective booties on its feet while running on ice and rocks. The booties keep the dog’s paws dry and prevent cuts, and a team can go through as many as 1,000 booties during an Iditarod.

pages.text: Huskies have also been bred to work as a team. This is important, since the whole team must work together to pull the sled. An Iditarod team can have as many as 16 dogs. Usually, an experienced lead dog runs at the front of the team and helps set the pace. Huskies are extremely friendly dogs, and, like most dogs, they love to please their owners. Lead dogs are tough, enthusiastic, and experienced.
pages.brief: A team of up to sixteen huskies pulls together, with an experienced lead dog running at the front to help set the pace. Huskies are friendly dogs bred to work as a team and to please their owners.

pages.text: A vet checks a resting husky. Care of the huskies before, during, and after the race is of utmost importance to the mushers and to the officials who run the Iditarod. Veterinarians wait at each checkpoint to examine the dogs as they come in. Dogs suffering from frostbite, exhaustion, or injury are pulled from the race. In fact, most mushers drop off one or more dogs that become tired or don’t want to run anymore. There are three mandatory stops during the race to let the dogs rest. The first one, taken at the musher’s choice of checkpoint, is 24 hours long. The other two are 8 hours long and are made at specific checkpoints. Mushers who mistreat their dogs are disqualified.
pages.brief: A veterinarian examines a resting husky at a checkpoint, checking the dog’s health during the race. Dogs with frostbite, exhaustion, or injury are pulled from the race, and there are three mandatory stops to let the dogs rest.

pages.text: The dogs eat a lot during the race to keep their energy high. One dog can consume up to 10,000 calories per day. The dogs’ diets are rich in fat and protein from meat, pure fat, and dry dog food. They also need a lot of water, which the mushers warm up so that the dogs will not lose heat. The dogs typically eat three meals a day during rests, and they also get lots of snacks on the trail. Food Consumed per Meal Food Type Quantity Dry dog food.4 kilograms (12 oz) Meat.5 kilograms (1 lb) Fat.25 kilograms (8 oz) Water 1 liter (1 qt) Like any athletic team, the dogs go through rigid training before the race. Sled dogs are trained to pull from the time they are puppies. Between September and February before the Iditarod, teams make practice runs of up to 2,253 kilometers (1,400 mi). They also compete in smaller races of 322 kilometers (200 mi) or more. In the end, the best-trained team is usually the winner.
pages.brief: A husky eats a meal of dry dog food, meat, fat, and warm water during a rest, with dogs consuming up to 10,000 calories a day. Sled dogs train from puppyhood and make long practice runs before the Iditarod.

pages.text: The Iditarod keeps alive the practice of dogsledding. Conclusion The Iditarod, also known as the “Last Great Race,” is a grueling competition between sled-dog teams. They race across the Alaskan wilderness for 10 to 12 days for a more than $50,000 prize. Mushers come from around the world to compete. Journalists, TV networks, and newspaper reporters from across the globe come to cover the race. But it is not the money or the fame that attracts the mushers. The mushers do not really race their teams against one another; they race against the hardships of the wilderness and against themselves. Any musher will tell you that the true heroes of the Iditarod are the huskies who run almost 2,000 kilometers (1,243 mi) over some of the harshest, most beautiful land on Earth.
pages.brief: A sled-dog team runs across the Alaskan wilderness as journalists and TV crews cover the Iditarod. The mushers race against the hardships of the wilderness and against themselves, while the huskies are the true heroes of the race.

books.title: Comic Cons
books.art_why: Keyword check indicates drawing for this title.

pages.text: Robin, the Joker, and Batman spend quality time together at the 2014 New York Comic Con. Welcome to Comic Con Packed with thousands of other fans in an auditorium, you wait for the stars to arrive. It’s warm inside your Chewbacca costume, and you’re impatient. Suddenly the audience is on its feet, cheering. You jump up to see the Iron Man himself, Robert Downey Jr., walk out onstage. The Avengers panel has begun. This is the world of comic cons: colorful, crowded, and built for fans of pop culture. If you collect comic books, watch movies, or play video games, there’s something for you at a comic con. These fan conventions, called cons for short, happen all over the country.
pages.brief: Robin, the Joker and Batman are together at the 2014 New York Comic Con, surrounded by thousands of fans. In a warm auditorium, a fan in a Chewbacca costume watches as Robert Downey Jr. walks out onstage as Iron Man and the audience stands cheering for the Avengers panel.

pages.text: College students browse comic books at a 2015 book fair. The Rise of an Art Form What has caused this explosive growth? First, comic books have become more popular in recent years. Comic books had many readers during the “Golden Age” of the 1930s and 1940s. They became much less popular for several decades afterward. During that time, many people thought of comics as kid stuff. But in the late 1980s and early 1990s, comic book series such as The Sandman and Watchmen broke new ground and were praised by critics as serious works of art. Since then, interest in comic books has soared, and writers and artists continue to explore new topics and styles.
pages.brief: At a 2015 book fair, college students browse comic books. The scene reflects the rise of an art form: comics had many readers in the 1930s and 1940s, lost popularity, then series such as The Sandman and Watchmen were praised as serious works of art and interest soared.

pages.text: A modern comic might tell a traditional superhero story, a story about war, or a story about family drama. Comic books known as graphic novels are popular with young adults. Graphic memoirs, another kind of comic book, often deal with serious themes. For example, Art Spiegelman won a Pulitzer Prize—a highly respected achievement—for his graphic memoir Maus. His work was based on interviews with his father, a Holocaust survivor. As topics for comic books have expanded, so have audiences. Fans of every color, age, and gender can find something to relate to in comic books. As a result, comic cons are booming. Second, the enormous success of recent Hollywood movies based on comic books has brought many people to comic cons. Movies such as The Dark Knight (2008), Wonder Woman (2017), and Black Panther (2018) attracted many new fans. Movies are now a big part of comic cons. Famous actors, writers, and directors from comic-book movies often appear on panels and draw Spider-Man first came huge crowds. to the big screen with a blockbuster film in 2002.
pages.brief: Modern comics tell superhero stories, war stories and family drama. Graphic novels are popular with young adults, and Art Spiegelman’s graphic memoir Maus won a Pulitzer Prize. Fans of every color, age and gender read comics, while comic-book movies such as The Dark Knight, Wonder Woman and Black Panther draw new fans.

pages.text: Artists draw manga-style illustrations during the 2017 Libya Comic Convention in Tripoli. Movies are only the beginning, though. Comic cons around the world also celebrate video games, novels, and television shows. The audience has become so large that some cons focus on just one art form. For example, many fans attend cons for anime and manga (animated films and comic books from Japan). There are cons for fans and collectors of classic comics. There are cons for fans of sci-fi and fantasy fiction. There are even cons for fans of steampunk, horror, and humor, among many others.
pages.brief: At the 2017 Libya Comic Convention in Tripoli, artists draw manga-style illustrations. Around them, fans celebrate video games, novels and television shows, with some conventions focused on anime and manga, classic comics, science fiction, fantasy, steampunk, horror or humor. Movies are only the beginning of what comic cons offer.

pages.text: Big Cons and Small Comic cons happen in cities all over the world. Outside the huge conventions in San Diego and New York, the crowds are smaller but just as enthusiastic. Check online or in your local newspaper to find out if there’s a comic con coming to a town near you. You might be surprised at what you’ll find: local fans mix with big-name cartoonists and movie stars at many smaller cons. If you go, you just might see the star of your favorite show or your favorite writer. You are also likely to meet local artists and make new friends. A brother and sister attend the 2019 Edinburgh Comic Con on their respective dragons, Night Fury and Light Fury.
pages.brief: At the 2019 Edinburgh Comic Con, a brother and sister attend with their dragons, Night Fury and Light Fury. Smaller crowds outside huge San Diego and New York conventions are just as enthusiastic. Local fans mix with big-name cartoonists and movie stars, and visitors can meet local artists, see favorite stars and make new friends.

pages.text: Captain America and Loki battle it out at the 2016 MCM Comic Con in London. Cosplay Many fans display their own creativity at comic cons. Some do this through cosplay. In cosplay, fans dress up in costumes as characters from comic books, anime, manga, and other fantasy genres. Cosplay is serious business for fans worldwide. Costumes can be bought, custom- built, or handmade. Many cosplayers make realistic props that go with their characters. Some cosplayers act like their favorite characters while they are in costume. Costumes can be simple or incredibly detailed. Figuring out how to make or build a costume is a big part of the fun for many fans. Cosplay is a major part of comic cons, with hundreds of costumed fans in the audience. Many conventions also hold cosplay contests, where cosplayers can pose for photos and act in skits based on their characters.
pages.brief: At the 2016 MCM Comic Con in London, Captain America and Loki battle in costume. Hundreds of cosplayers fill the audience in simple and detailed costumes, carrying handmade or custom-built props and acting like favorite characters. Some pose for photos and perform skits in cosplay contests.

pages.text: Celebrity Appearances At comic cons, fans can also meet creators personally. Stars often take part in panels where they speak about the experience of making comic books, films, and shows. Audience members can sometimes ask questions during panels, have their photos taken with celebrities, and get autographs. These personal meetings become treasured memories for many fans. Isaac Hempstead-Wright and Elle Fanning appear at CCI: San Diego to promote their animated film The Boxtrolls.
pages.brief: At CCI: San Diego, Isaac Hempstead-Wright and Elle Fanning appear to promote their animated film The Boxtrolls. Fans meet creators and stars at panels, where they hear about making comics, films and shows. Audience members ask questions, take photos with celebrities and get autographs, turning these personal meetings into treasured memories.

pages.text: Attendees flow through the giant exhibit hall at the New York Comic Con in New York City. The Exhibit Hall The center of most comic cons is the exhibit hall. Fans can buy and trade comic books here, along with action figures, toys, and other merchandise. Experienced collectors can find rare editions of comic books. New collectors can get a head start on their collections. There is often an author signing area in the exhibit hall where fans can meet artists and writers. Even if you’re not looking to buy anything, there is always a lot to see in the exhibit hall. Cosplayers wander by in colorful costumes; movies and movie trailers are shown regularly. Celebrity sightings are always possible, and there is an endless supply of colorful merchandise to browse through.
pages.brief: Attendees flow through the giant exhibit hall at New York Comic Con in New York City. Fans buy and trade comic books, action figures, toys and merchandise, while collectors hunt rare editions. An author signing area lets fans meet artists and writers. Cosplayers wander by, movies are shown, and colorful merchandise fills the hall.

pages.text: Growing Pains and Issues The popularity of comic cons has not come without some controversy, though. Some comic book fans feel that the bigger cons have become too large. They think that the focus has moved away from comic books. Many comic cons could, in fact, be described as pop culture conventions rather than comic book conventions. The audience for comic books and comic cons has changed as well. While comic con attendees used to be mostly male, about forty percent of recent CCI: San Diego attendees are female. More than half of the people attending recent cons are under twenty-nine. The increased diversity of the comic con audience brings larger crowds and is a welcome develop- ment for most fans. Comic cons can also be a place to discuss larger controversies. With the recent comeback of the comic book form, authors have taken on serious topics like race, gender, politics, and war. These comics are not to everyone’s liking. Some comics can even become the subjects of “banned book” campaigns, where a library is asked to take a book off the shelves. Spider-Man and Batman comics, for example, have been challenged in some places because of adult themes. Readers, teachers, and librarians often discuss censorship on panels at comic cons.
pages.brief: At a comic con panel, readers, teachers and librarians discuss censorship and banned-book campaigns. A diverse crowd—about forty percent female and more than half under twenty-nine—fills the convention. Comics about race, gender, politics and war sit alongside superhero stories, and Spider-Man and Batman comics have been challenged for adult themes.

pages.text: Stars from the film Black Panther attend a comic con panel in 2017. One result of these talks has been the rise of the labels “graphic novel” and “graphic memoir” to describe comics that are meant for adults. Some comics are still aimed at children, but comics as a whole are no longer “kids only.” Some comics are fictional and some aren’t; some are educational and some are meant for entertainment. Some deal with adult themes, while others provide an escape into fantasy worlds. Since comics are diverse, should all comics be shelved together in libraries and schools? What role do comics have in our society? These questions are frequent topics at comic con panels.
pages.brief: Stars from the film Black Panther attend a comic con panel in 2017. On panels, speakers discuss whether all comics should be shelved together in libraries and schools, and what role comics have in society. Graphic novels and graphic memoirs for adults sit alongside comics for children, fiction and nonfiction, education and entertainment.

pages.text: Pushing the Boundaries Keeping up with the variety of comic books can be challenging, but overall, it’s an exciting time for comic cons. The huge range of the comics available today has resulted in bigger and wider audiences for comics and conventions. Fans of every age, color, and gender can find themselves represented in a comic somewhere. Heroes might look like Superman, a young girl from Botswana, or a reporter on the ground in Bosnia. There is no limit to what can happen in a comic book or who can be its heroes. In the end, this is what draws people to comic cons. The cons (and the stories that inspire them) create worlds where can be transformed into heroes. Many people return to over and over. A young girl shows off her pink Star Wars stormtrooper costume at CCI: San Diego.
pages.brief: At CCI: San Diego, a young girl shows off her pink Star Wars stormtrooper costume. Around her, fans of every age, color and gender find heroes who look like Superman, a young girl from Botswana or a reporter on the ground in Bosnia. The variety of comics draws people back to comic cons again and again.

books.title: Catching Air
books.art_why: Modern wind sports and equipment are real-world subjects, not a biography of one named famous person.

pages.text: Skydivers jump from an airplane. Air and Flight Look, up in the sky! Is it a huge bird? Is it Superman? No, it’s a regular person flying high, or “catching air,” while hang gliding, skydiving, or parasailing. Maybe you’d like to try one of these wind-powered sports and soar and swoop through the wide-open skies. All you need is a sense of adventure, the right equipment, and an understanding of how wind works.
pages.brief: High above the ground, several skydivers in jumpsuits leap from an open airplane door into a wide blue sky. Below them, a hang glider and a parasailor glide through open air, showing different wind-powered sports.

pages.text: Wind-sport enthusiasts pay attention to their natural surroundings. They know areas of land heat up faster than areas of water. They need moving air, so they like tall slopes and cliffs. As warm air rises from land, a cooler wind from the sea rushes in to replace it. When this wind strikes the face of a cliff, it is deflected upward. This strong updraft of air creates lift —and a great ride! Often, wind-sporters look to birds for flying advice. Hawks or seagulls circling lazily overhead are riding a rising column of air called a thermal. Smart wind-sporters will also try to catch thermals for rides. t f Wind-sporters catch updrafts to give them a boost into the sky.
pages.brief: Along a coastal cliff, warm air rises from sunlit land while cooler sea wind rushes in and bends upward against the rock face. Hawks and seagulls circle in a thermal above, and wind-sporters watch the birds and catch the rising updraft.

pages.text: Hang Gliding The hot summer sun sits high in the mid- afternoon sky. A gentle breeze blows in from the sea. A woman with a triangular-shaped, winged contraption on her shoulders runs down a slope and leaps from the cliffs rising about 915 meters (3,000 ft) above the shore. Yikes! What is she doing? The wing fills with air and billows out, and up she goes! The pilot has stretched out flat and is hanging from a cocoon-like harness attached to the wing. To climb up or dive down, she pushes or A hang glider pilot launches from pulls back on a long a cliff-top ramp to sail over the beach far below. metal control bar. To turn left or right, she leans. The edge of the wing tips down, and the glider banks and turns gracefully through the air.
pages.brief: A woman hang glider pilot in a cocoon-like harness hangs beneath a triangular wing. She launches from a cliff-top ramp about 915 meters above the shore, then leans and pushes the metal control bar to bank and turn over the beach far below.

pages.text: Air moving over the top of a wing moves farther and faster than air under the wing. She is hang gliding! And she may sail in the sky for hours if conditions are good—and if she understands a few principles of aerodynamics (air-oh-die-NAM-iks), or, the study of how objects move through the air. The special shape of the wing produces lift as the glider moves through the air. The curved top surface of a wing is a longer distance than the straight underside of a wing. Air moving over the longer, curved top has to move faster than the air moving under the wing. As the air moving over the top of the wing speeds up, the air molecules spread out—which decreases the air pressure. The greater air pressure underneath the wing creates lift and causes the wing to rise.
pages.brief: Close in the sky, a hang glider pilot hangs below a curved wing as air moves over its longer top surface and straight underside. The wing’s shape creates lift, raising the glider and pilot through the open air.

pages.text: How to Hang Glide To take off, the pilot runs down a steep slope to gain speed, create airflow over the wing, and create lift for the glider. He’s off! Hanging from the harness, or a special chair seat, the pilot steers along the winds. He catches and rides one updraft, then another. But this isn’t a place to relax and daydream. The pilot has to pay attention as he turns, circles, climbs, and dives. When the pilot pulls the control bar back, the glider gains speed but loses altitude, or height. (For every 1.22 meters, or about 4 feet, that the forward, it also 30 centimeters, or 1 foot.) When he pushes the control bar forward, the wing edge tips up and the glider The glider’s harness keeps the pilot’s rises, but it loses body straight to cut wind resistance. speed. The natural downward force of Earth’s gravity will pull the hang glider down if it stalls, or stops moving forward. To stay up in the air and keep riding along the wind, the pilot keeps the glider moving forward.
pages.brief: A male hang glider pilot runs down a steep slope, then hangs from his harness and steers along the wind. He catches one updraft after another, pulling and pushing the control bar to climb, dive, turn, and keep moving forward above the landscape.
