pages.text: What It Takes Equipment: Harness, helmet, goggles, parachute, glider, and flotation gear if near water. Clothing: Wear a heavy jacket, jeans, and gloves. It can get very cold at higher altitudes. (Air temperature falls by about 2.2 degrees Celsius, or 4 degrees Fahrenheit, about every 300 meters, or 1,000 feet, up.) Size: Harnesses are designed to fit a person who is 1.5 to 2 meters (5 to 6½ ft) tall and weighs 40 to 113 kilograms (90 to 250 lbs). Skills: The ability to carry an 18-plus kilogram (40 lb) weight on your shoulders while jogging. But balance and endurance are more important than strength or speed. Good reflexes and an ability to make fast decisions are a must. Requirements: Age 16 or older and able to pass a three- to six-month training course. Cost: $5,000 to $6,500 to train and to purchase your hang-gliding equipment.
pages.brief: A hang glider pilot stands ready in a heavy jacket, jeans, gloves, helmet, goggles, and harness, with a parachute, glider, and flotation gear nearby. The equipment is arranged for a high-altitude ride where cold air and fast decisions matter.

pages.text: The Story of Icarus People have been fascinated by the dream of flight for thousands of years. A Greek myth tells of the inventor Daedalus (DEH-duh-lus) and his son, Icarus, who were imprisoned on an island. Their only way out: to fly. Daedalus watched birds. Then he fashioned wings for himself and his son from feathers held together by wax. They escaped! But Icarus ignored his father’s cautious warning and flew too high in the sky. The heat of the sun melted the wax, and Icarus fell to the sea and drowned. Icarus is a good story but not good science. People could never flap their winged arms fast enough to generate sufficient power to overcome the pull of gravity.
pages.brief: On an island prison, the inventor Daedalus and his son Icarus wear wings made of feathers and wax. They escape into the sky, but Icarus flies too high; the sun melts the wax, and he falls toward the sea below.

pages.text: Lilienthal’s first glider Do You Know? In the 1800s, German inventor Otto Lilienthal discovered that a properly engineered wing would help a person stay aloft for hours at a time. The Lilienthal glider from around 1895 is designed like a bird’s wing, with a curved upper surface. The Wright Brothers used information from Lilienthal’s experiments to invent the first airplane. Hang Glider F u n F a c t s: • The longest hang glider ride lasted 36 hours. • Hang gliders typically travel 160 to 320 kilometers (100 to 200 miles). The farthest flight on record is just more than 700 kilometers (435 miles), which was set July 17, 2001, in Zapata, Texas, by Austrian Manfred Ruhmer. • Flight heights can range from as low as 1.5 meters (5 ft) above the ground to more than 4.8 kilometers (3 miles) high!
pages.brief: Otto Lilienthal hangs beneath a bird-shaped glider with a curved upper surface in the 1800s. In the open sky beyond, a modern hang glider soars high over a Texas landscape, echoing Lilienthal’s wing design and long-distance flights.

pages.text: Skydiving A small plane buzzes overhead. At an altitude of 3,048 meters (10,000 ft), the passenger door opens. A person crouching in the doorframe leaps out, arms and legs spread wide. Within 10 seconds, the skydiver is free-falling at 193 kph (120 mph). That’s twice as fast as a car zooming by on a highway. You watch, astonished, as the skydiver sharply drops... and drops... and DROPS for the next 45 seconds. Release the parachute! Release the chute! you think. Finally, at about 762 meters (2,500 ft) above the ground, he pulls the ripcord. Out comes the small drogue chute that A skydiver begins her free fall. pulls out the canopy, or larger chute. It fills with air, and the skydiver is jerked upward. He continues to fall, but now at a leisurely 16 to 20 kph (10–20 mph). For the next 3 minutes, he enjoys the view and the ride before landing on his feet in a clearing.
pages.brief: A skydiver crouches in the open door of a small plane at 3,048 meters, then leaps with arms and legs spread. He free-falls fast for 45 seconds, pulls the ripcord, and the parachute canopy fills with air before he lands on his feet in a clearing.

pages.text: How a Parachute Works Gravity pulls the free-falling skydiver down toward Earth at speeds of 193 kph (120 mph) or more. When the parachute opens, it fills with air and slows the skydiver’s speed. Air trapped in the canopy (the “umbrella” part) presses up against the chute, providing resistance that slows the fall. The skydiver glides to Earth. Buttons Away! What you need: Four-holed button. Four 15-inch-long strands of thread. Scissors. Plastic bag. Tape. What you do: 1. Cut a 20-centimeter (8-in) square from the plastic bag. 2. Tape one end of each strand of thread to a corner of the plastic. 3. Thread each strand through a different hole in the large button. 4. Tie the threads together. 5. Gently hold or pinch the top side of the plastic in its center, and let the button dangle. 6. Drop your homemade parachute from a high spot, such as off the side of a deck. 7. Watch the button glide to the ground.
pages.brief: A homemade parachute made from a plastic square, threads, and a four-holed button dangles from a high spot. The button hangs below the plastic, which fills with air and glides gently to the ground, showing how a parachute canopy slows a fall.

pages.text: A diamond formation Skilled skydivers can free-fall in formations. To decrease their free fall speed, they hold their arms and legs outstretched in the “spread-eagle” position and join hands. Multiple bodies provide more wind resistance, so the divers can float for a longer time. To increase free fall speed, skydivers learn to fall in a standing, or vertical, position. Now that you know how to skydive, what’s next? Experienced skydivers, or sport parachutists, compete in such events as landing accuracy, free fall speed, and freestyle. They put on shows and do stunts in the air, such as passing a baton to each other or creating group formations in the sky.
pages.brief: Several skilled skydivers hold hands in a diamond formation, arms and legs outstretched in the spread-eagle position. Their bodies create wind resistance as they free-fall together, while other divers fall in a vertical position to move faster through the sky.

pages.text: What It Takes Equipment: Jumpsuit, helmet, backpack that holds both. An automatic opens the reserve chute if something goes wrong. Skills: Have enough strength to carry about 16 kilograms (35 lbs) of equipment and control the toggle switches that steer the chute. Be able to deal with the shock of the chute opening, as well as extreme changes in temperature. Size: Harnesses are designed to fit a person who is 1.5 to 2 meters (5 to 6½ ft) tall and weighs 40 to 113 kilograms (90 to 250 lbs). Requirements: Age 16 or older and in good shape. Pass eight training levels, including many jumps with instructors. A student must make 20 solo jumps and pass a written test. Cost: $3,000 to $6,000 for training and equipment.
pages.brief: A skydiver wears a jumpsuit, helmet, and backpack holding a parachute and automatic reserve chute. He grips the toggle switches that steer the canopy, carrying about 16 kilograms of equipment while preparing for the shock of opening and extreme temperature changes.

pages.text: BASE Jumping If skydiving from a plane doesn’t get your pulse racing, how about parachuting from a tall Building, Antenna tower, bridge Span, or cliff high above Earth? Welcome to the sport of BASE jumping. Most BASE jumps are made from around 305 meters (1,000 ft) high, which is considerably less than the height at which skydivers open their parachutes. BASE jumpers have just 20–30 seconds in the air to open their chutes and land in a small safety zone. Crazy? Maybe. But only expert skydivers with a minimum of 200 jumps can attempt such daredevil feats, and many places that could be used for BASE jumping have made it illegal because of the danger. A BASE jumper leaps from a cliff.
pages.brief: A BASE jumper leaps from a tall cliff high above the ground, wearing a parachute and aiming for a small safety zone below. The jumper has only 20 to 30 seconds to open the chute and land.

pages.text: Skydiving F u n F a c t s: • Expert skydivers can land on a tiny target that is about the size of a tennis ball. • The highest and fastest skydive on record occurred in 2012, when BASE jumper Felix Baumgartner jumped from a capsule attached to a high- altitude balloon floating at about 39 kilometers, or 128,000 feet. That’s over 24 miles high! During his free fall descent of 4 minutes and 22 seconds, Felix of over 1,340 kph, or 833 mph. He was the to break the Felix Baumgartner leaps from the an airplane or capsule to begin a record-setting other vehicle! free fall of over 24 miles.
pages.brief: Felix Baumgartner, in a protective suit, leaps from a capsule attached to a high-altitude balloon about 39 kilometers above Earth. He free-falls for 4 minutes and 22 seconds, reaching more than 1,340 kph before opening his parachute.

pages.text: Parasailing A 10-year-old girl standing on shore straps a harness over her life jacket. She adjusts her helmet and gives the driver of the speedboat the “thumbs-up” signal. The motor roars, the boat scoots forward, and the towrope connecting the girl to the boat tightens. She takes a few steps and begins to glide on the water. Is she water-skiing without skis? No, she is parasailing! As the boat zooms into the bay, the colorful parachute dragging behind her fills with air. The girl rises like a human kite, 61 meters (200 ft) into the sky. The boat moving forward provides thrust, the power to take off. The air rushing into the parachute provides lift. As long as the towrope stays tight, the flyer sits back and enjoys the ride —and the admiration of all those watching from the ground. A parasailor soars aloft as he launches from a beachside float.
pages.brief: A 10-year-old girl in a life jacket, harness, and helmet gives a thumbs-up to the speedboat driver. The boat speeds forward, the towrope tightens, and her colorful parachute fills with air, lifting her like a human kite 61 meters above the water.

pages.text: When towing a parasailor, the speedboat cruises between 24 and 48 kph (15–30 mph). It needs to go fast enough to create lift but not so fast that a wave will make it lose control. When turning, or if a strong gust of wind blows from behind, the boat needs to speed up. Slack in the towrope will cause the parasail to fall. Parasailing is not Parasailing high above the water when the wind is blowing stronger than 24 kph (15 mph). The height a flyer reaches depends on the speed of the boat and length of the towrope. On average, recreational parasailors reach the height of a 20-story building; maximum height is 183 meters (600 ft) over oceans and 91 meters (300 ft) over large lakes and bays. Some special- attraction parasail rides can go as high as 305 meters (1,000 ft).
pages.brief: A speedboat tows a parasailor high above the water, keeping the towrope tight. The boat cruises fast enough for lift, speeding up in turns or gusty wind, while the flyer rises to a height that depends on boat speed and towrope length.

pages.text: Unlike hang gliding and skydiving, para- sailing has no minimum age requirement. There is no special training for the parasailor, though the boat driver needs to have experience. There are many ways to parasail. Strap on a harness or sit in a specially designed chair. Ride alone or with a friend. Parasailing is usually done on oceans, lakes, and bays. Flyers take off from the shore from a barge in the water or from a boat equipped with a winch. Rides from parasailing companies typically last around 10 minutes and can cost $50 or more. A basic parasail, plus accessories, can cost $1,000 and up. Delta kite Parasailing History 1918 • Developed during WWI. A German U-boat (submarine) captain wanted to be able to see above the fog when his boat surfaced. 1948 • Dr. Francis Rogallo developed what he called a Delta kite, the basis for the kind of parachute used in parasailing. 1960s • Parascending was invented, an inexpensive way to teach parachuting. A parachuter and towrope were attached to a car driven fast enough to raise the parachuter to 305 meters (1,000 ft) before being set free. 1970s • Parasailing became a recreational activity.
pages.brief: A parasailor rides in a harness above a bay while a boat with a winch tows the colorful parachute. Another flyer could ride alongside, and the scene includes oceans, lakes, or bays where rides launch from shore, a barge, or a boat.

pages.text: Paragliding Paragliding combines elements of three wind sports: parasailing, hang gliding, and parachuting. Paragliders wear a wing-shaped parachute, and some attach a frame harness with a motor that looks like a big fan. They may take off from a tall cliff or snowy mountainside. Often, paragliders compete to see who can cover the greatest distance or make the best time along a specific airborne course. They may take photos of reference points along the way to prove they passed a designated spot. Paragliders can stay in the air for hours at a time and travel great distances.
pages.brief: A paraglider hangs beneath a wing-shaped parachute, launching from a tall cliff or snowy mountainside. Some paragliders use a frame harness with a motor that looks like a big fan, and they stay aloft for hours while traveling great distances.

books.title: The Transcontinental Railroad
books.art_why: The book describes 1860s railroad construction, a historical event best shown in an illustrated drawing.

pages.text: Settlers spent months on the road, and many died. Introduction Before the 1860s, a trip from New York City to San Francisco, California, could take six months. Over the long months of traveling, people had to carry all their food or hunt and gather it from the land. The trails west went through the lands of Indigenous peoples who had already had many negative dealings with outsiders and learned not to trust them. Still, thousands of settlers made the journey to California every year. The West Coast offered rich farmland, wonderful weather, and gold. At the time, the fastest way to travel was by railroad. Railroads crossed the eastern United States as far west as Chicago, Illinois, and Omaha, Nebraska. Building a direct railroad across the United States would allow settlers to get to California much more quickly. It would also allow settlers in the West to reach the East Coast to order goods, send and receive mail, and visit loved ones.
pages.brief: Families trudge along a long western trail carrying food and bundles, while a group of Indigenous people watches warily from a ridge; in the distance lie green farmland and hints of gold country.

pages.text: Immigrants did much of the work for the railroad companies. Pitting the companies against each other made sure that the railroad would be built quickly. Whoever built the most track would get the most money. The railroad work continued even though many workers died from accidents or natural disasters. The Central Pacific started work in January 1863 just outside Sacramento, California.
pages.brief: Outside Sacramento in January 1863, immigrant laborers begin the Central Pacific line, clearing ground and handling rails while company men watch, driven by a race for money and speed despite danger.

pages.text: Who Will Win the Race? The Civil War and financial trouble kept the Union Pacific Railroad from starting construction for two years. The war was taking up all the iron, gunpowder, and workers that the railroad needed for building track. But work got underway soon after the war ended in 1865. By 1866, it looked as if the Union Pacific would easily win the race. Preparing to lay track was a complicated process. First, surveying crews studied the land, putting stakes in the ground to mark exactly where the track would go. Second, a crew of graders went out. They removed any vegetation, filled in any low spots, and dug to make a flat, smooth track. Across the flat land of the plains, the graders often had little to do. Surveyors carefully measure distance and elevation.
pages.brief: On the flat plains, surveying crews measure distance and elevation and drive stakes into the ground while graders clear vegetation, fill low spots, and smooth a path for track; Union Pacific crews advance quickly.

pages.text: Chinese workers lay track in Utah in 1869. Laying the track required several groups of workers. First, a team of workers laid down wooden timbers called ties across the track. Next, other workers dragged the heavy iron rails into place. Then, another group pounded in iron spikes and bolts that held the rails to the ties. Finally, a last group carried in sand and gravel, called ballast, to fill in around the new tracks. Using this system, the Union Pacific Railroad could lay 2 to 3 miles (3–5 km) of track in a single day. Right behind all these crews, the very first train to cross the plains rolled down the new track. The train carried all the wood, rails, iron spikes, tools, and ballast the crews needed. It also carried sleeping cars, a kitchen and food storage, repair shops, and goods, such as clothing. It was like a rolling town that built itself as it went.
pages.brief: Chinese workers in Utah lay wooden ties, drag iron rails, pound spikes, and shovel ballast into place; behind them a supply train rolls along the new track, carrying tools, food, sleeping cars, and goods like a moving town.

pages.text: The citizens of this working town were mostly immigrants from Ireland, Germany, and the Netherlands; Civil War veterans; and formerly enslaved Black people. They built the railroad across the plains with incredible speed, quickly reaching the Rocky Mountains. The Sioux, Arapaho, and Cheyenne tribes were devastated by the railroad. The American bison, also known as buffalo, which the Indigenous people depended on for their existence, could not travel across the tracks. Settlers killed thousands of bison, until they were almost gone. Without bison, the Indigenous peoples of the plains could not survive. Tribes lost many people from the disease, hunger, and conflict that came with the massacre of the bison. Settlers hunted bison nearly to extinction.
pages.brief: A diverse railroad crew of Irish, German, Dutch, Black, and veteran workers lays track across the plains toward the Rocky Mountains; nearby, a herd of bison is blocked by the rails, and Indigenous families face hunger and loss.

pages.text: The railroad also brought a flood of settlers to the plains. The railroad companies sold the land of the Sioux, Arapaho, and Cheyenne to the settlers. They began farming and building their homes there. The trains also brought litter, noise, air pollution, and prairie fires caused by sparks from the wood- or coal-burning engines. Indigenous people raided some trains to try to halt the railroad. As the Union Pacific advanced across the West, Indigenous people fought against the illegal seizing of their land. They stole supplies and livestock, and even killed some workers. The Union Pacific demanded that the army protect the workers and the railroad. Soon, the U.S. government sent soldiers onto the plains, where they engaged in many battles with Indigenous people.
pages.brief: Settlers farm and build homes beside the new track while a train spark ignites a prairie fire; Indigenous warriors raid a train and drive off livestock, and U.S. soldiers arrive on the plains to protect railroad workers.

pages.text: Workers built the railroad through the rugged Sierra Nevada range. Who Will Conquer the Mountains? The work on the Central Pacific was going more slowly. Right away, the company had to cut a track into the steep and snowy Sierra Nevada. Because trains at the time could not climb steep hills or go around sharp corners, the workers somehow had to make the jagged mountains into a smooth, gently rising trail. The workers cut away the solid granite mountainsides and filled in gorges and ravines with rocks and soil, wheelbarrow by wheelbarrow. It was slow, painful work, and very few people wanted to do it. Almost all the white men hired by the Central Pacific Railroad quit within a week.
pages.brief: In the rugged Sierra Nevada, workers cut into solid granite mountainsides and fill gorges with rocks and soil hauled by wheelbarrow, trying to make a smooth, gently rising trail; most white laborers quit within a week.

pages.text: Central Pacific reluctantly hired some Chinese workers to see if they would do better. Chinese workers faced racism and discrimination. Yet, Chinese workers often lasted a long time on the job because of their cleanliness and healthy habits. By 1868, Chinese workers made up most of the Central Pacific’s workforce. To get the railroad over the Sierra Nevada, the Chinese workers had to cut fifteen tunnels through solid rock. They used only hand drills, sledgehammers, and loose gunpowder. Through the winter, a total of forty-four snowstorms buried the mountains. The workers built tunnels, sleeping areas, and workspaces under an average of 18 feet (5.5 m) of snow. All their supplies had to be brought up the side of the mountain by ox wagon or by hand. Chinese workers load ballast to fill in the area beneath a track.
pages.brief: Chinese workers cut tunnels through solid rock with hand drills, sledgehammers, and gunpowder; under deep Sierra snow, they build sleeping areas and workspaces, haul supplies by hand and ox wagon, and load ballast beneath a track.

pages.text: The most famous accomplishment of the Chinese workers was to cut a track into the side of an enormous cliff they called Cape Horn. People who wrote about the project later described workers in woven reed baskets big enough to hold two people. They were lowered in the baskets from the top of the cliff. The workers drilled holes into the sides of the cliff, stuffed the holes with black powder, and lit a fuse. The workers at the top hauled up the baskets as fast as they could, hoping to pull everyone out of the way before the cliff was blown apart. But with these accomplishments came tragedy. Accidents crushed some workers, and the cold weather froze many to death. Avalanches buried entire groups of people alive—some were not found until spring. The Central Pacific Railroad did not keep track of how many Chinese laborers were killed while building the transcontinental railroad. Some accounts estimate around 1,200 died. Finally, in 1867, the track broke the Central Pacific moved onto the deserts of Utah.
pages.brief: At Cape Horn, workers hang in woven reed baskets from a cliff top, drilling holes and lighting fuses before being hauled up; below, avalanches and freezing snow threaten the crews as they push the track onward toward Utah.

pages.text: Where Will They Meet? The Union Pacific had a much easier time crossing the Rocky Mountains than the Central Pacific had crossing the Sierra Nevada. They took a gentle route called the South Pass, and they also moved quickly onto the deserts of Utah. On May 10, 1869, workers, railroad owners, journalists, and politicians gathered at Promontory Point, Utah, for the completion of the transcontinental railroad. The race was over—the Union Pacific had laid 1,086 miles (1,748 km) of track, and the Central Pacific had laid 689 miles (1,109 km), though the Central Pacific got extra money for building through the Sierra Nevada. To celebrate the completion of the first railroad to cross the United States, the heads of the two companies would drive the last four spikes into the track. Special spikes were made of gold and silver. Leland Stanford, the head of the Central Pacific, and Thomas Durant, head of the Union Pacific, each swung a sledgehammer and missed! The crowd cheered anyway. The transcontinental railroad was complete.
pages.brief: At Promontory Point, Utah, on May 10, 1869, workers, owners, journalists, and politicians gather as Leland Stanford and Thomas Durant swing sledgehammers at four special gold and silver spikes; both miss, and the crowd cheers.

pages.text: The Route of the Transcontinental Railroad KEY Central Pacific Railroad Union Pacific Railroad Promontory Wyoming Central Pacific Point Railroad Nebraska Omaha Nevada Union Pacific Railroad Sacramento Utah California Colorado N Conclusion After all the years of labor and danger, California was only a few days’ travel away from New York. Railroads stretched to Salt Lake City, Oregon Territory, and the Southwest. More towns sprang up along the tracks now that goods and mail could travel easily. The railroad companies made millions of dollars from the sale of Indigenous land, while the laborers never got any further payment. Yet, for the first time, a transcontinental railroad connected the country from east to west.
pages.brief: A wide map of the western United States shows the Central Pacific route from Sacramento eastward and the Union Pacific route from Omaha westward, meeting in Utah; along the lines, new towns appear, with California now only days from New York.

books.title: The Amazing Amazon
books.art_why: The Amazon rainforest and its animals exist today, so photographs fit this science and nature book.

pages.text: Chapter 1: There Is a Place There is a place where monkeys swing and howl, jaguars leap from tree to tree, and insects create huge colonies underground. In this place, bananas, pineapples, coconuts, and chocolate grow in abundance. In this place, tiny frogs live in flowers and climb trees, and pink-colored dolphins swim in the river. Storms come often to this place, and the air is sweet. Some sunlight filters through the vines and leaves of the tall trees, but it is mostly dark here on the ground. It is hot, humid, and surprisingly still. Rainwater trickles down through the foliage from leaf to leaf. You hear a slow sound: drip, drip, drip. Your skin is sweaty, an insect lands on your neck, and an ant quietly walks across your sandal. Suddenly a little brown monkey swings to a nearby branch, a bright yellow eyelash viper slithers up a tree, and a bright green Amazon parrot flutters past. Welcome to the Amazon basin, a tropical rainforest. Rainforests Rainforests are located all over the planet. Tropical rainforests are close to the equator, between 23.5° N latitude and 23.5° S latitude.
pages.brief: A dense tropical rainforest rises with tall vines and broad leaves. A brown monkey swings from a branch, a yellow eyelash viper slithers up a trunk, and a green Amazon parrot flutters past. Tiny frogs sit in flowers, pink dolphins swim in the river, and bananas, pineapples, coconuts, and chocolate grow nearby.

pages.text: Tropical rainforests cover a small part (about 6 percent) of Earth’s surface. But more than half (50 percent) of the world’s plant and animal species are found in them—that’s close to thirty million species of plants and animals! Most of the world’s rainforests are in Africa, Southeast Asia, and South America. The Amazon The Amazon rainforest lies in South America. Most of its 5.5 million square kilometers (1.4 billion acres) are in Brazil, but parts of the rainforest are also in Peru, Venezuela, Ecuador, Colombia, Guyana, Bolivia, Suriname, and French Guiana. It is the largest tropical rainforest in the world, with more different types of insects, plants, and animals than any other place on Earth. Scientists discover new species of insects and plants there every year. The Amazon River flows through the heart of this rainforest. Flowing at a rate of up to 7 kilometers per hour (4.3 mph), the water is brown from all the silt it carries. It is like a huge sea of fresh water. It has more than one thousand tributaries. Catfish, piranhas, and dolphins all live in the Amazon River.
pages.brief: A globe view shows tropical rainforests clustered near the equator. A map of South America highlights the huge Amazon rainforest across several countries, with the brown Amazon River flowing through its heart. Catfish, piranhas, and dolphins swim in the river, and dense forest stretches in every direction.

pages.text: This book will take you on a tour of the Amazon rainforest, traveling from the tallest trees to the rainforest floor. Along the way, you will meet an eagle, monkey, jaguar, and ant. You will even hear what these Amazon natives would say—if they could talk. So just how big is the Amazon River? • The Amazon River can be more than 48 kilometers (30 mi) across at its widest point during the rainy season. • It flows almost 6,437 kilometers (4,000 mi) to the Atlantic Ocean. • Within its mouth is an island the size of Switzerland. • It is home to more than forty thousand plant species. • The river’s arapaima fish can grow to be 3 meters (10 ft) long and weigh 180 kilograms (400 lb)! • Its volume is greater than the next eight largest rivers combined! The Amazon is the world’s widest and largest river.
pages.brief: The wide Amazon River stretches across the rainforest during the rainy season, flowing toward the Atlantic Ocean. An island sits within its mouth. A long arapaima fish swims in the brown water. More than forty thousand plant species and many animals live along the river and in the surrounding forest.

pages.text: From the Amazon Yearbook Sloths are slow-moving animals. They seem to just hang out (upside down!) in the trees. Sloths sleep up to twenty hours a day. When they’re awake, they hardly move, which allows algae Sammy to grow on their fur. But, hey, it “Slowpoke” Sloth helps them blend into the forest. Sammy was voted: Most Likely to Survive, but Least Likely to Succeed The tapir is a large, hoofed Tamara the Tapir animal that is related to the horse and the rhinoceros. Tapirs often weigh well over 136 kilograms (300 lb), and they like to swim in the river, bathe in the mud, and they are nocturnal, preferring to look for food when it is dark. Tamara was voted: Best Personality At approximately 1.2 meters (4 ft) long and standing 60 centimeters (2 ft) at the shoulder, the capybara is the world’s largest rodent. Katie Capybara (But Katie doesn’t like to be.
pages.brief: Three rainforest animals appear together. A sloth hangs upside down in a tree, algae growing on its fur. A tapir swims in the river and bathes in mud. A capybara, the world’s largest rodent, stands near the water, its slightly webbed feet visible. The animals look calm and comfortable in their habitat.

pages.text: Katie was voted: Most Likely to Win a Rat Race The poison arrow frog has super-bright colors and designs. This ostentatious patterning warns other animals that its skin is poisonous. Some native Paulo the Poison Arrow Frog people in the Amazon rainforest have used the frog’s poison for centuries when they go hunting. Paulo was voted: Most Dangerous Amphibian Chapter 2: Layers of the Rainforest To better understand the rainforest, scientists have “divided” it into four layers, or sections. You can think of it like a four- Rainforest Layers story building, with the highest trees making up the top floor, called the emergent layer, and the next-highest trees making up the canopy layer. Below them is the understory layer. At the bottom is the rainforest floor. called a big rat.) Capybaras’ slightly webbed feet help them swim.
pages.brief: A brightly colored poison arrow frog clings to a leaf, its bold patterns warning other animals. A capybara stands near the water, showing its slightly webbed feet. In the background, Amazon people are shown using the frog’s poison for hunting. Dark understory foliage surrounds them.

pages.text: High Risers The tallest trees of the rainforest are the emergents. They are like big umbrellas that rise as much as 60.9 meters (200 ft) above the thick forest. Emergents are exposed to sun, wind, rain, and lightning. Big roots support these giant trees. Because rainforest soil is shallow, tree roots often grow above the ground. The kapok tree is deciduous, meaning it sheds its leaves during the dry season, and has tall roots that extend out like wooden walls. These roots are so big that your whole class could hide behind just one of them! Not many animals live in the emergent layer; however, some birds, bats, monkeys, and butterflies do visit to eat leaves and fruit. One huge bird, the harpy eagle, actually lives up there, high above the Amazon. Harpy eagle Spotlight Interview: The Harpy Eagle Interviewer: Hello there, Harpy. Is it true that you are the largest eagle in the Americas? Harpy: I think so. In your people terms, I am about one meter tall, which is more than three feet high.
pages.brief: Giant emergent trees rise like umbrellas above the thick rainforest. A kapok tree shows huge roots spreading above the shallow soil like wooden walls. High in the branches, a harpy eagle perches. Birds, bats, monkeys, and butterflies visit the emergent layer to eat leaves and fruit.

pages.text: Interviewer: It looks as if you have some big wings as well. Harpy: Oh, these things? I was born with these. If I stretch them out like this, they are longer than most people. You see? My wingspan is two meters across—about six and a half feet. Flying fast really helps me find food. Interviewer: What is your favorite food? Harpy: Oh, I like pizza delivered to my door. Just kidding—there’s no pizza here in the rainforest! I hunt sloths, monkeys, and fellow birds. Monkeys are probably the tastiest. Interviewer: Is that what your big talons are for? Harpy: Yep. Since they are thirteen centimeters long—that’s about five inches—these meat hooks can scoop unsuspecting animals right off tree branches. Interviewer: Do you ever fear revenge, like a monkey uprising? Harpy: No, I’m the top bird around here. I build my stick nests 27 to 43 meters, or about 90 to 140 feet, up in the tallest trees. I choose trees with widely spaced branches so I have a clear flight path in and out of my nest. That way I can see what’s around. Monkeys don’t normally go up that high. Hey, there’s a monkey now! I’ll see you later!
pages.brief: A harpy eagle perches high in a tall tree, its huge wings stretched wide to show a two-meter span. Long talons grip the branch. Its stick nest sits among widely spaced branches, giving a clear flight path. The eagle looks toward a monkey in the distance.

pages.text: Crazy Canopy The rainforest’s real action is in the canopy layer. This primary layer is where most of the rainforest plants and animals live. It is like a thick roof woven out of tree branches, plants, and vines that covers the two remaining layers. About 80 percent of the sunlight in the rainforest is absorbed by the trees in this layer, so very little gets to the lower layers. Many trees in the canopy are covered with climbing vines and epiphytes. Epiphytes are plants that grow on top of other plants and receive most of their moisture and nutrients from the air. Most of the rainforest’s flowers, fruit, and seeds are found in this layer. With so much good canopy food, it makes sense that animals hang out here. Many animals rarely come down to the ground, preferring to eat, sleep, hunt, and give birth high up in the trees. Many of them fly, jump, glide, and hop to get from tree to tree. Sloths, toucans, and parrots are just some of the canopy’s residents, but the hardest ones to ignore are probably the howler monkeys. Their name befits their behavior, as these monkeys (the largest of the New World monkeys) howl and scream to keep other animals out of their territories.
pages.brief: The canopy forms a thick roof of branches, vines, and epiphytes. Sunlight filters through, but most is absorbed before reaching lower layers. Bright flowers, fruit, and seeds hang among the leaves. Sloths, toucans, parrots, and howler monkeys live, eat, sleep, and give birth high above the ground.

pages.text: Spotlight Interview: The Howler Monkey Interviewer: Wow, that was one loud and distinctive howl! Excuse me, but could you please stop screaming for one moment? I would like to ask you a few questions! Howler: Okay, but hurry up. If I don’t scream like this regularly, other monkeys may come into our territory to claim our food. Interviewer: Do you always stay up here in the canopy? Howler: This is our home, my man. On the ground, there are some really big animals—it’s Howler monkey.
pages.brief: A howler monkey sits high in the canopy, mouth open in a loud scream. Its long tail wraps around a branch. Far below lies the dark jungle floor. The RAZ interviewer listens nearby, asking questions while the monkey defends its territory and food.

pages.text: Interviewer: Does your long tail help you? It looks prehensile. Howler: Yeah, if by prehensile you mean “grab onto.” My tail helps me climb, but my hands and feet are very useful for climbing, too. Interviewer: You sure use big words for a monkey. Hey, stop the howling! If you can be heard from five kilometers, or three miles, away, just think how loud it is for me. What makes you so loud anyway? Howler: I have a special bone in my windpipe. My throat is like a hollow sound box. See the big swelling under my chin? Here, touch it. Interviewer: Oww! That’s not funny—you have sharp teeth! Okay, Mr. Monkey, you can go back to howling now. The Darker Story The understory is the third level of the rainforest; it is below the canopy and above the ground. The ferns, plants, and young trees that grow in this layer rarely reach much more than 3.6 meters (12 ft) in height. It is dark in the understory because very little light shines through the thick canopy. Understory a jungle down there. When it comes to safety, we don’t monkey around. We’re herbivores, so up here we can eat fruit, leaves, and flowers, and we can live in safety.
pages.brief: A howler monkey hangs by its strong prehensile tail, hands and feet gripping a branch. It points to the large swelling under its chin. Its mouth opens, showing sharp teeth. The interviewer reaches toward the throat, then pulls back in surprise. The monkey prepares to howl again.

pages.text: The flowers these plants produce are brightly colored and emit strong scents to attract pollinators such as birds and insects. The understory is not nearly as busy as the canopy, but many animals do live here. About 220 species of poison arrow frogs hide in the foliage. Venomous and nonvenomous snakes wrap around trees like vines. Birds peck and pull insects from the wood. Large cats such as cougars and jaguars leap between branches. Spotlight Interview: The Jaguar Interviewer: Hey, put me down! And don’t bite. Bad cat, bad big cat! Jaguar: Sorry, I thought you were a monkey. Lucky for you that you’re not as tasty. Hey, what do you think you’re doing here anyway? Interviewer: I came to interview you, the Jaguar plants grow leaves that are big and wide in order to have a better chance of catching some rays.
pages.brief: In the dark understory, broad leaves and bright flowers catch scattered light. A jaguar leaps between branches and seizes the interviewer. Snakes coil around trunks like vines, poison arrow frogs hide in foliage, and birds peck insects from wood. Cougars and jaguars move through the shadows.

pages.text: Jaguar: That’s what they say. I weigh 136 kilograms (300 lb), too. Not many animals mess with me. By the way, you can just call me Jag. Interviewer: Okay, Jag, what do you do for exercise? Jag: I get bored with just one sport. That’s why I cross-train: I run, swim, climb, fish, and hunt. Interviewer: What do you hunt? Jag: Lots of things. My spots, called rosettes, camouflage me so my prey won’t see me coming until it’s too late. Sometimes I climb up in the canopy to eat sloths and monkeys. On the ground, I hunt peccaries, tapirs, and yummy capybaras. On lazy days, I lie near the river and catch fish with my claws. When I’m really hungry or want a challenge, I kill anacondas and caimans. Let’s face it, I’m one big carnivore. Interviewer: Wow, I don’t want to be in your powerful jaws ever again! If you’ll excuse me, I need to go now. Chapter 3: Keeping It Clean If you walked around the rainforest floor, you might be surprised. It is not just one thick jungle. Sure, you would see roots, ferns, herbs, and baby biggest cat in the Americas. Mr. Jaguar, are you really 2.6 meters (8.5 ft) long?
pages.brief: A muscular jaguar stands in the understory, its rosette spots blending with shadows. It shows its long body and powerful jaws. Nearby, it runs, swims, climbs, and fishes by the river. The interviewer keeps a safe distance, ready to leave before becoming a meal.

pages.text: Earthworms, termites, fungi, and bacteria eat up the fallen fruit, leaves, and branches, recycling it back into nutritious soil. Plants decay quickly on the rainforest floor. When a big tree falls, the insects quickly munch it down into small pieces. A leaf that falls from a tree decomposes in a mere six weeks in the rainforest, whereas in other ecosystems it could take up to a year. Also on the ground are big animals such as giant anteaters, deer, tapirs, peccaries, and capybaras, but they are far outnumbered by the smaller spiders, beetles, and ants. Ant highways crisscross the rainforest floor. One kind of ant, the famous leaf-cutter ant, even parades around with leaves and flower petals in its mouth, creating trails that stretch more than 30 meters (98 ft) across. Trivia Question In the Amazon rainforest, are there more mammals, birds, insects, or reptiles? kinds of butterflies. And just think of all the ants!) of mosquito alone. There are well over one thousand different Answer: Insects! (There are more than two hundred types trees, assuming you could see in the almost complete darkness. But most of the green would be high above you.
pages.brief: On the rainforest floor, fallen leaves, fruit, and branches decay quickly. Earthworms, termites, fungi, and bacteria recycle them into rich soil. Giant anteaters, deer, tapirs, peccaries, and capybaras stand among smaller spiders, beetles, and ants. Leaf-cutter ants parade with leaves and petals along long trails.

pages.text: Spotlight Interview: The Leaf-Cutter Ant Interviewer: Hey down there! Yeah, you—the one carrying the big leaf over your head! I’d like to ask you a few questions. Do you have a moment? Ms. Ant: Sure, but I do need to hurry back to the fungus garden. We’re low on food. Interviewer: Did you really just climb up a tree and cut off that leaf? Ms. Ant: That’s correct. And now I’m carrying it back to our underground colony, where smaller ants will chew it up into little spongy bits. Interviewer: So you don’t eat the actual leaf? Leaf-cutter ants.
pages.brief: A leaf-cutter ant carries a big leaf over its head, climbing down from a tree. It follows a trail back toward the underground colony. Smaller ants will chew the leaf into spongy bits for fungus. The interviewer kneels down to ask questions, careful not to step on the busy ant trail.

pages.text: Ms. Ant: No, even though we are herbivores, we use the leaves as a substrate for the cultivation of a special type of fungus. Then we eat the fungus. Want to try some? Interviewer: No, thank you—I, uh, just had lunch. So tell me, what is it like underground? Ms. Ant: We have deep nests with hundreds of chambers. We have a stratified society, meaning different ants perform different jobs in different places within the colony. In the middle rooms, smaller ants tend to our fungus gardens, and our only queen is in a different room laying up to thirty thousand eggs in one day. That’s why there are almost five million of us here! Now if you’ll excuse me, I need to sniff my way home. And please watch your feet—if you step on our trail, it might alter the scent and I might get lost! Bromeliads are cone- shaped plants that grow on trees. Their cones catch a lot of rainwater and form little swimming pools high above the ground. Tiny frogs, salamanders, and crabs live in these pools. Mosquitoes and dragonflies lay eggs in them.
pages.brief: Below ground, leaf-cutter ants tend fungus gardens in many chambers. Smaller ants work in middle rooms while the queen lays eggs in another. Above, a cone-shaped bromeliad holds rainwater like a tiny pool, with frogs, salamanders, crabs, mosquitoes, and dragonflies living around it.

pages.text: Chapter 4: Who, Me? Yes, you. Do you eat bananas? Do you like chocolate? Have you ridden a bicycle with rubber tires? Well, guess what! Bananas, chocolate, and rubber all grow in the Amazon rainforest. Many more things come from the Amazon, too, such as pain and cancer medicines, woods for furniture, pineapples and other fruits, and fresh air. The Amazon is a rich, living treasure. Insects buzz by that do not even have names yet. Trees grow, fall, and decompose into rich soil. Rainstorms fill up frogs’ swimming pools. And perhaps most importantly, plants of the rainforest take carbon dioxide from the air and replace it with oxygen. Rainforests contribute approximately 24 percent of the oxygen in Earth’s atmosphere. Humans and other animals need oxygen in order to live. The Amazon rainforest is a real place. Even if it is far away from you, the Amazon lives at this very moment. As you read these words, a jaguar slinks through the understory, a leaf-cutter ant marches back to a fungus garden, and the scream of a howler monkey echoes throughout the forest. The Amazon rainforest is home Can you hear it? to many living things.
pages.brief: Bananas, chocolate, and rubber all come from the Amazon. A bicycle with rubber tires stands near pineapples, wood furniture, and medicines. Rainforest plants release oxygen into the air. A jaguar slinks through the understory, a leaf-cutter ant marches home, and a howler monkey’s scream echoes through the trees.

pages.text: Explore More Did you like learning about the Amazon rainforest? Well, there is much more to see. If you do some research, you’re bound to find some very interesting animals! 1. At the Library Tell your librarian that you are interested in books about the Amazon rainforest. 2. On the Web In the address window, type: www.google.com Then type: Amazon rainforest. Click on “Google Search.” Read the colored links. Click on one that looks interesting. When you want to explore other links, click the “back” arrow on the top left. Or try a new search: Amazon River Capybara.
pages.brief: A young reader stands in a library with Amazon rainforest books stacked nearby. A librarian helps. At a computer, the reader searches for Amazon rainforest information. An open book shows the Amazon River and a capybara. The reader looks ready to explore more links and facts.

pages.text: 3. Try This! Where do you live? Do you live in the rainforest? What about in a desert, tundra, or pine forest? Do you live on the coast, up in the mountains, or out on the plains? You must live somewhere, right? If you live in a town or city, sometimes it can be hard to tell what kind of region you live in. But there are clues all around. What kinds of trees and bushes grow nearby? What kinds of birds fly overhead? What is the weather like? Look around and investigate. If you are not sure, ask your teacher, librarian, parent, or friend. Once you figure it out, make a report. Draw a picture like the one on page 9, but make it for your area. What kind of insects, plants, and animals are native to your home? You could find this information by walking around outside. You could also ask other people. Or you could read a book or search the Web. You’ll probably be surprised by the cool things you learn about your neighbors!
pages.brief: A child walks outside a home or school, looking at nearby trees, bushes, birds, and weather. A teacher, librarian, parent, and friend stand nearby to help. On a table, the child draws a picture of local insects, plants, and animals for a report about the home region.

books.title: King George III
books.art_why: A named famous person, so cartoon is appropriate.

pages.text: England, Ireland, and Scotland.
pages.brief: An overview page for a history book about England, Ireland, Scotland, and King George III, with chapter topics arranged from a historic meeting and the making of a king through officials clashing, a royal family, the colonies, America fighting back, illness and revolution, a new king, and a complex portrait.

pages.text: John Adams (left), from the United States, extends an offering to George III (right) of England in 1785. A Historic Meeting John Adams, one of America’s Founding Fathers, traveled to England in 1785 to meet with King George III. Adams stood before the king, who looked at Adams skeptically. The United States had declared its independence from Great Britain just nine years earlier, and relations between the two nations were rocky. Adams humbly offered the United States’ hand in friendship. He spoke of honor and affection between the two nations and expressed good wishes for the king’s health and happiness. The king smiled, replying that he accepted Adams’s offer, and the brief meeting ended. Great Britain, the country King George III ruled and loved, had suffered due to the loss of the American colonies. He was determined, and vowed to lead his nation to greatness again.
pages.brief: In 1785, John Adams of the United States stands before King George III of England in a formal meeting. Adams extends an offering of friendship, while the king looks at him skeptically. The king smiles and accepts Adams’s offer, and the brief meeting ends.

pages.text: North American British Territories in 1763 This map shows Great Britain’s territory in North America before the French and Indian War (purple) and the areas they gained after the war (red). In the mid-1700s, Great Britain was a powerful ruler in different places around the world. Its colonies in India and North America provided markets where British merchants sold goods. The British monarchy led the way for the nation. However, the British Parliament often clashed with the king. In 1760, George II died, and at the age of just twenty-two, George became King George III. At that time, Great Britain was in the middle of fighting for control of land in the Seven Years’ War against France and other countries in Europe. Battles also took place in North America, where the war was called the French and Indian War. When Great Britain won the war, it gained many French territories and grew larger than ever before.
pages.brief: A map of North American British territories in 1763 shows Great Britain’s land before the French and Indian War and the areas gained after it. At the same time, in the mid-1700s, Great Britain’s colonies in India and North America provide markets, and the young King George III takes the throne after George II dies.

pages.text: Two Officials Clash The victories in the Seven Years’ War thrilled King George III, but the British public did not give him much credit. Instead, William Pitt, war minister to King George, earned the praise. William Pitt was an enemy of Lord Bute, the king’s mentor. Pitt and Bute argued at the end of the war. Pitt wanted to expand the war into Spain, but Bute and the king did not. The conflict became so heated that Pitt resigned his post in the king’s ministry. The king appointed Bute prime minister, the leading position in the king’s ministry. Bute formally ended the Seven Years’ War with a treaty signed in 1763. He resigned shortly after that. William Pitt was the driving force behind Britain’s victory. Even so, Lord Bute opposed him and urged George III to do the same.
pages.brief: William Pitt, war minister to King George III, argues with Lord Bute, the king’s mentor. Pitt wants to expand the Seven Years’ War into Spain, but Bute and the king disagree. The conflict becomes heated, Pitt resigns, and the king appoints Bute prime minister. Bute ends the war with a treaty in 1763.

pages.text: King George selected Sophia Charlotte as his wife without having met her. She arrived in England, met the king, and married him the next day. A Royal Family George III may have lost his closest political advisor, but he had gained a partner for life. In 1761, the king married a German princess named Sophia Charlotte. Their long, successful marriage lasted more than fifty years, and they had fifteen children together. Happy at home, George was determined to be a great leader. He worked hard to learn more about the British Parliament and how it could be improved. The king remained keenly aware of global affairs as well. A Simple Man Despite his royal rank, King George enjoyed the simpler things in life. He loved agriculture and spent many days inspecting his kingdom’s farms. His favorite activities included horseback riding, music, attending the theater, and playing cards.
pages.brief: King George III chooses Sophia Charlotte as his wife without meeting her. She arrives in England, meets the king, and marries him the next day. Their marriage lasts more than fifty years and they have fifteen children. Despite his royal rank, George enjoys farming, horseback riding, music, the theater, and playing cards.

pages.text: The Colonies The greatest challenge King George III faced was the American Revolution. The war began with a series of parliamentary acts that outraged the American colonists. Great Britain levied taxes on goods the colonists used: the Sugar Act taxed molasses; the Stamp Act taxed all printed paper; and the Townshend Acts taxed paint, glass, and tea. The colonists opposed the taxes and issued boycotts of British goods. Then, on the night of December 16, 1773, a group of colonists dressed as Native Americans boarded a British ship docked in Boston Harbor. The ship carried crates of tea, and the colonists dumped the crates into the water. King George responded to the Boston Tea Party with a challenge: “The colonies must either triumph or submit.” The Boston Tea Party rallied the colonists who felt oppressed by British taxes.
pages.brief: American colonists oppose British taxes on molasses, printed paper, paint, glass, and tea. They boycott British goods. On December 16, 1773, colonists dressed as Native Americans board a British ship in Boston Harbor and dump crates of tea into the water. King George III responds with a challenge to the colonies.

pages.text: America Fights Back The American Revolution began in 1775, when soldiers fired shots at the Battles of Lexington and Concord in Massachusetts. King George realized he needed more troops to lead Great Britain to victory, so he hired the services of about thirty thousand German soldiers, called Hessians. Teamed with the Hessians, the king’s army defeated the colonists in some early battles. However, when General George Washington led a surprise attack in late 1776, the British were pushed back. In 1778, a decisive event occurred: the French joined the American side. Supported by their allies, the Americans won the war in 1781. King George, sensing he might be blamed for the defeat, claimed, “I am innocent of the evils that have occurred.” Upon declaring independence from Britain in 1776, some colonists tore down a statue of King George in New York City.
pages.brief: The American Revolution begins in 1775 with shots at Lexington and Concord. King George III hires about thirty thousand German soldiers called Hessians. George Washington’s surprise attack pushes the British back, and the French join the Americans in 1778. The Americans win in 1781, and some colonists tear down a statue of King George in New York City.

pages.text: At times, King George III’s illness resulted in violent outbursts, and he was restrained. Illness and Revolution In the late 1780s, after the loss of the colonies, people around King George III began to notice his failing health. He seemed nervous. He said strange things and talked to imaginary people. He could be violent, too, shouting and pushing people. These were just the emotional symptoms —he weakened physically as well. Deeply alarmed, the king’s family and ministers asked doctors to help. They conducted treatments common during that era. They had the king drink medicine, and they opened his veins and bled him. They also began a course of strict discipline, punishing the king harshly if he acted strangely. This treatment appeared to help, and soon the king began working again.
pages.brief: In the late 1780s, King George III’s health fails. He seems nervous, says strange things, talks to imaginary people, shouts, pushes people, and weakens physically. Doctors make him drink medicine, bleed him by opening his veins, and punish him harshly for strange behavior. The treatment appears to help, and the king begins working again.

pages.text: The political Rival Gardeners” both George III had their own to attend to. A revolution in Ireland also commanded the king’s attention around that time. The conflict centered on religion. Ireland was a Catholic nation, and Great Britain’s Parliament had passed laws limiting the rights of Catholics living there. After the British army stifled a rebellion, Great Britain’s Parliament merged with Ireland’s in 1800, creating the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland. The king’s challenges were not over, though, and the early 1800s saw Great Britain at war with France once again. After the French Revolution of 1789, a young general named Napoleon Bonaparte rose to power in France. Napoleon wanted to conquer lands in Europe, including Great Britain. England had to defend itself. The Napoleonic Wars ended in 1815 with Great Britain and its allies again defeating Britain’s old rival.
pages.brief: A revolution in Ireland commands King George III’s attention, with conflict centered on religion. Ireland is Catholic, and Parliament has limited Catholic rights. After the British army stifles a rebellion, Parliament merges with Ireland’s in 1800 to create the United Kingdom. In the early 1800s, Great Britain is again at war with France, and Napoleon Bonaparte rises to power.

pages.text: A New King George In 1809, Great Britain celebrated George III’s fiftieth year on the throne. Despite his reign’s rough beginnings, the king had reached new heights of popularity, and most subjects believed that George III had led his country well for half a century. Thousands of his subjects cheered him. The following year, the king suffered a terrible tragedy. His youngest daughter died suddenly of tuberculosis at the age of twenty-seven. The king was shocked and heartbroken. Soon the symptoms of his earlier illness returned. He went into a steep physical and mental decline. In 1811, it became clear that the king could no longer perform his duties. The British Parliament named his eldest son, George, as regent, or temporary ruler. When George III finally passed away in January 1820, young George ascended to the throne just as his father had done decades earlier. George IV served as king from 1820 to 1830.
pages.brief: In 1809, Great Britain celebrates King George III’s fiftieth year on the throne, and thousands of subjects cheer him. The following year, his youngest daughter dies suddenly of tuberculosis at twenty-seven, and the heartbroken king’s illness returns. In 1811, Parliament names his eldest son, George, as regent. When George III dies in January 1820, George IV ascends the throne.

pages.text: A Complex Portrait King George’s legacy offers a picture of a complicated yet strong leader. Some people think of George III as the king who let the American colonies win their independence. Others think of him as the ruler who went insane. Many historians, however, have begun to rethink their opinions of him. Some historians believe symptoms of his mental illness are linked to physical disease. As a leader, George III always put his country first. He rallied and led his nation to victories in the Seven Years’ War and the Napoleonic Wars. He also fought hard to keep the British colonies in America. The king’s personal life has also been given more history has shown that George was a hard worker, a loyal husband, and a loving father. King George reigned for sixty years—longer than any monarch before him.
pages.brief: King George III’s legacy is complicated. Some remember him as the king who let the American colonies win independence, while others remember his mental illness. Many historians now link his symptoms to physical disease. They see a leader who put his country first, led victories in two wars, and was a hard worker, loyal husband, and loving father.

pages.text: The Life of George III 1738: George is born on June 4 1751: Frederick, Prince of Wales and George’s father, dies 1756: Seven Years’ War begins 1760: King George II, 1763: Seven Years’ George’s grandfather, dies, War ends and George becomes king 1775: First shots of the American Revolution 1781: The British surrender to the American colonists 1788: George III shows signs of a serious mental illness; resumes duties a year later, appearing to be cured 1798: Britain stops the Irish Rebellion 1809: The king celebrates fifty years on the throne 1815: The British 1820: Thousands attend George III’s funeral.
pages.brief: A timeline of George III’s life marks his birth in 1738, his father’s death in 1751, the Seven Years’ War, his becoming king in 1760, the first shots of the American Revolution in 1775, British surrender in 1781, signs of mental illness in 1788, fifty years on the throne in 1809, and his funeral in 1820.

books.title: Hungry Right Here?
books.art_why: The book covers present-day American hunger, food assistance, and real people; photographs are possible.

pages.text: Electronic Benefit Transfer (EBT) cards given out by states look like credit cards and have replaced food stamps.
pages.brief: Several EBT cards, shaped like credit cards, lie on a table near a stack of old food stamps. A state worker hands one card to an adult at a service desk, while another adult waits in line.

pages.text: The Invisible Epidemic It’s the last day of school! Everyone is excited about the long summer break—everyone except a boy named Aaron. His stomach rumbles. The only food he’s had today is the school lunch, and he knows the cupboards at home are empty. His mom works two jobs, but by the end of the month they always run out of money for food. He sighs, thinking of the long summer ahead.
pages.brief: On the last day of school before summer break, excited children stream past a boy named Aaron. Aaron sits apart with one hand on his rumbling stomach, thinking of empty cupboards at home and his mother working two jobs.

pages.text: Why People Can’t Afford Food When families don’t have enough money, they often have to make tough choices. Sometimes that choice is to either pay the bills or eat. Millions of Americans work full time and sometimes still go hungry—women in particular. USDA numbers show that more than 60 percent of adults receiving food assistance are women. According to the U.S. Census, more than 80 percent of single parents caring for children are women. These women are twice as likely to live in poverty as single men caring for children. When mothers are living in poverty, their children often are, too. A mother uses government assistance to buy fresh food.
pages.brief: A mother in a grocery store uses a government assistance card to buy fresh produce while her children wait beside the cart. At a kitchen table, another single mother looks at bills beside an empty plate.

pages.text: During the Great Depression, the government gave out surplus food to help feed hungry Americans. How Food Assistance Works Federal food assistance began in 1933 as a way for the government to help farmers. The USDA bought farmers’ extra crops and gave them to those in need. In 1939, the government began giving actual stamps that people used to buy that extra food. By 1964, the program allowed people to buy any type of food, not just extra from farmers. In 2008, the Food Stamp Program was renamed the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) to reflect the program’s new focus on nutrition.
pages.brief: During the Great Depression, a government worker gives surplus food to a line of hungry Americans. Nearby, farmers load extra crops onto a truck for the USDA, and a family uses paper stamps to buy food at a store.

pages.text: Who Receives SNAP Benefits? 23% elderly people or 44% 33% In 2018, nearly two-thirds of SNAP recipients were children, elderly people, or people with disabilities. In 2019, SNAP helped more than thirty-five million Americans. The average monthly food stamp benefit is less than $5 a day. Another federal program helps pregnant women and children under the age of five. It provides specific nutritious foods such as milk, baby formula, and baby food. For more than thirty million children, the National School Lunch Program (NSLP) also provides free or reduced-cost lunches at public schools, regardless of income.
pages.brief: A grandmother, a child, and a person using a wheelchair stand together at a food assistance office. A pregnant woman receives milk and baby formula, while children line up for free or reduced-cost school lunch.

pages.text: The Politics of Hunger The government offers a safety net to many hungry Americans. Yet the amount of money budgeted for federal food programs varies from year to year. Who draws up the budget? Congress, our national lawmakers in Washington, D.C. In some years, Congress cuts billions in spending for SNAP; in other years, it increases spending for school lunch programs. People disagree about how much the federal government should spend on these food programs. They disagree about who the government should help feed and how the government should determine who gets that help. Because of other rising costs, such as childcare, housing, and education, many families today struggle to pay their bills. To help with that struggle, some people think more Americans should receive food assistance. A five-year-old holds a sign to help protest a 2013 House farm bill. The bill would have cut SNAP by $20.5 billion. Actual cuts in November 2013 affected more than Americans.
pages.brief: In Washington, D.C., members of Congress debate a federal budget around a table. Outside, a five-year-old child stands with adults at a 2013 farm bill protest, while a family looks at bills for childcare, housing, and education.

pages.text: Filling the Gap When government funding is not enough to meet the needs of hungry Americans, local food programs help fill the gap. Food banks in every state collect food from growers, restaurants, and grocery stores. They give the food to charities, such as food pantries or soup kitchens, that serve the public. Food banks often provide canned or boxed foods because storing fresh fruits and vegetables is difficult. For people with lower incomes, the need for these fresh foods can sometimes be filled by community gardens. Here, people plant, care for, and harvest food to use at home or share with the community. Many community gardens grow vegetables for their local food banks. Food Deserts High-poverty areas are often “food deserts”—places not served by large grocery stores. Some are in inner cities where stores have closed. Others are in rural areas with small populations. People in these areas often can’t afford to travel ten or fifteen miles to buy groceries, so they buy basic food at small, local stores. Prices are generally higher, and small stores often don’t carry nutritious foods like quality meat or fresh produce. Food deserts can make life particularly difficult for communities of underrepresented people that lack access to supermarket chain stores.
pages.brief: Volunteers sort canned and boxed foods at a food bank, then hand bags to people at a food pantry. Nearby, a community garden grows vegetables. In a food desert, a small corner store stands in an inner-city neighborhood far from a large grocery store.

pages.text: A mother and her children plant tomatoes in a middle-school garden in Colorado. They plan to donate their produce to a local food bank. Feeding America, the largest organization helping American families, has more than two hundred food banks and sixty thousand food pantries that feed about twelve million kids each year. However, charities provide less than 6 percent of the food assistance in the United States. As costs rise, wages stay the same, and federal food programs are cut, these organizations are finding that they cannot meet the needs of hungry people. They often run out of food and have to turn families away. Do You Know? The nonprofit organization AmpleHarvest.org connects more than 7,500 food charities with gardens that want to donate produce.
pages.brief: A mother and her children plant tomato seedlings in a middle-school garden in Colorado. They plan to donate the garden’s produce to a local food bank, where volunteers fill bags for families and a line of people waits at a pantry.

pages.text: Kids Can Make a Difference Many kids help fight hunger in America. Students in New Hampshire held a “hunger banquet” for their parents. The “cost” to attend the banquet was canned food for the food pantry. A sixth-grade class in Massachusetts made an award-winning video about hunger to educate people in their community. Other students have raised money for food banks through bake sales, art sales, car washes, walk-a-thons, and read-a-thons. Sam Adamo played his cello at a local farmer’s market and collected $700 for his local food bank in Rhode Island. Carson Pazdan created a cookbook for and by kids. The cookbook sales raised more than $20,000 for the Northern Illinois Food Bank. Macy Stewart collected 844 pounds (383 kg) of food by handing out bags in her school and asking classmates to fill them for St. Mary’s Food Bank in Surprise, Arizona. When seven-year-old William Winslow realized that kids in his part of North Carolina would not have food over spring break, he asked a local grocery store to let him stand outside and talk to people. He told them about BackPack Buddies, a program that sends meals home on weekends for students in need.
pages.brief: Students in New Hampshire host a hunger banquet for parents, a sixth-grade class in Massachusetts films a video about hunger, Sam Adamo plays cello at a Rhode Island farmer’s market, Carson Pazdan sells a kid-made cookbook, and Macy Stewart hands out food bags at school.

pages.text: William collected 8,100 pounds (3,674 kg) of food for BackPack Buddies in 2016. In only one weekend, William collected 1,400 pounds (635 kg) of food and $305 in cash donations. Now in fourth grade, he still holds a fundraiser each year. In 2016, he organized 171 volunteers to collect donations at ten grocery stores. Donations provided eleven thousand meals to children in his area. In 2017, he hopes to expand throughout the state of North Carolina. William says, “I’m just an involved, regular kid. Any kid can make a difference if they want to. It’s just whether they want to or not.” Higher Wages, Less Hunger Raising the minimum wage is one way to fight hunger. Several states have raised their minimum wage to $10 to $15 per hour, which lowered their hunger rates.
pages.brief: William Winslow, now a fourth grader, stands outside a grocery store with volunteers collecting food donations for BackPack Buddies. Crates of food and cash donations pile up, and a minimum-wage worker counts higher pay at a register.

pages.text: Map the Meal Gap Food Insecurity Rates Use this map to compare rates of hunger within your state. Next, compare your state and region with others. Where is the percentage of food insecurity highest? Lowest? How Can People Help? People with a family garden can donate extra vegetables to a local food pantry—or plant an extra patch to donate! Kids can also donate part of their allowance and encourage others to do the same. Kids in Virginia came up with a plan to allow kids to donate a dime to the food bank each time they bought lunch. Create a plan at your school to support food banks.
pages.brief: A map of the United States shows regions shaded by food insecurity rates. Below it, a family garden yields extra vegetables for a food pantry, and children in Virginia drop a dime into a collection each time they buy school lunch.

pages.text: Volunteers prepare meals at the Central Kitchen in Washington, D.C. Find out what the local food bank and charities need and at what time of year the need is greatest. Share what you find with friends, family, and neighbors. Write letters to Congress and to your state and local governments. Encourage your leaders to support programs that help make sure no child goes hungry. We have what it takes to make sure that children like Aaron never go hungry again. We just need the will to make it happen. Calling for Help If you or someone you know is hungry and needs help, call 1-866-3-HUNGRY or 1-877-8-HAMBRE (for Spanish). The National Hunger Hotline connects callers with emergency food providers, government assistance programs, and various social services.
pages.brief: Volunteers in aprons prepare meals at the Central Kitchen in Washington, D.C. Nearby, a person writes letters to Congress and local leaders, and a family shares information with neighbors. A hotline call connects someone to emergency food providers and government assistance.

books.title: The Balloon Brothers
books.art_why: The book centers on named historical figures, the Montgolfier brothers, so a cartoon treatment fits.
