pages.text: Two Brothers with Big Ideas The Montgolfier brothers were part of a large family from a small town in southern France. Their father, Pierre Montgolfier, was a successful paper manufacturer. His factories were the official suppliers of stationery to the court of King Louis XVI. Joseph and Étienne took over the family business in the 1770s. Their successful business left them plenty of free time to pursue other interests. In his early forties, Joseph became intrigued with the possibility of flight. Since the 1600s, scientists had been exploring the possibility of making a lighter-than-air craft that would fly because of the principle of buoyancy. No one had yet figured out how to build such a vehicle, however. Buoyancy was first understood by the ancient Greek mathematician Archimedes (ark-uh-MEE- deez). It involves the density of an object—its weight for a given volume—compared with that of a fluid around it. ( Fluid in this sense can mean either a liquid or a gas.) If the density of an object is less than that of the fluid surrounding it, the object will experience an upward force. A cork floats because its density is less than that of water. A balloon filled with hot air rises because the.
pages.brief: Joseph and Étienne Montgolfier stand in their family paper business in a small southern French town. Their father, Pierre, a successful paper manufacturer, supplied stationery to King Louis XVI’s court. Joseph, in his early forties, looks thoughtfully upward, thinking about flight and the principle of buoyancy.

pages.text: Joseph suspected that a light gas contained within a lightweight enclosure might make flight possible. He read about such a gas that several past researchers had reported from their experiments. Scientists had known about this mysterious gas for many years. In 1766, English chemist Henry Cavendish identified the gas as an element. He gave it the name “ inflammable air” because it was highly explosive. French chemist Antoine Lavoisier (la-VWAH-zee-ay) renamed it “hydrogen.” Joseph filled small paper spheres with hydrogen and released them, but his experiments were disappointing. The spheres rose just a few meters before coming back down. Hydrogen atoms are so small that they passed right through the paper into the surrounding air. Elements and Atoms Elements are the chemical building blocks of the universe. Every element is made up of atoms. They are the smallest particles of substances that still have the properties of that substance. Oxygen and hydrogen are both elements. One oxygen atom and two hydrogen atoms can combine to form one molecule of water. heated air in the balloon is less dense than the surrounding air. An object with a density greater than the fluid in which it is immersed will sink.
pages.brief: Joseph Montgolfier releases small paper spheres filled with hydrogen. They rise only a few meters before sinking back down. He looks disappointed. Nearby, a cutaway view shows tiny hydrogen atoms passing through the paper into the surrounding air, explaining why the spheres could not stay aloft.

pages.text: Joseph looked for another way to build a flying machine. One day, he noticed that shirts drying over a smoky fire puffed upward. Like most people, he had often seen smoke rising from chimneys. This, he concluded, was the answer: smoke! Joseph-Michel Montgolfier In early 1783, the Montgolfiers began burning different materials to find ones that produced a lot of smoke. They found that a mixture of damp straw and chopped-up wool worked best. It also smelled terrible. But the smoke did indeed give buoyancy to any sort of light container. The brothers concluded that smoke must contain something Jacques-Étienne Montgolfier unknown with a lifting property. They named this marvelous substance “Montgolfier gas.” Of course, there was no such substance. The lifting effect was caused by the hot air itself. When air gets heated, the molecules within it move around faster. This causes the air to expand and become less dense. When contained within a balloon, the lighter air makes the balloon rise.
pages.brief: Joseph watches shirts drying over a smoky fire puff upward. He and Étienne then burn damp straw and chopped wool in a work area, producing thick, terrible-smelling smoke beneath a light container. The smoke makes the container rise, and they believe they have found a marvelous lifting substance.

pages.text: Constructing “Smoke-Powered” Balloons Without understanding the real science behind hot-air balloons, Joseph and Étienne continued to build and test new balloons. The brothers experimented by using different materials for the envelope, including silk, paper, and linen. As their work moved forward, they also made their balloons larger. The balloons rose ever higher into the air. The brothers’ experiments began to attract attention. A crowd filled the town square of a village in southern France on June 4, 1783, for the test of a large balloon made of cloth lined with paper. The crowd watched in amazement as the unoccupied balloon soared some 2,000 meters (6,560 ft.) into the sky. After a ten-minute flight, the balloon landed about 2 kilometers (1.2 mi.) away. Successful test flights such as this one launched a balloon craze in France. From “Ascending Machines” The balloons that got the French people so excited were not called that until after the Montgolfiers made history. Earlier, they were called “ascending machines”—or later, “aerostats.” The name “balloon” was taken from the French word ballon, meaning “a large ball used in games.”
pages.brief: The Montgolfier brothers build and test balloons of silk, paper, and linen, making each one larger. A crowd fills a village square in southern France to watch their large cloth-and-paper balloon, with no passengers, soar high into the sky before landing far away.

pages.text: Jacques Charles A Balloon Rivalry The Montgolfier brothers asked the French Academy of Sciences to officially recognize their work. The academy withheld approval, however. It decided to wait in case someone else invented a better balloon. The Montgolfiers’ chief rival was a physicist named Jacques Charles (ZHOCK SHARL), who proposed building a hydrogen balloon. The Montgolfiers had long since given up on using hydrogen in favor of their hot-air balloons, but Charles saw great possibilities in this approach.
pages.brief: Jacques Charles, a physicist, presents his plan for a hydrogen balloon while the Montgolfier brothers ask the French Academy of Sciences to recognize their hot-air work. The academy members withhold approval, waiting in case a better balloon appears, and a rivalry grows between the two teams.

pages.text: In July 1783, with the academy’s approval, Charles began work on his balloon. He was assisted by two brothers, Nicolas-Louis and Anne-Jean Robert (roh-BEAR), both professional engineers. The three constructed a small test balloon made of silk and coated with rubber to keep the hydrogen from escaping. In the meantime, King Louis invited the Montgolfier brothers to Paris. He wanted them to build a dazzling balloon that would display his glory to all of France. As the court favorites, the brothers now received government funding for their work. The two teams each wanted to be the first to launch a balloon with human passengers. The race was on. A Better Gas for Balloons: Helium Hydrogen is the lightest element—only one-fourteenth the weight of air. At first glance, it seems like the perfect gas for balloons. However, hydrogen is dangerous to work with because it catches fire and explodes easily. A much better gas for balloons is helium, the second-lightest element. Helium does not catch fire or explode. It is therefore completely safe for use in lighter-than-air flight. Helium was not discovered until the 1880s, so it was not available to balloon makers in the 1700s.
pages.brief: Jacques Charles and the Robert brothers, both professional engineers, construct a small silk test balloon coated with rubber to keep hydrogen inside. In Paris, King Louis invites the Montgolfier brothers to build a dazzling balloon for his glory, giving them government funding as the two teams race toward human flight.

pages.text: Soaring into the Blue On August 27, 1783, a large crowd gathered at a grassy area in Paris where the Eiffel Tower now stands. They had come to witness the launch of the Charles balloon. Among the onlookers was a famous American, Benjamin Franklin, who was serving as U.S. ambassador to France. The balloon was relatively small—about 4 meters (13 ft.) in diameter—with alternating red and white stripes. The Scientific Method The Montgolfier brothers and Jacques Charles aimed to answer a question: Is it possible to construct a lighter-than-air device that will enable people to fly? To answer that question, they followed a procedure known as the “scientific method.” The scientific method has several steps: • Ask a question. • Do background research. • Construct a hypothesis. • Test your hypothesis with observations or experiments. • Analyze your data and draw a conclusion. • Communicate your results.
pages.brief: A large crowd gathers on a grassy area in Paris, where the Eiffel Tower now stands, to watch the launch of Jacques Charles’s small balloon, about four meters wide with alternating red and white stripes. Benjamin Franklin, the U.S. ambassador to France, stands among the onlookers.

pages.text: In the late afternoon, the unpiloted balloon was released. It rose quickly and flew northeast for less than an hour, landing about 15 kilometers (9 mi.) away in a small village. Terrified villagers attacked this strange monster from the heavens with their pitchforks. Now it was the Montgolfiers’ turn to wow Paris. On September 19, they launched their test balloon with its animal passengers at Versailles. When the animals landed safely, the time for a human trial was finally at hand. Since the flight would be very dangerous, the king felt it should be done by a pair of prisoners who had been sentenced to death. However, a science teacher and a soldier volunteered. Their historic flight took place on November 21, this time from the outskirts of Paris. The balloon towered 23 meters (75 ft.) high. It was covered with various golden designs in honor of the king and royal family. With the science teacher and the soldier aboard, the balloon rose into the air. Twenty-five minutes later, it landed about 8 kilometers (5 mi.) away, settling between a pair of windmills outside the city. The two men were hailed as heroes.
pages.brief: Terrified villagers with pitchforks attack a fallen balloon in a small village. At Versailles, the Montgolfiers’ animal balloon has landed safely. Later, their tall balloon decorated with golden designs carries a science teacher and a soldier from the outskirts of Paris, landing between two windmills as people hail the two men as heroes.

pages.text: Benjamin Franklin observed the historic flight. Asked by another spectator what this balloon was good for, he reportedly answered, “What good is a newborn baby?” On December 1, just ten days after the Montgolfiers’ triumph, Jacques Charles and Nicolas-Louis Robert made the first human ascent in a hydrogen balloon. Taking off from the Tuileries (TWEE-luh-reez) Garden in Paris, they flew for more than two hours. They came down in a town about 36 kilometers (22 mi.) away. In the following years, the Montgolfiers launched several more balloons. The brothers were honored by the French Academy of Sciences, and their father, Pierre, was made a nobleman by King Louis.
pages.brief: Benjamin Franklin stands among spectators as another man questions what the balloon is good for. Later, Jacques Charles and Nicolas-Louis Robert rise in a hydrogen balloon from the Tuileries Garden in Paris, flying for more than two hours before landing in a distant town. The Montgolfier brothers are honored by the French Academy.

pages.text: The Legacy of Lighter-Than-Air Flight The passion for ballooning soon spread throughout Europe. It was not long, however, before the risks involved became clear. In June 1785, two men were killed while attempting to fly across the English Channel in a balloon. Despite the risks, pioneers continued to develop balloon designs long after the balloon craze of the late 1700s had ended. In the 1800s, lighter-than-air vehicles were given rudders and motorized propellers. By the 1930s, huge airships were flying passengers back and forth across the Atlantic Ocean. The golden age of airships ended abruptly when the German airship Hindenburg caught fire and crashed while landing in New Jersey in 1937. Today, airships are mostly used for advertising. They can often be seen flying above open-air stadiums during large sporting events. Gas balloons are mostly used for gathering weather data, while hot-air balloons are mostly used for recreation. Many areas hold festivals each year in which hundreds of colorful hot-air balloons fill the sky. These events can make it appear as though balloon mania never ended.
pages.brief: At a modern festival, hundreds of colorful hot-air balloons fill the sky. An airship advertises above an open-air stadium, while a gas balloon gathers weather data nearby. A separate scene recalls the Hindenburg, a huge German airship catching fire and crashing while landing in New Jersey in 1937.

pages.text: Canada Where Is It? Canada is the northernmost country in mainland North America and the second-largest country on Earth. Large countries usually have many neighbors, but Canada has only one—the United States. The border between them is about 8,893 kilometers (5,525 mi.) long, making it the longest border in the world between two countries. Canada’s national motto is “From sea to sea” because the country stretches from the Pacific Ocean in the west all the way to the Atlantic Ocean in the east and the Arctic Ocean to the north.
pages.brief: A broad drawn map of northern North America shows Canada stretching from the Pacific to the Atlantic and Arctic Oceans, with the United States along its long southern border. The land is vast and northern, with ocean on three sides, illustrating why the country’s motto speaks of sea to sea.

pages.text: People With one in every five people born in other countries, Canada is diverse. Most Canadians, however, do not think of themselves as a “melting pot,” in which different cultures blend together. Instead, many think of Canada as a “mosaic,” in which immigrants retain their culture and strengthen the nation through diversity. Some of the first European settlers in the land we now call Canada were from France and England. Before Canada became a country, these people settled separate colonies that were often at war with each other. They had different languages and religions, but eventually the groups learned to get along. Because of this, Canada has two official languages: French and English. France and Britain helped build the nation of Canada on the ancestral lands of Indigenous peoples who had been living in the area for thousands of years. Today, less than five percent of Canadians are Indigenous peoples, with most belonging to three groups: First Nations, the Inuit, and the Métis (may-TEE). First Nations people and Métis live throughout the country, and the Inuit continue to live in the far north. Life in Indigenous communities has changed over the years, but many who live in them continue to.
pages.brief: A group portrait of Canadians shows a diverse country of people born in many lands. Early French and English settler families stand in separate colonial communities, while First Nations, Inuit, and Métis people appear across the land. The scene suggests a mosaic in which different cultures keep their identities and strengthen the nation.

pages.text: For example, they teach about their history and learn to languages. Inuit children play at school. Through the years, many immigrants came from Germany and other European countries, as well as China, India, the Americas, and the Middle East. While richly diverse, this vast country is sparsely populated. Probably due to better farmland and access to waterways, most of its population—90 percent, by some estimates—lives within 160 kilometers (100 mi.) of the country’s southern border. Many urban Canadians work in service industries such as tourism, transportation, or banking. Away from the cities, some people work to extract Canada’s many resources such as oil, copper, and gold. Others farm the land or cut timber from the vast forests that blanket the country. Resources and manufactured goods are sold as far away as China, but most are traded across the border with the United States. traditional culture.
pages.brief: Inuit children play at school while people from Germany, China, India, the Americas, and the Middle East arrive as immigrants. Near the southern border, city workers serve in tourism, transportation, and banking, while others extract oil, copper, and gold, farm, or cut timber. Goods travel by trade across the border and overseas.

pages.text: Regions of Canada Land Canada holds majestic mountains, vast plains, lakes, and endless forests. Parts of the north have ice and snow all year. Geographers divide the country into seven landform regions. In the east is the Appalachian region, with rolling forested hills dotted by farms. Waterways define another region, the Great Lakes–St. Lawrence lowlands. It is the smallest region but an important one, known as “Canada’s heartland.” About half of all Canadians live in large cities in this region.
pages.brief: A sweeping drawn landscape shows Canada’s varied land: majestic mountains, plains, lakes, and endless forests, with ice and snow in the far north. In the east, rolling forested Appalachian hills are dotted with farms. Beside the Great Lakes and St. Lawrence River, the small lowland region holds large cities where about half of Canadians live.

pages.text: The forested Canadian Shield is a huge region that wraps around Hudson Bay. Long ago, glaciers scraped the area clean of soil and exposed the rocky surface. When the glaciers melted, thousands of lakes formed. Within this wet Tourists camp, hike, region lies a cold, marshy area and canoe in parks in known as the Hudson Bay lowlands. the Cordillera region. The interior plains are grasslands in the south and forests in the north. Today the grasslands are used for raising livestock and growing grains. In the far west is the Cordillera region with great mountain chains. The highest are the Rocky Mountains, with snow-covered peaks reaching 3,954 meters (13,000 ft.). In between the mountains are fertile valleys where farmers grow fruit and other crops. To the north of all these regions and their forests lies the Arctic tundra, where freezing temperatures prevent any trees from growing. Niagara Falls In the Great Lakes–St. Lawrence lowlands, water plunges down 57 meters (188 ft.) at Niagara Falls. The part of the falls in Canada—Horseshoe Falls—is 670 meters (2,200 ft.) long.
pages.brief: Drawn panorama shows the forested Canadian Shield wrapping Hudson Bay, with rocky lakes and marshy lowlands. Interior plains hold southern grasslands with livestock and grain and northern forests. In the west, the Cordillera’s Rocky Mountains rise snow-covered above fertile fruit valleys, where tourists camp, hike, and canoe. Far north, treeless Arctic tundra stretches, and Niagara Falls plunges in the east.

pages.text: Animals In the Arctic, a land of ice and snow, animals tend to be white in color. Their camouflage helps them survive. Polar bears have black skin, but their fur looks snow white. Harp seal pups are hard to see because they, too, are white. The arctic fox has a white coat in winter but sheds it for a brown one when the snow melts. Beluga whales are white, as are birds such as the tundra swan. In the forests south of the Arctic, moose, beaver, black bears, and wolves all blend in with the colors of the forest floor. The small animals of the grassy plains, such as ground squirrels and pocket gophers, dig underground tunnels to live in and raise their young. The best way to survive in the mountains is to be sure-footed. In the Rocky Mountains, goats and bighorn sheep have hooves that are great for running, jumping, and rock climbing. harp seal pup.
pages.brief: In Arctic ice and snow, polar bears, harp seal pups, beluga whales, tundra swans, and winter-white arctic foxes blend into the white landscape; the fox turns brown when snow melts. South in forests, moose, beaver, black bears, and wolves match the forest floor. Grassland ground squirrels and pocket gophers dig tunnels, while Rocky Mountain goats and bighorn sheep climb sure-footedly.

pages.text: All around Canada are animals that survive the cold winter and lack of food by migrating. Many birds migrate, but so do some fish, whales, turtles, grazing animals, and even dragonflies. Huge herds of grazing caribou move hundreds of miles from one part of Canada to another. Other animals go farther south, leaving Canada for a warmer climate. The champions for long-distance migration are the small but swift arctic terns. They fly from their breeding grounds in the Arctic all the way to Antarctica, a forty-day journey of some 35,500 kilometers (22,060 mi.). Then, six months later, they fly all the way back again. Canadian Wildlife Rocky Mountain Canadians share their huge homeland with countless species of birds, fish, mammals, and plants. The country works to protect the land, air, and water for people as well as the lives there.
pages.brief: Migrating animals cross Canada’s skies, waters, and lands to survive cold and hunger: birds, fish, whales, turtles, dragonflies, and huge caribou herds moving hundreds of miles. Other animals head south for warmth. Tiny arctic terns fly from the Arctic to Antarctica in about forty days, then return six months later. Canadian wildlife shares protected land, air, and water.

pages.text: History For many thousands of years, what is now Canada was home to self-governing First Nations people and the Inuit. The first Europeans to arrive were the Icelandic Vikings who sailed from Greenland more than one thousand years ago. Survival was difficult, and they eventually left. In 1497, British explorer John Cabot arrived in what today is eastern Canada and claimed land for England. Later, French explorers also claimed lands. The French and English found two resources that helped make money back in Europe: codfish and fur. More traders came and colonies developed. The foreign nations formed alliances with the First Nations people and a network to sell beaver pelts. During the 1400s to 1700s, France and England were often at war, as were their colonies. Canadian lands were handed from winner to winner until Great Britain eventually maintained control. As the colonies grew, they displaced First Nations people and took over their lands. The growing colonies began to desire more independence. In 1867, Britain made the colonies a dominion, with its democratic government’s capital in Ottawa. In 1931, Canada became fully independent when it became part of the British Commonwealth of Nations.
pages.brief: Long before Europeans, First Nations and Inuit communities live across the land. Viking sailors arrive from Greenland; John Cabot claims eastern land for England in 1497; French explorers follow. Beaver-pelt traders and growing colonies displace First Nations as conflicts shift control to Britain. In 1867 the colonies become a dominion with Ottawa as capital; in 1931 Canada becomes fully independent.

pages.text: Canada Day Calgary Stampede Quebec Winter Carnival Celebrations Canada Day, the nation’s birthday, is on July 1. People celebrate with parades, barbecues, and fireworks. The largest celebration is held in Ottawa. The Calgary Stampede celebrates Canada’s Old West with bull riding, barrel racing, steer wrestling, bronc riding—even chuck wagon racing. Called “The greatest outdoor show on Earth,” it attracts about a million visitors. Canadians have winter festivals, too, with dogsled races, skiing, and ice-skating. The Quebec Winter Carnival is the largest such festival in the world. There you can enjoy the snow-sculpture contest, visit an ice castle, and even stay in a hotel made of ice and snow that is built every winter and melts away every summer.
pages.brief: Canada Day brings parades, barbecues, and fireworks, with the largest celebration in Ottawa. The Calgary Stampede shows the Old West through bull riding, barrel racing, steer wrestling, bronc riding, and chuck wagon racing. Winter festivals add dogsled races, skiing, and ice-skating. At the Quebec Winter Carnival, people enjoy snow sculptures, an ice castle, and a hotel of ice and snow.

pages.text: Conclusion Canada, one of the largest countries on Earth, includes regions of towering mountains, rolling plains, dense forests, frozen tundra, and endless rocky shores. Each region has its own plants, animals, resources, and people. The people who live there may speak French, English, or one of many other languages, but they are all Canadian and proud of their cultural mosaic. Ice hockey originated in Canada and is the country’s national sport (left). People gather for a public event in Ottawa (top). Children from Nunavik, an Inuit village, go to hockey practice (bottom).
pages.brief: A broad view of Canada shows towering mountains, rolling plains, dense forests, frozen tundra, and endless rocky shores. In each region, local plants, animals, resources, and people live together. French, English, and other languages are heard among proud Canadians. Ice hockey, the national sport born in Canada, appears as people gather in Ottawa and Inuit children from Nunavik attend practice.

pages.text: Introduction The Ebbets Field stands were full on April 15, 1947. Brooklyn Dodger Jackie Robinson picked up his baseball bat. The crowd watched as the only African American in Major League Baseball (MLB) walked to the plate. Insults rang out from the other team’s dugout. The Dodgers’ Branch Rickey, had warned him this would happen. The words hurt, but Robinson had promised not to respond. He would play ball and let his bat do the talking. Many people Robinson waits for the pitch during an took note of the exhibition game at Ebbets Field the day before his MLB debut. great courage Jackie Robinson showed that day. His courage would make him a baseball legend and a champion for equal rights.
pages.brief: At Ebbets Field, Jackie Robinson in a Brooklyn Dodgers uniform holds his baseball bat at the plate. The stands are packed with spectators watching him. Across the field, players in the opposing dugout lean out and shout insults. Robinson stands calm, ready to play.

pages.text: Jackie Robinson attended the University of California at Los Angeles (UCLA). He was a star on the school’s football, track, basketball, and baseball teams. Robinson was the first student in the school’s history to win special awards in four sports in a single year. In spite of this success, Robinson did not graduate from UCLA. The Robinsons had little money. He left school in 1941 to help support his family. In addition to baseball, Robinson ran track and played basketball and football at UCLA—and excelled at all of them.
pages.brief: At UCLA, Jackie Robinson plays football, runs track, and plays basketball and baseball. He wears athletic uniforms for each sport and excels in all of them. In one scene, he receives special awards for four sports in a single year before leaving school in 1941 to help support his family.

pages.text: Taking a Stand Robinson played semiprofessional football after college. Then, in December 1941, the United States entered World War II. Like many young men at the time, Robinson was called up to serve in the U.S. Army. Robinson served at Fort Hood, Texas. One day in 1944, he and a group of soldiers got on an army bus. The bus was segregated —white soldiers sat in the front and black soldiers in the back. Yet Robinson knew he was no less a soldier than the white men. He refused an order to move to the back of the bus. For Robinson poses in his U.S. Army uniform. this, he was arrested. The army wanted to punish Robinson, but many people defended him. He was a good soldier who had only stood up for what was right. In the end, he was found not guilty.
pages.brief: Jackie Robinson in his U.S. Army uniform sits among Black soldiers at the back of a segregated army bus at Fort Hood, Texas. White soldiers sit at the front. Robinson refuses an order to move, is arrested, and later stands before people who defend him until he is found not guilty.

pages.text: You’re Hired! After his time in the army, Robinson worked at a Texas college coaching basketball. In 1945, he received a letter from the Kansas City Monarchs, a professional baseball team. They offered Robinson a contract to play with them for four hundred dollars a month. The Monarchs were part of the Negro Leagues. At that time, baseball was segregated. White and black athletes played in separate leagues. Robinson signed on to play for the Monarchs, thinking it might be a way to someday get into the all-white major leagues. Robinson played shortstop for the Kansas City Monarchs in the mid-1940s.
pages.brief: Jackie Robinson coaches basketball at a Texas college. He holds a letter from the Kansas City Monarchs offering him a contract to play professional baseball for four hundred dollars a month. Later, in a Monarchs uniform, he plays shortstop on a segregated baseball field, hoping to reach the major leagues.

pages.text: Wesley Branch Rickey, pictured here around 1945, wanted to see baseball’s “color barrier” (the rules keeping white and black athletes separate) broken. Robinson showed everyone he was a skilled player. He caught the eye of Branch Rickey, general manager of the Brooklyn Dodgers. Rickey felt that there should not be separate baseball leagues based on race. Instead, as he put it, professional baseball should be “color-blind.” He wanted the Dodgers to sign a player from the Negro Leagues, a first attempt to integrate major league baseball. Rickey knew that this player would not only have to be a great athlete. He would also have to show strong character in the face of abuse. In 1945, Rickey met with Robinson. Rickey offered to hire him on one condition: Robinson could not respond to any prejudice against him because of his race.
pages.brief: Brooklyn Dodgers general manager Branch Rickey, wearing a suit, sits at a desk in 1945 and meets with Jackie Robinson. Rickey leans forward, explaining that baseball should be color-blind and that Robinson must not respond to prejudice. Robinson listens seriously, understanding the difficult condition of his new contract.

pages.text: A Team of Two A Team of Two Robinson shakes Rickey’s hand after signing his 1948 contract. Robinson was at first very surprised. How could this man expect him to not fight back against prejudice? Rickey explained that the best way to fight back would be to play well. Robinson would show just how good he was.
pages.brief: Jackie Robinson and Branch Rickey shake hands after Robinson signs his 1948 contract. Rickey, in a suit, smiles as he explains that playing well is the best way to fight prejudice. Robinson looks surprised but determined, holding the signed contract in a Dodgers setting.

pages.text: Number 42 Takes the Field On October 23, 1945, Jackie Robinson signed on to play for the Dodgers’ minor league team. Spring training for the team was held in Florida. There, Robinson had a taste of what he would face as MLB’s first African American player. He could not stay in the same hotels as the rest of the team. Other minor league teams refused to play because of Robinson. Opposing pitchers threw the ball at him. Even some of his teammates didn’t want to play with him. Punishing Pitches Punishing Pitches The umpire motions Robinson to first base after Robinson is hit in the arm by a pitch during his 1947 season in the major leagues.
pages.brief: At spring training in Florida, Jackie Robinson stands apart from white teammates outside a hotel, holding his equipment. On a baseball field, an opposing pitcher throws the ball at him, hitting his arm. The umpire points Robinson toward first base while some teammates turn away.

pages.text: None of this abuse stopped Robinson. He played well enough to move up to the Dodgers the next year. Wearing number 42, Jackie Robinson took the field on April 15, 1947, before a crowd of more than twenty-six thousand spectators. The Dodgers earned a victory that day, not only over the Boston Braves but also over prejudice against African Americans. Robinson and Dodgers team captain Pee Wee Reese smile after both hit home runs to help win Game 1 of the 1952 World Series. As teammates they became close friends, and Robinson and Reese were they remained so for the rest of their lives. both stars in 1952.
pages.brief: Jackie Robinson, wearing number 42, takes the field at Ebbets Field before more than twenty-six thousand spectators on April 15, 1947. Later, Robinson and Dodgers captain Pee Wee Reese smile together after both hit home runs in Game 1 of the 1952 World Series.

pages.text: Another Great Steal Another Great Steal Yankees catcher Yogi Berra attempts to tag Robinson during the 1955 World Series. Robinson also went on to have a great career. He was chosen Rookie of the Year in 1947. In 1949, he was voted Most Valuable Player in the league. Robinson was a fast runner who led the league in stolen bases. He helped the Dodgers win six league championships and a World Series victory. In 1962, he became the first African American to enter the Baseball Hall of Fame.
pages.brief: During the 1955 World Series, Jackie Robinson slides into a base as Yankees catcher Yogi Berra reaches to tag him. Robinson is a fast runner, stealing another base. Around him, a stadium crowd watches the play, showing his great baseball career and his place in the Hall of Fame.

pages.text: Beyond Baseball After retiring from baseball in 1957, Robinson joined the coffee maker and fast-food chain Chock Full o’ Nuts. In doing so, he became the first black vice president of a U.S. national company. In 1964, he cofounded the Freedom National Bank, which grew to become one of the largest black-owned banks in the United States. Six years later, he launched a construction company. Robinson also became a civil rights leader who continued to work for equality for all people. He died in 1972 from heart problems and diabetes complications. books.title: Rainforests
books.art_why: Rainforests, wildlife, and people exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: Rainforest soils are often shallow. Many tall rainforest trees grow large branching support structures called buttress roots to help them stay upright.
pages.brief: Tall rainforest trees stand in shallow soil, their large branching buttress roots spread wide at the base to keep them upright. The roots and trunks rise in a dense forest, showing how the trees are supported in the rainforest.

pages.text: Scarlet macaws fill the sky with color in Peru. A Place of Wonder Picture a forest so tall that the trees seem to touch the sky. Beneath these giants, a dense weave of leaves and branches shades the layers below. Squawking birds flash brilliant colors as monkeys scramble from branch to branch, filling the air with their howls. Snakes slither silently up tree trunks, hiding in wait for prey. Far below on the dark, damp forest floor, creatures scurry and creep through mushrooms, dead leaves, and fallen fruit. When nighttime arrives, larger animals will come out to hunt. Water is everywhere: it falls from the sky, drips from leaves, pools on the ground, and flows downhill into streams. Even the air is thick with moisture. All of nature celebrates the life-giving power of water and the abundant growth it supports. This is a rainforest—a place of astonishing beauty and wonder.
pages.brief: In a tall Peruvian rainforest, scarlet macaws fly through the sky as monkeys scramble from branch to branch. Below a dense canopy, snakes climb tree trunks and small creatures move among mushrooms, dead leaves, and fallen fruit. Water drips from leaves, pools on the dark forest floor, and flows into a stream.

pages.text: Earth’s Rainforest Regions Tropical rainforests are mainly located in the tropical zones, which are between the Tropic of Cancer and Tropic of Capricorn. These zones are closest to the equator and receive the most direct sunlight. They also receive about the same amount of sunlight throughout the year. South America’s Amazon rainforest is the largest and best-known tropical rainforest. Others are found in Central America and parts of Africa, southern Asia, and Australia. Almost all rainforests are tropical rainforests. Temperate rainforests are mainly located along coasts in cool temperate regions farther from the equator. In North America, temperate rainforests stretch from Alaska to Oregon. They are also found along the coast of Chile, in Norway and the United Kingdom, and in parts of eastern Russia, Japan, Australia, and New Zealand.
pages.brief: A wide view of Earth shows tropical rainforests near the equator between the Tropic of Cancer and Tropic of Capricorn, including the Amazon, Central America, Africa, southern Asia, and Australia. Cooler coastal temperate rainforests appear from Alaska to Oregon, Chile, Norway, the United Kingdom, Russia, Japan, Australia, and New Zealand.

pages.text: Tropical Rainforests Climate and Soil Tropical rainforests are generally warm and humid year-round. As a rule, average temperatures range from about 20° to 30°C (68°–86°F), and humidity is often 80 percent or higher throughout the year. Yearly rainfall is at least 200 centimeters (80 in.) and can reach 1,000 centimeters (400 in.). Rainfall can be very heavy, as much as 5 centimeters (2 in.) in an hour. Most tropical rainforests lack distinct rainy and dry seasons. Soils in tropical rainforests are rarely rich. This is in part because the plants themselves contain so many nutrients that not much is left in the soil. Also, rainforest soil is often waterlogged because rainfall is almost always greater than the rate at which water evaporates. Water flows downhill into rivers and streams, carrying nutrients with it. The Importance of Rainforests During photosynthesis, plants produce oxygen as a waste product. Because the rate of photosynthesis is so high in rainforests, this biome produces most of Earth’s oxygen, which humans and other animals depend on for our survival. Rainforests also absorb carbon dioxide, which keeps this gas from entering Earth’s atmosphere and adding to global warming. These forests provide homes for enormous numbers of life-forms. The list of ways that rainforests benefit the environment goes on and on.
pages.brief: Heavy rain falls in a warm, humid tropical rainforest, where the air is thick with moisture. Waterlogged soil lies beneath dense plants, and runoff flows downhill into a river or stream, carrying nutrients away. The scene shows the wet climate and the often nutrient-poor ground beneath the forest.

pages.text: Tropical rainforests have the highest biodiversity of any biome. Even though they cover only about 7 percent of Earth’s surface, they contain more than half of the planet’s plants and animals. This is a result of several factors. The Lesulas live in Central almost-constant sunlight and Africa. They were unknown to scientists until 2007. warm temperatures support photosynthesis, which produces food for not only plants but also the animals they feed, either directly or indirectly. The availability of water, which all living things require, is another factor. In addition, tropical rainforests offer many and diverse kinds of food and shelter. This biome contains more than two-thirds of all known plant species, and new animal species are discovered every year. Plants Plants in tropical rainforests grow in four layers. The emergent layer contains the tallest trees, which can grow to over 60 meters (200 ft.) in height. Because they rise above the other trees, they receive the most sun, rain, and wind. The heavy exposure to sunlight causes their water to evaporate. These trees have adaptations to survive in dry conditions, including small, waxy leaves.
pages.brief: A Lesula monkey stands in a Central African rainforest, a species unknown to scientists until 2007. Around it, the tallest emergent trees rise above the other trees, their small, waxy leaves exposed to strong sun, rain, and wind. The scene shows the forest’s rich variety of life and plant layers.

pages.text: The canopy, roughly 18–45 meters (60–125 ft.) in height, is where most plants and animals live. Trees and vines grow so densely that they shade the layers below. Most flowers and fruit grow in the canopy. It also contains many epiphytes (EH-puh-fytes), or “air plants,” which live on other plants for support. Epiphytes get nutrients from rain and humidity in the air rather than from soil. In rainforests, they often grow on trees in order to reach sunlight. Tropical Rainforest Layers.
pages.brief: High in the rainforest canopy, dense trees and vines form a shaded layer about 18 to 45 meters above the ground. Flowers and fruit grow there, and epiphytes—air plants—cling to tree branches, reaching sunlight while getting nutrients from rain and humid air rather than soil.

pages.text: The understory receives much less sunlight than higher layers—only about 2 to 15 percent. Plants here have adaptations to survive in shade, including large, wide leaves to capture sunlight for photosynthesis. The understory also contains young trees as well as many climbing plants that seek sunlight. Mosses, algae, and fungi often grow on understory plants as well. The forest floor, or ground level, is dark and humid, receiving only about 2 percent of sunlight. The almost complete lack of sunlight prevents most plants from growing in this layer. It contains decomposing leaves and fallen trees, fruit, and branches. Decomposition supports rainforest food chains in important ways. Mosses, ferns, ginger, mushrooms, and fungi are also common here. Animals Animals vary widely from one tropical rainforest to another. However, certain adaptations are common among them. Many have adaptations for living in trees, including flying, climbing, leaping, and gliding. Communicating with loud calls is common since the dense trees block visibility. Bright colors help many birds spot each other. Other rainforest animals don’t want to be spotted; instead, they use camouflage to hide from predators.
pages.brief: Beneath the canopy, the understory receives little sunlight, so young trees and climbing plants reach upward with large, wide leaves. Mosses, algae, and fungi grow on understory plants. Lower down, the dark, humid forest floor holds decomposing leaves, fallen trees, fruit, and branches, with mosses, ferns, ginger, mushrooms, and fungi.

pages.text: Because of the abundance of animals, competition for food is widespread. Some animals deal with this by having specialized diets or body parts. For example, a toucan’s huge, long bill allows it to reach fruit growing on branches too thin to support its weight. Many rainforest animals are active at night. This adaptation helps them avoid daytime heat and also reduces competition for food. Grasping and Gliding Some canopy animals have developed special adaptations to get across large spaces between branches. Especially in Central and South America, some have a grasping, or prehensile, tail that can be used like a fifth limb. For example, spider and howler monkeys use this body part when scrambling from branch to branch high above the ground. In Asia, some animals glide to cross gaps in the canopy. Flying squirrels, flying geckos, and several other animals have this don’t actually fly; instead, they soar from higher to lower branches using skin flaps around their body that catch air a parachute. A flying squirrel glides from one tree to another at night.
pages.brief: A toucan uses its huge, long bill to reach fruit on thin branches. Nearby, a spider monkey scrambles high above the ground using its grasping tail like a fifth limb. At night, a flying squirrel glides between trees with skin flaps catching the air like a parachute, crossing a gap in the canopy.

pages.text: The algae growing on a sloth’s fur helps it blend in with green plants. Bats, butterflies, small monkeys, eagles, and other birds live in the emergent layer. The canopy is home to the most animals, including some that spend their entire life there. Sloths, toucans, and howler and spider monkeys are found in Central and South America. Orangutans live in Southeast Asia, and sugar gliders live in Australia and parts of Indonesia. Parrots live in all rainforest canopies. Frogs, salamanders, snakes, lizards, birds, and insects are found in the understory, and ground-dwelling animals live on the forest floor. Tapirs, deer, peccaries, boars, and capybaras live in the Amazon. Asian rainforests have elephants and tigers. Elephants are also found in African rainforests, as are gorillas and pygmy hippos. All rainforests except those in Australia have some kind of cat, such as tigers, jaguars, or leopards, and all but those in the Americas have crocodiles. Rainforests around the world have an abundance of insects, spiders, and earthworms.
pages.brief: A sloth hangs in the canopy, its fur tinted green by algae that helps it blend with plants. Around the rainforest layers, toucans and howler monkeys share the canopy with orangutans and parrots, while frogs, snakes, and insects live in the understory. On the forest floor, tapirs, deer, and capybaras move among many insects, spiders, and earthworms.

pages.text: Temperate Rainforests Temperate rainforests receive less rain than tropical rainforests, but still quite a lot—150 to 500 centimeters (60–200 in.) yearly. Moisture from coastal fog adds another 18 to 30 centimeters (7–12 in.) of precipitation each year. Mild winters, cool summers, and rainfall throughout the year are typical, although summers tend to be drier. Plants grow in three layers instead of four, with no emergent layer. The tallest canopy trees grow to roughly 90 meters (300 ft.) tall. Temperate rainforests have far fewer species of trees and other plants than tropical rainforests. In the Northern Hemisphere, evergreens with needle-shaped leaves are common in the canopy. Mosses and deciduous shrubs—shrubs that drop their leaves in winter—grow in the understory. In the Southern Hemisphere, broadleaf evergreens grow in the canopy, and evergreen and deciduous shrubs and trees are found in the understory. Epiphytes are generally limited to ferns and mosses. Temperate rainforests have many animals living on the forest floor, where they are sheltered from rain and wind. pages.brief: In a temperate rainforest in Northern California, tall redwood trees and ferns rise through coastal fog. The forest has three layers and no emergent layer, with needle-leaved evergreens in the canopy and mosses and shrubs below. Tree frogs, squirrels, deer, black bears, bobcats, wolves, mountain lions, insects, and spiders find shelter on the forest floor.

pages.text: The Huli people of Papua New Guinea’s rainforests are known for their headgear and face painting. There are about ninety thousand Huli today. People in Rainforests Native peoples have lived in rainforests for thousands of years, and an estimated fifty million still live there. The changes caused by European settlers have had a significant impact on most traditional lifestyles, and some groups no longer exist. The largest number of remaining Native peoples live in the Amazon rainforest. In recent years, many people have moved to rainforests and cleared land of trees to start small farms and ranches. Logging and mining have also caused significant areas of forest to be cleared. Tropical rainforests provide a vast number of resources for modern life, including food, spices, wood, medicines, and minerals. Tourism in rainforests, especially in the Amazon, is very popular because of the diversity of wildlife.
pages.brief: Huli people in Papua New Guinea’s rainforest wear distinctive headgear and face paint, with about ninety thousand Huli today. In rainforests worldwide, Native peoples have lived for thousands of years. Elsewhere, people clear trees for small farms and ranches, and logging and mining remove forest areas, while tourists come to see wildlife.

pages.text: A Celebration of Abundance Life exists almost everywhere on Earth— from Antarctica to the Sahara desert and from the ocean floor to Mount Everest. However, conditions in many places present challenges for living things. Those places may be cold for much or all of the year, or they may lack shelter or a steady water supply. Rainforests are different—nothing is lacking. They offer so much water, warmth, and shelter that life erupts in abundance. To get a sense of this biome’s biodiversity, think about this: more kinds of ants live on a single bush in the Amazon rainforest than in the entire United Kingdom. Rainforests are among Earth’s most precious jewels, where nature shines in all its glory. A cave opening frames a misty view of the tropical rainforest in Borneo, a large island in Southeast Asia.
pages.brief: A cave opening frames a misty view of a tropical rainforest in Borneo, Southeast Asia. Inside the lush forest, water, warmth, and shelter support abundant life. On a single Amazon bush, more kinds of ants live than in the entire United Kingdom, showing the rainforest’s extraordinary biodiversity.

books.title: Deserts
books.art_why: The book describes present-day real deserts, wildlife and places that can be photographed.

pages.text: Saguaro (suh-WAR-oh) cacti only grow in the Sonoran Desert, mainly in southern Arizona and northwestern Mexico. Saguaros can live more than two hundred years.
pages.brief: Tall saguaro cacti with thick upright stems and raised arms stand spaced apart on dry desert ground in the Sonoran Desert of southern Arizona and northwestern Mexico, under open sky. The oldest of these huge plants have stood in the same place for more than two hundred years.

pages.text: Spring wildflowers carpet the Mojave Desert in Southern California. Space and Stillness If you search online for descriptions of deserts, you’re likely to come across phrases like “empty wasteland” and “barren, desolate landscape.” Deserts have a reputation for being harsh, unpleasant places where life hangs by a thread and no one in their right mind would dare to go. If you talk to people who love deserts, however, you’ll hear a different story. To them, deserts are places of stillness and beauty where you can hear yourself think and see for miles in every direction. They’re also places with living things that have developed fascinating ways to survive where water is rare and precious.
pages.brief: A wide spread of spring wildflowers carpets the floor of the Mojave Desert in Southern California, covering the dry ground with colour as far as the eye can see, with open desert stretching away behind the flowers.

pages.text: Earth’s Desert Regions About one-fifth of Earth’s land is deserts. Every continent has deserts, including Antarctica, most of which is considered a cold desert. Cloudless skies for many days in a row are common in hot deserts. That’s because the humidity—the amount of water vapor in the air— is often too low for clouds to form. When they do, they may produce rain that evaporates before it reaches the ground. This kind of rain is called virga. Precipitation varies, depending on the type of desert. Some deserts may go a year or longer without any rain at all. Long dry spells can put deserts at risk for wildfires. In fact, wildfires are more common today than they were long ago. Global warming is causing droughts as well as higher temperatures in many desert regions.
pages.brief: A broad view of dry desert land stretching away beneath a cloudless sky, the air so dry that no clouds form. The scene shows how about one-fifth of Earth's land is desert, and how clear skies can last for many days in a row.

pages.text: A large haboob rolls across Mali, in West Africa. In cold deserts, much of the precipitation falls as snow rather than rain. Warmer deserts may have one rainy season or two. Sudden, violent rainstorms in some deserts can cause flash flooding. Thunderstorms often produce strong winds, and in hot deserts, these winds kick up a great deal of sand and dust. On occasion, the winds create haboobs—huge walls of sand and dust that may be nearly 3 kilometers (2 mi.) high. Wowser! • The hottest temperature in the world was recorded at Death Valley, in California, in 1913. The temperature was 57 degrees Celsius (134°F). • Daytime and nighttime temperatures in deserts can be very different because of the lack of humidity. (In wetter parts of the world, the humidity tends to hold in heat after sunset.) In Chihuahua, Mexico, daytime temperatures can reach 37°C (100°F), while nighttime temperatures on the same day can drop below freezing (0°C, or 32°F).
pages.brief: A huge wall of sand and dust, a haboob, rolls across the open land of Mali in West Africa, rising nearly three kilometres high and darkening the sky above the desert as it moves forward.

pages.text: Types of Deserts While Earth’s deserts have an amazing amount of variety, they can be grouped into four main types. Hot, Dry Deserts These deserts are the hottest type and also the best known. Although the weather is generally warm all year long, temperatures can reach extremes in summer—as high as 49 degrees Celsius (120°F). They can drop quickly after dark, especially in winter. Rainfall may be low year-round or occur in short bursts between long dry seasons. The largest hot, dry desert—the Sahara, in Africa—is almost as large as the continental United States. Other deserts of this type are located in southwestern North America, Central and South America, South Asia, and Australia. Semiarid Deserts Semiarid deserts have summers that are long and dry, though not as hot as those in hot, dry deserts. Winters are cold, with little rain or snow. In North America, Nevada’s Great Basin Desert is a semiarid desert. So is the Colorado Plateau, a large region that covers parts of Utah, Colorado, Arizona, and New Mexico. Spain’s Tabernas Desert, which is Europe’s only true desert, is also classified as a semiarid desert.
pages.brief: Hot, dry desert country in the Sahara in Africa, the largest desert of its kind, stretching wide beneath a blazing summer sun. Bare, sunbaked ground reaches to the horizon in a place where temperatures can climb to 49 degrees Celsius.

pages.text: What’s a Rain Shadow Desert? rising air cools, clouds form, rain or snow falls dry air moves down Some deserts are dry because mountains block moisture from reaching them. Warm, wet air moves up one side of a mountain range. Clouds form, then drop rain and snow. When that air starts down the range’s other side, it warms again, and the clouds disappear. The result on the far side is a rain shadow. Coastal Deserts Coastal deserts are usually located along the western edges of continents. Cold ocean currents along the coast produce winter fog and often block sunlight. The weather in coastal deserts is very dry but not extremely hot. Summers are warm, and winters are cool. Average yearly rainfall is usually 8 to 13 centimeters (3–5 in.). The Atacama Desert (South America) and the Namib Desert (Africa) are both coastal deserts. Cold Deserts Cold deserts have long, cold winters with high snowfall. Summers are short, and the snow can stay frozen for years. Most of Antarctica is cold desert, as is the Gobi Desert (Asia), the Patagonian Desert (South America), and most of Greenland.
pages.brief: A mountain range seen in cross-section: warm, wet air climbs one side, clouds form and drop rain and snow, then the air sinks down the far side and the clouds vanish, leaving the land beyond the mountains dry in a rain shadow.

pages.text: Desert Plants Because deserts are so dry, very little liquid water is available for living things to use, but adaptations allow them to live in habitats with low precipitation. Desert plants have three main survival strategies. One group of plants—succulents— store water in their roots, stems, or leaves. Cactuses are succulents, and there are many others as well. Most succulents have thick, waxy skin that holds in water. They often have shallow roots that enable them to quickly absorb any rain that falls. A second group of desert plants drop their leaves and become dormant during the dry season, then quickly spring to life when the rains return. Some plants in this group, including mesquite trees, have a long taproot that reaches deep underground to find water. This plant, baby toes, is a succulent but not a cactus. It does not have spines.
pages.brief: Close view of desert plants: a succulent with thick, waxy, water-holding stems and shallow roots spreading just below the surface, beside a low baby toes succulent with no spines, and a mesquite tree whose long taproot reaches deep underground for water.

pages.text: A third set of adaptations involves avoiding drought altogether. Plants in this group, including many desert wildflowers, mature quickly and complete their life cycle before the dry season begins. They devote their energy to producing seeds that germinate when the rains return. Photosynthesis in the Desert Plants produce their own food through a chemical process known as photosynthesis. This process involves taking in carbon dioxide gas through tiny holes called stomata, which are mainly located on the underside of leaves. Chlorophyll, a green pigment in the leaves, helps plants capture sunlight to make a simple sugar called glucose from carbon dioxide and water. Because photosynthesis requires sunlight, most plants conduct this process during the day. However, opening their stomata causes them to lose large amounts of water, which would be a problem for desert plants. Many desert plants conduct photosynthesis without losing much water. They keep their stomata closed during the day and open them at night, when the air is cooler and moister. They store carbon dioxide overnight and use it the next day to make food. Palo verde trees have a different way to conserve water. They drop their leaves during especially dry periods to avoid losing water. However, they can still make food because of the chlorophyll in their palo verde bark green bark.
pages.brief: Desert wildflowers growing fast and setting seed before the dry season begins, and beside them a palo verde tree that has dropped its leaves during a dry spell, its green bark still able to make food in the sunlight.

pages.text: An African bullfrog hides beneath sand (left). A ground squirrel uses its tail to shield it from sunlight (right). Both live in Africa’s Kalahari Desert. Desert Animals The lack of water is also a challenge for animals, as are the high temperatures in many deserts. Few large mammals live in hot deserts compared to most other biomes because they don’t tolerate the heat and lack of water well. Many desert animals, including squirrels, avoid the heat and conserve water by staying in the shade during the hottest times of the day. They hide away in a burrow or under rocks or vegetation. Others, including owls and small Australian marsupials known as bilbies, are nocturnal, or active at night. Still others, such as rattlesnakes, are typically crepuscular—active at dawn and dusk. Some desert animals, including bats, migrate to other locations during the hottest or driest times of the year. Desert toads become dormant while waiting for rain or cooler temperatures to return.
pages.brief: An African bullfrog half-buried and hidden beneath the sand, and a ground squirrel holding its tail up to shield itself from sunlight, both living in Africa's Kalahari Desert during the heat of the day.

pages.text: Desert animals have other ways to stay cool as well. Coyotes pant, while owls flutter their throat. Jackrabbits and fennec foxes release body heat through their large ears. Bighorn sheep shed their winter coat in stages, with their belly and other shaded parts losing hair first to help body heat escape. Getting enough water is another challenge for desert animals. Many feed on succulents, nectar, or sap. Others, especially reptiles and birds, release waste that contains very little water. Some desert animals have very unusual adaptations that help them get water. For example, thorny devil lizards have grooves between their spikes that absorb collected dew and send it to their mouth. thorny devil lizard.
pages.brief: A fennec fox and a jackrabbit releasing body heat through their large ears, a coyote panting, a bighorn sheep shedding its winter coat in patches, and a thorny devil lizard whose spiky grooves collect dew and carry it to its mouth.

pages.text: People in Deserts People have lived in deserts for many thousands of years. Today, roughly one billion people live in this biome—about one-seventh of Earth’s population. Like plants and nonhuman animals, people have had to adapt to find enough water to make their homes there. Traditionally, desert dwellers have been nomadic, moving with the seasons to find water and food. Protective clothing has shielded them from sunlight as well as sandstorms. In African and Asian deserts, The nomadic Tuareg people camels, sheep, goats, and of the Sahara Desert are horses have often provided sometimes referred to as the “blue people.” transportation as well as milk. Modern adaptations to desert life often involve bringing water in from elsewhere. Dams and irrigation have allowed millions of people to live in deserts. Residents of modern desert cities and towns consider air-conditioning essential. Deserts are popular destinations for tourists. Attractions include hiking, camping, and appreciating the stillness and natural beauty.
pages.brief: Nomadic Tuareg people of the Sahara Desert, dressed in protective clothing that shields them from sunlight and sandstorms, moving with the seasons to find water and food, travelling with camels that carry them and provide milk.

pages.text: In addition to animals, crepuscular describes other things related to twilight. Here, crepuscular rays shoot out from clouds during a Sonoran Desert sunset. So Much to See The plants, animals, and landscapes in deserts are all unique and fascinating—and there’s still more to appreciate. Because deserts have fewer tall trees than most other biomes, it’s easier to see the sky, which often puts on shows too dramatic to miss. Storm clouds can loom so large that they take on a life of their own. The sky sometimes fills with unusual sunrays so amazing that it’s hard to believe they’re real. Meteor showers and the huge arc of the Milky Way are also special nighttime treats. Although deserts have a reputation for being harsh places, in reality they’re treasures with wondrous gems just waiting to be discovered.
pages.brief: Crepuscular rays shoot out from clouds across a Sonoran Desert sunset, spreading across the land below. The sky above is wide and open because deserts have fewer tall trees than other places, making the sky easier to see.

books.title: Oceans
books.art_why: Modern oceans, marine life, and fishing crews are real-world subjects that can be photographed.

pages.text: Waves crash on the Indian Ocean. A Vast, Hidden World The ocean is a vast and mysterious place. A quick glance from the deck of a ship might make you think you’re in the middle of nowhere. The endless water may seem lifeless on the surface, with nothing but dark, choppy waves stretching out in every direction. In truth, the ocean is filled with life, movement, and color. Marine organisms range in size from single-celled green algae to enormous colonies of seagrass and from microscopic viruses to blue whales—the largest animals ever known to have lived on Earth. The ocean is also home to mountain ranges, active volcanoes, huge plateaus, and deep trenches. This endlessly fascinating world still has much left for humans to explore. It is also one of Earth’s most important biomes, affecting everything from weather and climate to global food supplies.
pages.brief: Dark, choppy waves crash across the Indian Ocean beside the deck of a ship. Beneath the surface, a blue whale swims past drifting green algae and seagrass, while underwater mountain ranges, active volcanoes, plateaus, and a deep trench shape the hidden seafloor.

pages.text: Four or Five Oceans? Long ago, schoolchildren only learned about four oceans: the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, and Arctic. During that time, scientists debated whether there were four or five oceans. In 2000, the International Hydrographic Organization, which surveys and charts Earth’s oceans and seas, officially added the Southern Ocean to the list of oceans. It surrounds Antarctica and extends north to the latitude line at 60° south. Not all countries recognize the Southern Ocean, and some schoolchildren still learn that Earth has only four oceans.
