pages.text: Water and Air Although Earth’s oceans all contain salt water, they differ in many other ways. At a basic level, regions of the ocean can be classified according to Earth’s three main climate zones: tropical, temperate, and polar. The tropical zones, which surround the equator, are the warmest, and the polar zones, which are near the poles, are the coldest. However, many other factors also play a part in ocean features. Water moves in currents, both on the ocean’s surface and deep below. Currents may carry warm water to cold regions or cold water to warm regions. Surface currents are caused by blowing wind as well as Earth’s rotation on its axis. Deep currents form as a result of differences in temperature and salinity, which is the amount of salt in the water. Wind is the most common cause of ocean waves. Waves may also form as a result of tides, which rise and fall each day. Tides are caused by the Because the Moon is so much closer to Moon’s gravity pulling our planet than the Sun, its tidal effect on Earth. on Earth is stronger.
pages.brief: Warm tropical water near the equator and cold polar water near the poles meet in a wide ocean. Wind blows across the surface, raising waves and pushing currents, while the Moon hangs above and pulls the daily tides.

pages.text: The temperature of the ocean also varies a great deal from the surface to the seafloor. Water is warmer near the surface partly because it’s warmed by the Sun. In addition, cold water sinks because it’s denser than warm water. It’s also under much more pressure. The ocean affects weather and climate by absorbing most of the Sun’s rays. It works much like a huge solar panel, especially in the tropical zones, and moves this heat around the world. Because of its enormous size, the ocean also helps drive the water cycle because of the amount of evaporation that takes place above it. This process sometimes creates huge storms. Climate Change and the Ocean The ocean absorbs carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, which helps lessen the effects of climate change. At the same time, the ocean is greatly affected by climate change. Rising temperatures and melting ice are altering weather patterns, ocean currents, coastal erosion, marine ecosystems, and more. Tropical cyclones, including hurricanes, are violent spinning storms that form over warm ocean water. They usually weaken as they move over land but can still cause a lot of damage.
pages.brief: Sunlight warms the ocean surface while colder, denser water sinks below it. Above the water, evaporation feeds clouds and heavy rain, and a violent tropical cyclone spins over warm ocean water, its winds and waves affecting weather and climate.

pages.text: Ocean Landforms Land along the edge of the ocean, called a coast or shoreline, may be sandy, rocky, or muddy. It lies next to shallow water located above slightly lower land called the continental shelf. Beyond this zone is the continental slope, a steep drop-off that leads down to the deep ocean. The seafloor is always changing because of the movement of tectonic plates in Earth’s crust, or rocky outer layer. Seafloor features include underwater volcanoes and seamounts as well as plateaus and plains. A notable feature of the seafloor is mid-ocean ridges, a system of mountain chains nearly 65,000 kilometers (40,390 mi.) long. This system formed and continues to change as a result of tectonic plates moving apart. Melted rock, called magma, fills in the space between the plates. The highest areas of the seafloor, which extend above the ocean’s surface, have formed volcanic islands such as Iceland and the Hawaiian Islands. Tectonic plates are huge pieces of Earth’s crust that move as hot, weak rock moves in the mantle, the layer underneath the crust. The movement of these plates causes earthquakes, volcanoes, and many other changes in Earth’s surface.
pages.brief: A coastline runs from sandy, rocky, and muddy shore into shallow water above the continental shelf, then drops steeply down the continental slope. Beyond it, tectonic plates move apart along a mid-ocean ridge, magma rises, and a volcanic island stands above the sea.

pages.text: The Ocean Floor Another feature of the seafloor is trenches, which are the deepest parts of the ocean. They form when two tectonic plates move toward each other and the lighter plate pushes the denser plate beneath it. When this happens, a steep, long V-shaped valley forms in the seafloor. Some of the largest earthquakes ever recorded have been caused by this process. It also causes volcanic islands to form. Japan’s islands as well as a group of islands off the coast of Alaska formed in this way. Most trenches are located in the Pacific Ocean. The deepest among them is the Mariana Trench, which is located south of Japan near the Mariana Islands. Trenches are completely dark and near freezing. Water pressure is over a thousand times greater than it is on the ocean’s surface.
pages.brief: Two tectonic plates push together, forming a long, steep V-shaped trench in the dark, freezing seafloor. The water pressure is immense. Far above, volcanic islands rise from the ocean, and the deepest trench lies south of Japan near the Mariana Islands.

pages.text: Zones and Organisms The ocean is divided vertically into zones by the amount of sunlight they receive. The surface receives the most sunlight, and darkness increases with greater depth. In addition to varying light, the zones have different temperatures, pressures, amounts of oxygen, and mineral nutrients. The sunlit, or surface, zone makes up only about 5 percent of the ocean’s depth. It receives enough sunlight for photosynthesis, the process by which plants and certain other organisms make their own food using sunlight, air, and water. Microscopic algae called phytoplankton, along with seagrass and giant kelp, another type of algae, are the ocean’s main photosynthesizers. They are crucial to all life on our planet because they produce at least half of Earth’s oxygen. Ocean Zones about 200 m (660 ft.) about 1,000 m (3,300 ft.) about 4,000 m (13,100 ft.) as deep as 6,000 m (20,000 ft.)
pages.brief: Sunlight fills the upper sunlit zone, where phytoplankton, seagrass, and giant kelp use photosynthesis. The sunlit surface makes up only a small part of the ocean’s depth; below it, the water darkens through deeper zones until sunlight fades into blackness.

pages.text: Phytoplankton are also the foundation of many ocean food chains. They and other photosynthesizers provide food for a huge variety of animals, either directly or indirectly. These animals include sea jellies, crustaceans, fish, seabirds, sea turtles, and marine mammals such as seals and whales. Because of photosynthesis, this zone is home to about 90 percent of all ocean life. Coral reefs are also found in the sunlit zone. These are made of the built- up skeletons of hard corals, support an Most coral reefs are found in the sunlit zone because most corals depend on algae, which need of organisms. Algae sunlight for photosynthesis. living with the corals produce food for them as well as for reef fish and other animals. The twilight zone is located beneath the sunlit zone. It receives some sunlight but not enough for photosynthesis, so it contains no plants or other photosynthetic organisms. The sunlight it receives isn’t enough to warm the water, which is always cold.
pages.brief: In the sunlit zone, a coral reef rises from the water, built from the skeletons of hard corals. Fish, sea jellies, a sea turtle, seabirds, and a seal share the bright water, while phytoplankton at the base of the food chain drift around them.

pages.text: Animals in the twilight zone include squid, octopuses, sperm whales, and certain kinds of fish. Creatures in and below this zone have adaptations for dealing with the increased darkness, cold, and pressure. Some glow, while others have no eyes and depend on senses besides vision. The midnight zone makes up about 90 percent of the ocean. It is completely dark and near freezing all the time. Sea cucumbers, gulper eels, and unusual fish are among the animals that make their homes here. We know very little about this zone because it is so hard to explore. Trenches are part of the midnight zone. Conditions in trenches are harsh, but a small number of organisms live here, too. Bacteria are the foundation of food chains. Instead of sunlight, they use hydrogen sulfide gas to produce energy. Glow-in-the-Dark Animals Some animals that live in the twilight and midnight zones have adapted to the dark by glowing. Some are bioluminescent; they make their own light by means of a chemical reaction in their body. Others are biofluorescent, which involves taking This pyrosome flashes in blue light, changing it, and giving brightly in the water off different colors of light. around Hawaii. It is bioluminescent.
pages.brief: In the cold, dark twilight and midnight zones, a squid, an octopus, a sperm whale, and a gulper eel move through black water. A pyrosome flashes bright blue near Hawaii, while bacteria on the trench floor make energy without sunlight.

pages.text: A fishing crew in Alaska loads their catch of silver salmon. People and Oceans Scientists study the ocean to learn about Earth’s landforms, weather, climate, animals, and much more. This biome is such a fascinating place that it would be easy to think its main value is to satisfy scientific curiosity. However, it also provides an enormous amount of food for people around the world—so much so that overfishing has become a serious problem. It also supplies ingredients for medicines used to treat cancers, ease pain, and help wounds heal. In addition, the ocean has allowed people to travel by water since ancient times. People also appreciate the ocean for the recreational opportunities it offers. These include scuba diving, snorkeling, surfing, boating, fishing, and whale watching as well as visiting distant islands.
pages.brief: A fishing crew in Alaska stands on a boat, loading their catch of silver salmon. Around them, the ocean stretches wide, a place people also use for study, medicine, travel, scuba diving, snorkeling, surfing, boating, fishing, and whale watching.

pages.text: Treasures from a Hidden World The next time you wander along a beach examining seashells, stones, and bits of seaweed, take a moment to appreciate the ocean and the treasures it brings. Think about how deep it is and the organisms and landforms it contains. Where did each interesting thing that washed up onshore come from? What was its journey like? Most of us only get to experience a small part of the ocean. The sparkling surface of the water hides a world as fascinating and complex as any biome on land. From the sunny upper layer to the cold, dark depths of the ocean’s trenches, there will always be new and amazing things to discover. A sperm whale disappears into the Pacific Ocean near New Zealand.
pages.brief: A beach holds seashells, stones, and bits of seaweed washed up onshore. Beyond the shore, a sperm whale dives into the Pacific Ocean near New Zealand, disappearing into the deep water that hides the ocean’s complex world.

books.title: Amazing Animal Adaptations
books.art_why: The book includes evolutionary and 1800s pollution history where photographs of the events are impossible.

pages.text: A Penguin Surprise When you think of penguins, what image comes to mind? You probably imagine black- and-white birds sliding down snowy slopes and diving into icy waters, not sunning themselves on tropical islands near the equator! You might be surprised to learn that one kind of penguin inhabits just such a place. The Galapagos penguin lives on warm islands in the eastern Pacific Ocean. How does a species originally from Antarctica survive in such a climate? It changes over time, gradually developing physical and behavioral adaptations that suit the conditions. The Galapagos penguin is not the only species to do this. Most animal species exist today because of how they changed and adapted to their surroundings. Galapagos penguins are the only penguins found at the equator.
pages.brief: A black-and-white Galapagos penguin stands on a warm tropical island in the eastern Pacific Ocean near the equator, sunning itself in bright sunlight, a surprising sight far away from icy Antarctic waters and snowy slopes.

pages.text: Hibernation is another kind of behavioral adaptation that occurs when seasons change. Instead of moving to a new place, some animals stay put and go into a state somewhat like sleep. True hibernators include frogs, ground squirrels, and bats; many animals once thought to hibernate, such as bears and skunks, actually enter a lighter state of sleep called torpor. Both groups of animals enter these states during cold winter months when food is scarce because they use less energy and need less food. When outside conditions improve in the spring, they become active again. A whiskered bat hibernates in a Netherlands limestone quarry (inset). A black bear mother sleeps with her cub inside their den in Minnesota (main). Bats are true hibernators, while bears enter a lighter state of sleep.
pages.brief: A whiskered bat hangs in hibernation inside a limestone quarry in the Netherlands, while a black bear mother sleeps with her cub inside their den in Minnesota during cold winter months when food is scarce.

pages.text: By contrast, structural adaptations are changes in body structure that make it easier for animals to live in their environment. These changes happen slowly over many generations. Chameleons, for example, developed skin that can change color, which helps them blend in with their surroundings and makes it hard for predators or prey to see them. Foxes have structural adaptations that help them use camouflage, too. The Arctic fox has a white coat, which makes it hard to see in the snow, while the desert fox has a tan coat, which blends in with the desert sand. Both foxes have other structural adaptations as well. The Arctic fox has much smaller ears than its cousin because foxes lose body heat through their ears. The Arctic fox lives in a cold environment, so it needs to hold in body heat. The desert fox, on the other hand, lives in a hot environment and needs to stay cool, so it has very large ears that help it shed heat. Arctic fox.
pages.brief: A chameleon blends into its surroundings with color-changing skin. An Arctic fox with a white coat and small ears stands in snow, while a desert fox with a tan coat and very large ears stands in sandy desert, each body suited to its environment.

pages.text: A walking shark takes a seabed stroll at night. Oddly Adaptable Some adaptations are odder than others. Take walking sharks. Found in waters near Australia and Indonesia, these small sharks have very strong front fins. At times, they use their muscular fins not to swim but rather to crawl across the ocean floor. Giraffes have a few odd adaptations of their own. Dig deep into a giraffe’s coat and you’ll end up holding your nose. That’s because giraffe fur works as a chemical defense. It is full of antibiotics and other smelly chemicals that keep parasites away. Giraffes also need very little sleep. Even when Most giraffes get by on just two hours of shut-eye a day, and nearly all of that is while standing! Both behaviors help protect them from predators. held high.
pages.brief: At night, a small walking shark uses its strong front fins to crawl across the seabed near Australia and Indonesia. A giraffe stands with its coat and long neck held high, showing the fur that keeps parasites away and the animal that sleeps very little.

pages.text: A Slow Process Animal species don’t think about ways to change. Adaptation happens naturally over time. Early bears that entered a state of torpor survived cold winters. The bears that didn’t died. As a result, only the first group of bears was around to reproduce. Something similar happened with foxes. Arctic foxes with small ears survived, while those with large ears did not. The survivors mated, and, in time, all the foxes in that environment had small ears because that feature was passed down. Animal species evolve through a combination of behavioral and structural adaptations. The Galapagos penguin is a good example. Galapagos penguins found their way to the tropics by way of the Humboldt Current. This South current carries cold water north America from Antarctica and is rich in squid and fish like sardines. The penguins are right at home in the cold water. They must PACIFIC come on land to nest, however, OCEAN and land in the tropics is much warmer than water.
pages.brief: Early bears that entered torpor survive cold winters, and Arctic foxes with small ears survive and pass that feature on. Galapagos penguins travel by the cold Humboldt Current from Antarctica, feed in water rich in squid and sardines, then come onto warmer tropical land to nest.

pages.text: Galapagos penguins have ways to cope with the heat. They pant to keep cool, and they stretch out their flippers to shade their feet and keep them from getting sunburned. The penguins build their nests in burrows between rocks, hidden from the Sun’s rays. While other penguins molt once a year, Galapagos penguins molt twice. Shedding their feathers helps them stay cool. These penguin behaviors and features developed over time. Penguins that lacked them died off. Prime nesting sites like this one are limited. In 2010, researchers built 120 shady penguin nest sites to help these endangered birds.
pages.brief: Galapagos penguins pant and stretch their flippers to shade their feet from the Sun. They nest in burrows between rocks, hidden from bright rays, and molt twice. Shady nest sites built by researchers in 2010 help these endangered birds.

pages.text: Odd Diets Diet is a behavioral adaptation. Some animal species have habits that help them survive. Kangaroo rats, for example, live A kangaroo rat hops in a manner similar to the much larger kangaroo, in deserts with little but the rat lives in North America. water or rainfall, yet somehow survive without ever drinking water. They get the moisture they need from eating grass seeds and mesquite beans. A parrot known as the scarlet macaw eats seeds, too, except these seeds contain a deadly poison. What may keep the macaw safe is its gnawing habit of also on rocks that contain clay. The clay absorbs the poison, which allows the birds to digest the seeds safely. Then again, new studies suggest the birds may be eating the clay in order to increase the salt in their diet. Either way, this instinctive behavior is a dietary adaptation that helps the birds survive.
pages.brief: A kangaroo rat hops through a dry North American desert, surviving without drinking water by getting moisture from grass seeds and mesquite beans. A scarlet macaw eats seeds and gnaws on clay-containing rocks, a dietary habit that may absorb poison or add salt.

pages.text: Strange ocean creatures known as tube worms have their own way of dealing with poison. Tube worms live in total darkness at the bottom of the Pacific Ocean and cluster near hot vents that pump out dangerous gases from deep inside Earth. The gases would kill most life-forms, but tube worms survive and even thrive, thanks to their odd body structure. They lack body parts we would expect to see in animals, such as eyes and a stomach. They are basically bags of bacteria. The bacteria inside the tube worms use the gases as an energy source. Tube worms cluster near a warm gas vent in the North Pacific.
pages.brief: Strange tube worms cluster in total darkness at the bottom of the Pacific Ocean near hot vents that pump out dangerous gases. They lack eyes and a stomach; bacteria inside their bodies use the gases as an energy source, helping them thrive.

pages.text: Their Blood Runs Cold Subfreezing temperatures can kill an animal. Animals’ body cells are mostly made of water. When cells freeze, the water turns to ice and expands. The cells burst, which causes death. Animals have developed different ways to keep this from happening. When temperatures drop, some species migrate to warmer places, while others sleep in warm dens. Still others stay alive by “supercooling” their body fluids. Many insects produce chemicals that act as a kind of antifreeze. The chemicals keep ice crystals from growing, so red flat bark beetle body cells get supercool but never freeze. This adaptation helps cockroaches and caterpillars survive freezing temperatures for days. Alaska’s red flat bark beetle can supercool its body fluids to –50°C (–58°F). Wood frogs can survive for weeks at a time when temperatures drop as low as –14°C (7°F). Although ice does form within frogs’ bodies, it forms between cells rather than inside them. That way, cells are not at risk of bursting.
pages.brief: In freezing conditions, a red flat bark beetle supercools its body fluids to very low temperatures, while a wood frog survives with ice forming between its cells rather than inside them. Chemicals act like antifreeze, keeping ice crystals from growing and cells from bursting.

pages.text: Other animals adapt by simply getting rid of the water in their body through a process called dehydration. Tiny insects known as Antarctic midges dry up, appear frozen, and seem to be dead. When they come in contact with water, however, they spring back to life. Only one mammal can supercool its body— the Arctic ground squirrel. This squirrel’s body temperature can drop as low as –3°C (26°F). Just how it does this is a mystery. It doesn’t make its own does it get rid of fluids. Yet temperatures. An Arctic ground squirrel in Alaska finds a snack.
pages.brief: Tiny Antarctic midges dry up and appear frozen and dead, then spring back to life when they touch water. An Arctic ground squirrel in Alaska finds a snack; it is the only mammal that can supercool its body, though how it does so remains a mystery.

pages.text: Wondrous Water Bears The tiny water bear is not a bear at all. It’s a microscopic animal known as a tardigrade that has some pretty impressive adaptations. Water bears can withstand cold to –200°C (–328°F) and heat higher than 149°C (300°F). They can survive high levels of radiation, a dangerous form of energy, and pressure six times greater than that found at the bottom of the ocean. In many conditions, they survive by curling into a ball and entering a nearly lifeless state. They also produce many substances known as antioxidants, which keep vital organs intact. And they produce a protein that protects their cells from the effects of radiation. These adaptations make tardigrades nearly indestructible. Scientists think that tardigrades will outlast humans, thanks to their amazing adaptations!
pages.brief: A microscopic water bear, or tardigrade, curls into a nearly lifeless ball to survive extreme cold, heat, radiation, and pressure. It produces antioxidants that protect vital organs and a protein that shields cells from radiation, making this tiny animal nearly indestructible.

pages.text: Masters of Disguise Another structural adaptation is the ability to camouflage. Some animals are true masters of disguise, such as the leaf mantis. Parts of its body are the exact shape and color of dead leaves, a remarkable adaptation that makes it easy for this insect to hide and hunt on the forest floor without being seen. Like the mantis, the cuttlefish can masquerade as part of the landscape. It looks like a small squid. Its skin changes color and texture to match almost perfectly. The cuttlefish has three skin layers and fleshy growths called papillae, which it uses to make itself look like bumpy coral or stone. This makes it practically invisible to prey and also keeps this effective hunter from being hunted itself! Adaptations are only helpful if they work, though. Changes to an animal’s habitat can turn an effective adaptation into a fatal flaw. This is what happened to an insect known as the peppered moth.
pages.brief: On the forest floor, a leaf mantis looks exactly like a dead leaf in shape and color, hiding while it hunts. A cuttlefish, resembling a small squid, changes skin color and texture with papillae to match bumpy coral or stone and avoid being seen.

pages.text: Most early peppered moths had white wings with dark spots. The moths easily blended in with lichen-covered tree bark. Predators such as birds couldn’t see the moths. Some peppered moths, however, were only dark. Those moths were easy targets for birds and, as a result, there were many more white moths than dark ones. During the Industrial Revolution in the 1800s, pollution from factory smokestacks killed the lichen and turned the tree bark black. Now the dark peppered moths could blend in and hide. The white moths stood out against the dark bark. Birds could easily see them now. The number of white moths dropped, while the number of dark moths rose. When pollution controls took effect in the 1900s, the tree bark turned lighter again, and the moth populations shifted once more. Dark moths became rare once again. Even though the color variation may have been a fatal flaw for some individual moths, it allowed the species as a whole to survive in a changing environment.
pages.brief: Peppered moths rest on tree bark. Most are white with dark spots and blend in with lichen-covered bark, while some are only dark and easy for birds to see. Factory pollution in the 1800s blackens the bark; later pollution controls lighten it again, shifting moth populations.

pages.text: Life Finds a Way Adaptation is especially important in environments that are going through change. For most living things today, that change is climate change. Animals like the Galapagos penguin must once again adapt to conditions around them. As ocean waters warm and food supplies grow scarce, the penguins must change how, what, or where they eat. The same holds true for animals around the planet. Most will survive as long as they continue to adapt in response to their changing environment—if they have time to adapt. A Galapagos penguin feeds its chick. If the cool waters that supply their food warm permanently, the penguins may have to move.
pages.brief: A Galapagos penguin feeds its chick. As ocean waters warm and food supplies grow scarce, this bird must change how, what, or where it eats. If the cool waters that supply its food warm permanently, the penguins may have to move.

pages.text: A Race Against Time Many species are being pushed to adapt to climate change, but adaptation takes time. In their race against the clock, the outlook is better for some than others. Tawny owls come in different shades. With milder winters in recent decades, researchers in Finland have seen an increase in darker owls. Less snow means these owls blend in better and are more likely to survive and reproduce. Polar bears may have evolved from their brown bear ancestors as far back as six hundred thousand years ago. It took the species time to adapt to its conditions. Black skin, white fur, and fur-covered feet are adaptations that make the bears well-suited for Arctic survival. Now, loss of their sea ice habitat due to global warming poses a dire threat to polar bears. They were listed as a threatened species under the Endangered Species Act in May 2008. American pikas are cute but tough. Because they live high on mountains, they have adapted to a cold climate. When exposed to warm temperatures, pikas can overheat and die. But since pikas live so high already, there is nowhere for them to go. Trapped at the top, they could be one of the first species to go extinct due to climate change.
pages.brief: A tawny owl in Finland shows a darker shade that blends in with less snow. A polar bear with black skin, white fur, and fur-covered feet stands in its Arctic habitat, where sea ice is shrinking. A small American pika sits high on a mountain, adapted to cold and trapped by warming.

pages.text: World-Famous Wonder: Serengeti National Park and Masai Mara Reserve Tanzania and Kenya— Films and photographs from the Serengeti (SARE-en-GET-ee) are some of the most famous images of Africa. Dry grasses rustle across broad landscapes colored brown, red, and orange by the African sun. Lions, gazelles, zebras, and antelopes lounge peacefully on the immense plains. The Masai people have called this land home for thousands of years. Serengeti National Park was established in 1951 by the British in Tanzania. The park’s creation forced many Masai to move away from their lands. They now have only a small part of the land that was once theirs. The Masai have always called the Serengeti Siringitu: “the place where the land goes on forever.”
pages.brief: On the broad Serengeti plains, dry grasses ripple under the African sun while lions, gazelles, zebras, and antelopes rest peacefully. Masai people stand nearby on land their families have called home for thousands of years, looking across the famous savanna landscape.

pages.text: The Serengeti, one of Earth’s oldest, largest savannas, or dry grasslands, is the last home of many famous African animals. Every year, hundreds of thousands of wildebeests and zebras migrate, moving across the plains, following seasonal rains. Amazing predators, including lions, crocodiles, cheetahs, and hyenas, follow them. Several of the Serengeti’s animals, including rhinos, cheetahs, and some antelopes, are severely endangered due to poaching and human-caused habitat loss. Without the park and its rangers to protect their habitat, these creatures would probably become extinct.
pages.brief: Hundreds of thousands of wildebeests and zebras move across the Serengeti plains, following seasonal rains. Lions, crocodiles, cheetahs, and hyenas follow the herds. A ranger watches over the savanna, where rhinos, cheetahs, and antelopes face poaching and habitat loss.

pages.text: A Country’s Proud Heritage: Santa Rosa National Park Costa Rica —Costa Rica, a tiny Central American country, includes many natural and cultural treasures. In Santa Rosa Park, many special features come together. Along the Pacific coastline, many endangered sea turtles gather by the thousands to nest. The oceans here are also great for surfing.
pages.brief: Along Costa Rica’s Pacific coastline in Santa Rosa National Park, thousands of endangered sea turtles gather on the beach to nest. Waves roll in nearby, where a surfer rides the ocean. The shoreline and sea meet under bright tropical light.

pages.text: The inland portions of the park feature savannas and the largest area of dry tropical forest in Central America. This habitat supports howler monkeys, wild pigs, and over fifty species of bats that nest in the park’s many caves. Many scientists visit this rich natural landscape to study how the plants and animals of the forest and ocean interact. Two historical sites preserve the memory of important battles in Costa Rica’s struggle for independence from Spain. Visitors can tour these sites and enjoy hiking, camping, and surfing.
pages.brief: Inland Santa Rosa National Park shows dry tropical forest and savanna. Howler monkeys, wild pigs, and many bats gather near caves while scientists study how forest plants and animals interact with the ocean. Visitors hike and camp near historical sites from Costa Rica’s independence struggle.

pages.text: Park Among the People: Rock Creek Park Washington, D.C., U.S.A. —It’s easy to imagine national parks as expanses of wild territory. It’s not so easy to imagine a park inside a major city. Yet that’s just what Rock Creek Park is. It is a small, 1,700-acre area of preserved cultural and natural heritage, right in the center of the U.S. capital city. Established in 1890, this park a spot of nature. They can escape among the plants, rushing water of a forest. A theater plays in the summer. The park is also filled with historical artifacts from the founding of the U.S. capital, the Civil War, and the displaced Piscataway people.
pages.brief: In the center of Washington, D.C., Rock Creek Park offers a small preserved forest with rushing water and plants. People walk and escape the city among trees, while an outdoor theater hosts a summer play. Historical artifacts from the city’s founding, the Civil War, and the displaced Piscataway people are part of the park.

pages.brief: Mountains rise sharply from the shores of the narrow, extremely deep Saguenay Fjord in Quebec, an arm of the sea. The water stretches between steep slopes under open sky. The scene shows the dramatic meeting of mountain and deep marine water in the conservation area.

pages.text: The mix of freshwater and salt water in the fjord provides many nutrients that attract all sorts of sea creatures. Plankton, fish, birds, and mammals all call it home. Many species of whale, including minke, fin, pilot, humpback, and blue whales, come here during warmer months. The rare beluga, or white whale, lives here year-round. Seals, fish, and invertebrates such as crabs and shellfish are also abundant. So, how do you visit an underwater park? Many people choose to get close to whales and other animals by boat. The park offers whale watches and trips in kayaks—small, canoe- like boats. Visitors also can go scuba diving, hiking, and ice fishing.
pages.brief: In the fjord, freshwater and salt water mix, feeding plankton, fish, birds, and mammals. Humpback, minke, fin, pilot, and blue whales swim in warmer months, while a rare white beluga stays year-round. Seals, crabs, and shellfish live below. A whale-watch boat and kayaks carry visitors.

pages.text: Unique Spots Around the World Volcanoes National Park, Hawai’i, U.S.A. — This park boasts the world’s largest, most active volcano. Visitors watch red-hot, glowing lava roll in fiery streams from the volcano. Falling into the ocean, it sends up plumes of steam. This is the formation of the island, up close! Wilderness areas provide hiking and camping among Hawai’i’s unique landscapes and plants. Everglades National Park, Florida, U.S.A.—North America’s largest subtropical wilderness, this park sits on the homelands of Seminole, Taino, and Tequesta people. Fragile swamps, grasslands, and marshy coastline are preserved here. Rare mammals such as the Florida panther and the manatee also live here.
pages.brief: In Hawai’i Volcanoes National Park, visitors watch glowing red lava stream from the world’s largest active volcano and send up steam as it reaches the ocean. In Florida’s Everglades, a Florida panther and a manatee live among fragile swamps, grasslands, and marshy coastline, homelands of Seminole, Taino, and Tequesta people.

pages.text: Sareks National Park, Sweden —Sweden was Europe’s first country to create national parks. This one, far north above the Arctic Circle, is Western Europe’s largest area of wilderness. It is filled with majestic mountains and glaciers. It is also the ancestral home of the Saami, or Lapp people, who herd reindeer. Tassili N’Ajjer National Park, Algeria (tah-SEE-LEE n-AH-jer)—Algeria, in Northern Africa, is situated in the fierce Sahara. The left behind more engravings in caves and on the sides of cliffs. The art documents the history of humans since 6000 bce!
pages.brief: In Sarek National Park, Sweden, majestic mountains and glaciers rise above the Arctic Circle, the ancestral home of Saami reindeer herders. In Algeria’s Tassili N’Ajjer National Park, ancient engravings cover cave walls and cliff sides in the Sahara, documenting human history since 6000 BCE.

pages.text: Current and Future Challenges Even after a national park is established, preserved lands face many threats. In some countries, people use parklands for growing crops, grazing livestock, and gathering firewood to warm and feed hungry people. Wars and government instability, when political parties clash violently, can also damage these fragile environments. Because some preserved lands house like oil fields, mineral resources, or forests, some people believe these resources should be used to create economic growth. The boundaries of national parks are sometimes questioned and changed as people negotiate power over these natural resources.
pages.brief: Parkland is used for growing crops, grazing livestock, and gathering firewood. Wars and unstable governments damage fragile environments, while oil fields, mineral resources, and forests tempt economic use. People argue over park boundaries and negotiate power over natural resources, leaving the protected land under pressure.

pages.text: Even in a well-protected national park, too many visitors can cause plenty of problems, leaving behind litter, trampling trails, or polluting the air with snowmobile exhaust. It also can be difficult to experience wilderness while surrounded by people. National parks provide refuge for endangered wildlife. They protect millions of plant species, which give us oxygen and help lower the atmosphere’s temperature. As people continue to destroy natural ecosystems to build roads and buildings, it is more vital than ever to protect these beautiful places. If future generations are to enjoy these wild spaces, governments around the world need to work with Indigenous populations to preserve the land.
pages.brief: Too many visitors crowd a trail, leaving litter, trampling plants, and filling the air with snowmobile exhaust. Endangered wildlife finds refuge nearby, and plants help provide oxygen and lower temperatures. Beyond the park, roads and buildings replace natural ecosystems, while governments and Indigenous populations are called to work together.

pages.text: The fur trade became big business in North America.
pages.brief: In a wide North American landscape, several traders in heavy coats sort and stack thick bundles of animal pelts beside a rough wooden trading post and a loaded pack, showing how the fur trade became a large business.

pages.text: Introduction As soon as the bell rang, Robert stuffed that night’s homework into his backpack. He ran for the front steps of the school. Every day, Robert and his friends sat and played a trading card game. People play in a Yu-Gi-Oh! tournament. Robert, William, and Rudolfo liked to play, but sometimes they would just sit and trade cards. William often got good cards from his cousin in California, and Rudolfo got cool cards from his family’s shop downtown. Robert always liked to trade, but today was special. There was a new student in the class who had just moved from Japan, and Haruki liked to trade cards, too. Haruki wanted to trade cards with William, and had cool cards from Japan that William had never seen! All of Haruki’s cards were in Japanese, and no one at Robert’s school had them. Haruki traded cards to William that William had never played with, and William gave Haruki some cool cards in return. Haruki shared these English language cards with his friends in Japan.
pages.brief: Robert stuffs homework into his backpack as the school bell rings and runs toward the front steps, where William and Rudolfo sit trading cards; a new student, Haruki, holds out Japanese cards to trade with William.

pages.text: Trade routes from 6300 BC — AD 1200 Asia N. America Europe ATLANTIC OCEAN PACIFIC OCEAN PACIFIC Africa INDIAN S. America OCEAN OCEAN Australia Prehistoric world These are just some examples of the routes ancient people used to KEY trade goods, such as silk, Antarctica gold, olive oil, gems and minerals, and more. Ancient people, who lived thousands of years before us, also traded objects over long distances. In Europe, men would spend months crossing oceans and traveling up rivers to trade swords or hairpins. In North and South America, people lived and traded for thousands of years before meeting Europeans. Prehistoric North American trade is a perfect example of how people moved valuable objects thousands of miles to trade them for other special objects. (Prehistoric means it happened before those people made written records, such as books.)
pages.brief: A broad prehistoric world map shows long trade routes crossing Asia, Europe, Africa, and the Americas, while ancient traders carry silk, gold, olive oil, gems, and minerals by boat and on foot over great distances.

pages.text: How can we learn about prehistoric trade? One way is through oral tradition. Oral tradition is the set of stories that one generation tells to the next. Because many people like to add things to stories to make them more exciting or easier to understand, stories that are part of oral tradition change over the years. Another way to learn about prehistoric trade is through archaeology. Archaeology is the study of people through the things they leave behind. By looking at the remains of buildings, graves, and especially the trash people leave behind, we can learn about what people did. How can archaeology help figure out how prehistoric North American people traded? If an archaeologist finds a broken seashell in the trash of an ancient village in Colorado, she knows those people in Colorado traded with people who lived near an ocean. Archaeologists years ago.
pages.brief: An elder tells stories to a circle of children beside an archaeologist who studies old buildings, graves, and a village trash heap; the archaeologist holds a broken seashell found far inland in Colorado, far from any ocean.

pages.text: Asia North America Nevada How might Japan Japanese trading cards make the PACIFIC OCEAN trip to Nevada? Think about William and his trading cards. If William’s family moved houses, and someone found a Japanese card in his old room, that person would know that, somehow, William was trading with Japan! If the person who found the card didn’t know about Haruki, she might think lots of different people traded the card, bringing it from Japan to William. But since it’s impossible to buy Japanese cards anywhere near William’s hometown, it must have come from Japan. People often travel farther for a rare and valuable commodity. A commodity is something that is traded, such as gold, seashells, or a trading card. Commodities that were traded in prehistoric North America include copper, shells, and animals. In prehistoric North America, people traveled long distances on foot or by boat. Because of this, trade commodities were usually light, valuable objects that would not spoil.
pages.brief: A Japanese trading card lies in an old Nevada room while a map connects Asia and North America; nearby, travelers carry light, valuable goods such as cards, shells, and copper across long distances on foot or by boat.

pages.text: Copper Objects made from the reddish metal called copper are found in many North American archaeological sites. An archaeological site is a place where people have left behind evidence of their lives, such as trash or parts of buildings. Objects found on these sites are called artifacts. An artifact is an object that has been shaped or Gold and copper artifact from Peru, South America changed by people. Whole copper artifacts have been found in graves in archaeological sites, and broken objects have been found in old garbage. Copper artifacts found in North America include fishhooks, knives, jewelry, and bells. Some of the copper used to make those artifacts was mined in the area around the Great Lakes, particularly around Lake Superior. In most of North America, it was hard for prehistoric people to make metal because metal is often mixed up in rock and that rock is only found in certain areas. Rock with metal in it is called ore. To get the metal out of the ore, people have to get it really hot. This is called smelting metal.
pages.brief: At an archaeological site near the Great Lakes and Lake Superior, copper fishhooks, knives, jewelry, and bells lie beside old graves and garbage; workers heat metal-rich ore in a fire to smelt copper from rock.

pages.text: Native Copper Trade Lake Superior G R E A T L A M K E S s i Bedford Mound R a major prehistoric have been traded Near Lake Superior, there were very large deposits of native copper. Native copper is special because it is very pure copper that can be found in large chunks or as sheets in cracks of rocks. Native copper also does not need smelting. Hundreds of thousands of tons of native copper were mined in this area. Artifacts made from native copper have been found in areas on either side of the Mississippi River and far downstream.
pages.brief: Along the rocky shores of Lake Superior, prehistoric miners pull large chunks and sheets of pure native copper from cracks in the rock; far downstream near the Mississippi River, copper artifacts lie in a mound site.

pages.text: We can tell that this copper was traded great distances in several ways. Many sites where archaeologists find copper artifacts have no natural copper nearby, so we know the copper must have come from far away. Also, by examining copper through a microscope, or examining small amounts of chemicals in the copper, we can tell native copper from smelted copper. Copper ore needs to be smelted before the metal in the rock can be used. Native copper does not need to be smelted before the metal can be used.
pages.brief: In a laboratory, an archaeologist examines a copper artifact under a microscope and tests tiny amounts of chemicals; beside a map, copper artifacts sit far from any natural copper source, showing the metal was traded long distances.

pages.text: A different example of long-distance copper trade involves copper bells. Copper bells found at sites in Arizona and New Mexico were made from smelted copper. Ancient people living in Mexico and Central America made copper bells. pages.text: Obsidian Obsidian is a glassy volcanic rock. Many tools in prehistoric North America were made by chipping flakes off rock to make sharp edges. Obsidian is much better for making sharp edges than regular rock because it has been through a heating process. It can make sharper and harder blades than ordinary glass. Obsidian is found in places that had volcanic activity, and obsidian from different areas has different, tiny amounts of chemicals. We can guess where it came from by examining the chemicals in obsidian, just as we can with the chemicals in copper. Obsidian sculpture Obsidian rock from Panum Crater in northeastern California.
pages.brief: A worker chips sharp flakes from a piece of glassy black obsidian to make a blade; nearby lie a glossy obsidian rock from Panum Crater and a smooth obsidian sculpture, showing the volcanic glass used for tools.

pages.text: People can learn about many objects, not just copper or obsidian, based on trace chemicals. For example, the type of paper used in William’s trading cards, or the kind of ink used to print his cards might reveal where a card comes from. Prehistoric North American people living in the Northwest could easily find obsidian. Obsidian came from areas such as Washington, Oregon, Northern California, and western Canada. Obsidian deposits are often in areas that have volcanoes. Many of the tallest mountains in the Northwest are volcanoes, such as Mt. Rainier near Seattle, Washington, and Mt. Saint Helens. When a volcano erupts and the conditions are right, lava that cools rapidly can form obsidian. Mount St. Helens before its 1980 eruption.
pages.brief: In the volcanic Northwest, Mount Rainier and Mount St. Helens rise above dark slopes; a scientist studies trace chemicals in an obsidian tool, while hot lava cools quickly into glassy obsidian near Washington, Oregon, California, and western Canada.

pages.text: Shells Shells from the ocean are beautiful and can be used for many purposes. Humans have used shells for jewelry, as small plates, and even as musical instruments. At archaeological sites near the ocean, huge piles of shells can be found in trash heaps. Often these piles are the garbage left over after eating the meat in the middle of shellfish. We know that seashells found in the Arizona desert or the upper Mississippi River Valley are not from food, because it would have taken too long to carry shellfish that far inland before it would have become rotten and dangerous to eat. An archaeologist examines seashells found in an ancient trash heap.
pages.brief: Near the ocean, huge piles of discarded shells fill an ancient trash heap; inland in the Arizona desert and upper Mississippi Valley, seashells lie far from the coast, showing they were carried as valuable goods rather than spoiled food.

pages.text: These prehistoric shell earrings were found in northern Arizona. How do we know that some shells found on archaeological sites were used for jewelry? Many of the shells have small holes, usually in the same place. By placing the shells on a string, they could have been made into a necklace. Also, some people wore jewelry when they were buried. Many people were buried with their valuable possessions. When an archaeological site includes ancient graves, archaeologists sometimes find objects in them that were traded great distances. In undisturbed graves, shells have been found in the pattern of a necklace. The string may be gone, but the shells are in the same place they would have been if there had been a string.
pages.brief: In northern Arizona, prehistoric shell earrings and shells with small holes lie near an ancient grave; the shells rest in a necklace pattern around a buried person, hinting that strung shell jewelry was traded from far away.

pages.text: Shells can be helpful in identifying trade connections. Some types of shellfish only live in certain areas. For example, if a type of shell from a shellfish that lived in the Gulf of Mexico is found in Colorado, we know that the people in Colorado traded with someone from near the Gulf of Mexico. Stop & Think Many grocery stores have a counter where seafood is sold. Where does the fish you eat come from? Read the labels or ask someone at the seafood counter where the store’s fish comes from. fish sold at market.
pages.brief: A shell from the Gulf of Mexico lies in Colorado, linking inland people to distant coastal traders; at a grocery seafood counter, a shopper looks at fish from far away, comparing modern food sources with ancient shell trade.

pages.text: The bones of a dog uncovered in an ancient Israeli cemetery Birds and Animals All over the world, animals are a common trade item. When Europeans first came to North America, they brought horses. Horses can be used for transportation or to pull and carry things. After European contact, many animals became part of transatlantic trade. Valuable animals were transported across the Atlantic Ocean. Sometimes we find the bones of birds and other animals in archaeological sites. The bones of animals that live in the area, particularly those that are used as food, are common. For example, in eastern North America, deer bones are often found at sites where ancient people lived.
pages.brief: In an ancient Israeli cemetery, a dog’s bones lie uncovered; across the Atlantic, Europeans bring horses to North America, and at many eastern North American sites deer bones from local food animals appear among the remains.

pages.text: Copper, Shell, and Parrot Trade Four Corners area Ancient Puebloan Chaco Canyon, a major prehistoric MEXICO Sometimes we find the bones of exotic animals in an archaeological site. Exotic animals are those that come from a different place. An elephant is an exotic animal in North America, but normal in parts of Africa. Exotic animals are evidence of trade. For an elephant to come to a zoo in North America, it needs to be traded from a faraway place. Archaeological sites in the Southwest, such as Arizona, sometimes have bones from parrots. Parrots are exotic animals because they ordinarily only live in Central or South America. Archaeologists think these birds were valued for their colorful feathers. The remains of birds, such as parrots, being found thousands of miles north of where they usually live is evidence of long- distance trade.
pages.brief: In the Southwest’s Four Corners area near Chaco Canyon, archaeologists uncover parrot bones thousands of miles north of Central and South America; the colorful exotic birds were likely valued for feathers and show long-distance trade.

pages.text: Conclusion In prehistoric North America, some people traveled thousands of miles to trade. Many times, traders used boats to travel along rivers or on the coast. For example, the Mississippi River was an important trade route that connected much of North America. Other times, people had to walk. Crossing mountain ranges, such as the Rocky or Appalachian Mountains, could take weeks of difficult walking. Today, it is easier to transport heavy trade goods long distances. Ships, trucks, trains, and planes are all used to carry trade goods among the countries of the world. Containers full of trade goods travel by barge.
pages.brief: Prehistoric traders paddle boats along rivers and coasts, including the Mississippi River, while others walk for weeks across the Rocky and Appalachian Mountains; today ships, trucks, trains, planes, and barges carry heavy goods around the world.

pages.text: Trade doesn’t require a truck full of valuable objects such as televisions. Trade can occur when one person gives another person something in exchange for something else. Remember how William got his Japanese trading cards? Next time you take a trip, think about all the things you take with you. Afterward, think about the things you left behind. Did you exchange gifts with someone? Did you buy something you couldn’t get at home? That’s just what the prehistoric people of the world did. Germany Peru Holland Mexico.
pages.brief: A traveler unpacks gifts and souvenirs after a trip, recalling how William traded for Japanese cards; small exchanged objects from Germany, Peru, Holland, and Mexico show that trade can be a simple swap between people.

books.title: Dust Bowl Disaster
books.art_why: Period drawings suit a 1930s historical account of the Dust Bowl and Great Depression.

pages.text: Introduction Hurricanes. Floods. Forest fires. Earthquakes. Every year these natural disasters strike somewhere on Earth. But during the late 1920s and 1930s, two disasters of another kind swept the United States, inflicting pain and suffering on its people. These disasters were particularly troublesome because they lasted for years rather than hours or days, creating hardships for thousands upon thousands of people. The first blow was not a natural disaster but an economic one. This disaster became known as the Great Depression. It began with the crash of the stock market in 1929. The stock market began falling and by the time it stopped falling, stocks were worth about 20 percent of their previous value. People lost their life savings, their jobs, and many of their possessions. Banks and factories closed.
pages.brief: A stormy sky, floodwater and fire show natural disasters striking Earth. In a city street, a closed bank and factory stand beside worried people who have lost their savings, jobs and possessions during the Great Depression.

pages.text: Wheat fields cover the plains as far as the eye can see. From Prosperity to Poverty Farmers in the Great Plains had been prospering for decades before the Dust Bowl struck. World War I (1914–1918) prevented European farmers from growing wheat, so farmers in North America sold their wheat to buyers who shipped it overseas. The demand for wheat drove prices upward. Farmers plowed up more and more of the grasslands to feed the needs of European countries. The farmers of the Great Plains continued to prosper while many others suffered under the Great Depression. But the prosperity would soon end.
pages.brief: Wide wheat fields stretch across the Great Plains as far as the eye can see. Farmers plow up more grassland to plant wheat, and wheat is loaded for buyers overseas. The farmers prosper while many others suffer during the Great Depression.

pages.text: Plowing up the grasslands to grow more wheat caused two problems that the farmers did not expect. First, it made so much wheat available that wheat prices began to drop. Storage bins became filled to capacity, and farmers began to dump their harvested wheat onto the ground and onto roads. Math Minute From July 1930 to July 1931, wheat prices dropped from 68¢ a bushel to 25¢ a bushel. In 1930, farmer Beck planted 100 acres of wheat and harvested 12 bushels per acre. In 1931, he planted another 100 acres and harvested 12 bushels per acre. How much more did he make in 1930 than he did in 1931?
pages.brief: Farmers dump harvested wheat onto the ground and onto roads beside storage bins filled to capacity. A farmer stands near a field where 100 acres of wheat were planted and harvested. Wheat prices have dropped sharply.

pages.text: A choking dust storm whips across the plains. Second, when the Great Plains entered a period of prolonged drought, plowing up the grasslands caused the fields to dry up. With too little moisture to support crops, the fields were left bare. From one hot summer to another, the sun baked the soil. When winds increased, the exposed dry dirt was whipped up into dark clouds of choking dust that swept across the land. The thick, billowing walls of dirt hid the sun and forced people to light lamps in the midday darkness.
pages.brief: A choking dust storm whips across the Great Plains, a dark wall of dirt hiding the sun. Bare, dried fields lie below. Inside a home, people light lamps in the midday darkness while dust fills the air.

pages.text: Living in a Dust Bowl For years, the Dust Bowl gripped the Great Plains. Every time the wind whipped up the dirt and carried it skyward, another dust storm moved across the Great Plains. These storms took on names like dusters and black blizzards. People living in the plains did everything they could to keep the dust from entering their homes and their lungs. pages.brief: Inside a plain farm home, men, women and children stuff newspapers and rags around windows and doors. They tie rags over their faces, and children lie in bed with damp cloths over their mouths and noses to keep dust out.

pages.text: Still, the dust found its way into homes and into the bodies of every living creature. It clogged up motors in cars and trucks. Livestock wandered blindly in the clouds of dust. Many animals fell dead when their lungs became caked with dust. Outside, dust piled up like snowdrifts during a blizzard. The only difference was that the dust drifts did not melt. They just got higher and higher, burying tools, farm equipment, and small buildings. Roads had to be plowed, and trains were literally stopped on tracks covered by heaps of dirt. Conditions got so bad that winds carried the dust eastward to fall across cities such as Chicago, Atlanta, and New York. Dust even blew over the Atlantic Ocean and fell upon decks of ships at sea. A tractor sits by the dust. Word Wise During the winter, winds often whipped up a mixture of snow and dust. These storms became known as snusters.
pages.brief: Dust drifts pile up like snow, burying tools, farm equipment and small buildings. A tractor sits beside a high bank of dust. Livestock wander blindly, and a train stands stopped on tracks covered by heaps of dirt; roads are plowed.

pages.text: Visualize Take a moment and think of what it must have been like on April 14, 1935. Draw a picture of the scene as you visualize it. The Black Sunday storm approaches a town in the Texas panhandle. Perhaps the worst day of all during the Dust Bowl occurred on Black Sunday—April 14, 1935. The day began with the sun rising in a clear blue eastern sky and a gentle breeze whispering from the west. Without warning, a gigantic wall of dirt and dust appeared on the horizon and rushed across the rolling plains at 60 miles (96.5 km) per hour. It rushed eastward so fast that the storm swallowed up birds and rabbits trying to out-fly and outrun it. Animals dropped to the ground, dying of exhaustion and suffocation. People ran for any shelter they could reach—sheds, barns, homes, and cars.
pages.brief: On Black Sunday, April 14, 1935, a gigantic wall of dirt and dust rushes across the Texas panhandle toward a town. People run for sheds, barns, homes and cars. Birds and rabbits try to outrun the storm, and animals drop to the ground.

pages.text: The Black Sunday storm nearly overwhelms a couple of people. Living to Tell Their Story Some people who lived through the Dust Bowl recorded accounts of their experiences. Melt White of Dalhart, Texas, was just a child when Black Sunday occurred. He described his memories of that day in interviews for a documentary film about the Dust Bowl. He described the wind blowing very hard and the house shaking violently. He was frightened that the house might blow away. Outside, the dust filled the sky until it became very dark. He tried to see his hand in front of his face and couldn’t. He kept bringing his hand closer to his face. It was so dark that even when he touched his nose with his hand, he couldn’t see it.
pages.brief: A couple of people are nearly overwhelmed by the Black Sunday storm. Inside a shaking house in Dalhart, Texas, a child named Melt White holds his hand close to his face in the darkness; he cannot see it even when he touches his nose.

pages.text: One Kansas farmer, Lawrence Svobida, kept an extensive written record of his experience and later wrote a book about being a farmer on the Great Plains before, during, and after the Dust Bowl. Here is a description of what he said: Before Svobida described the beauty of seeing many miles of waist-high wheat fields swaying in the breeze. He could think of nothing in the world more beautiful than a golden wheat field in the summer sun. The sight would take his breath away. During the Dust Bowl, farmers hoped to see blowing wheat instead of blowing dust.
pages.brief: Kansas farmer Lawrence Svobida stands beside a waist-high golden wheat field that sways in the summer breeze and stretches for miles under the sun. He holds a written record. During the Dust Bowl, farmers hoped to see blowing wheat instead of blowing dust.

pages.text: During With the Great Plains gripped in a drought, Svobida’s thoughts were much different. He described the wind and the dust that cut visibility to almost nothing. People’s eyes would be filled with dust and wearing goggles didn’t even help. In a documentary film, Svobida talks about the ferocity of the wind and how it seemed to never stop. He had never even imagined such a wind. It felt to him like everything would be blown away, and wherever he looked, his fields were empty. In his book, Svobida wrote about how the experience changed his feelings on farming, which had once provided him with joy. When he knew his crops were irrevocably gone, he described feeling as if there had been a death. Nature had flouted his desire to work the land and the dreams he had of being a farmer. He felt like giving up on everything, including any attempts to make something of his life.
pages.brief: Lawrence Svobida stands in an empty field during the drought, wind and dust cutting visibility to almost nothing. His eyes are filled with dust; goggles do not help. Around him the fields are empty, and he looks defeated, as if everything will be blown away.

pages.text: Farmers wait for rain that won’t come for years. After Svobida, like many others, still clung to the hope that rain would end the drought. In his book, he talked about searching the sky every day for rainclouds. He watched his neighbors’ crops die out one by one, until finally the skies poured out five inches of precipitation over two days. The water soaked into the soil and finally stopped the dust and drought. Eventually, inhaling blowing dust for years seriously affected Lawrence Svobida’s health. He had to admit defeat and leave the Great Plains.
pages.brief: Farmers wait for rain that will not come for years. Lawrence Svobida searches the sky for rainclouds while his neighbors' crops die one by one. Then five inches of rain fall over two days and soak into the soil, stopping the dust and drought. Years of inhaling dust affect his health.

pages.text: Not much was left for cattle to eat in Oklahoma in 1936. Leaving the Dust Bowl People living in the Great Plains were hearty souls who settled the area when there were no houses, water wells, roads, or fields. They were accustomed to difficult times. Many persevered one way or another through the Dirty Thirties. When they couldn’t grow wheat, they turned to raising thistles and a plant called soapweed, which could be chopped up and fed to livestock. Soapweed Many farmers turned to raising dairy cattle at the beginning of the Dust Bowl years. Part of the milk was skimmed off and fed to pigs and chickens. But as the drought worsened, farmers could no longer raise enough feed for their cattle and other livestock.
pages.brief: In Oklahoma in 1936, little is left for cattle to eat. A farm family feeds chopped thistles and soapweed to livestock. Dairy cattle stand on dry land; part of the milk is skimmed off and fed to pigs and chickens as the drought worsens.

pages.text: With no source of income, farmers grew tired and hungry. Many could not keep up payments on their farms. They eventually left the Great Plains to seek a better life elsewhere. Thousands were drawn westward to Do You California to seek work in Know? the state’s rich farmlands. But By the end there were fewer jobs there of the 1930s, than there were people. 2.5 million people had left the Plains states. Two hundred them ended up in California.
pages.brief: Farmers with no income grow tired and hungry and cannot keep up payments on their farms. Families leave the Great Plains and travel westward toward California's rich farmlands, seeking work. There are fewer jobs there than there are people.

pages.text: John Steinbeck John Steinbeck and his book The Grapes migration in his famous 1939 novel The Grapes of Wrath. He wrote about the hundreds of thousands of people who came over the California. They came in cars loaded with all their worldly possessions and often slept in their cars or in tents. Some formed caravans, or groups of cars that traveled together, for safety. People didn’t stay in one place long. They were always moving, searching for work, and desperate for food. Think About It Imagine coming to the Great Plains in the early 1900s and starting a farm. You have built a home, dug a well for water, plowed up grassland to grow wheat, and raised a family. A drought comes and makes it difficult to grow crops. What do you do? Do you stick it out? How do you survive? Or do you pull up stakes and move to another place?
pages.brief: Author John Steinbeck holds a book as families travel toward California in cars loaded with worldly possessions. Some cars form caravans for safety. People sleep in cars or tents, always moving, searching for work and desperate for food.

pages.text: The Government Steps In It was clear that people living in the Great Plains needed help. They were losing their land, their farms, and their hope. Franklin Roosevelt Millions more had lost their jobs because of the Great Depression and had no hope of finding new jobs. All were hungry and poor. Many were dying. In 1932, the citizens of the United States had elected Roosevelt’s inauguration Franklin Roosevelt as their next president. He quickly offered a program for recovery known as the New Deal, which included government agencies and programs to help farmers and unemployed workers. Roosevelt appointed Hugh Bennett, a man well-known for his work in soil conservation, as director of a new agency called the Soil Erosion Service. Bennett worked to change farming methods in order to help stop blowing dirt in its tracks. He worked to convince Congress to pass the Soil Conservation Act of 1935.
pages.brief: At his inauguration, President Franklin Roosevelt announces a New Deal program to help farmers and unemployed workers. Hugh Bennett, known for soil conservation, works to change farming methods and stop blowing dirt. Congress passes the Soil Conservation Act of 1935.

pages.text: Roosevelt also provided other programs to help the weary farmer. Some of these programs were: 1933 – The Emergency Farm Act The act set aside $200 million to help farmers who could not make payments on their farms to refinance their bank loans. 1935 – Drought Relief Service The government bought cattle from farmers to prevent farmers from becoming bankrupt. The government paid them more than they could have received from selling on the regular market. 1935 – Soil Conservation Service This service developed programs to stop soil erosion and paid farmers to use soil-conserving methods to farm. 1937 – Shelterbelt Project This project paid farmers to plant trees all across the Great Plains. Trees planted along fencerows would stop wind from carrying away soil. The plan of the Shelterbelt project was to plant four million from the Canadian into Texas.
pages.brief: Farmers receive help through New Deal programs. Government agents buy cattle from farmers to prevent bankruptcy, pay farmers to use soil-conserving methods, and pay them to plant trees along fencerows across the Great Plains. Rows of young trees stretch from Canada into Texas.

pages.text: In addition to these programs, the New Deal offered many programs aimed at creating jobs for all those who were out of work. The largest of these programs was known as the Works Progress Administration (WPA). The WPA employed millions after it was created in 1935. A Song of the Dust Bowl Stories and songs were written about the Dust Bowl. Perhaps the most famous songs coming out of the Dust Bowl years were written by popular folk singer and writer, Woody Guthrie. Of his many songs, So Long It’s Been Good to Know Yuh (Dusty Old Dust) and Dust Bowl Blues were two of his best known. Above, Guthrie plays to a New York City crowd in the 1940s.
pages.brief: A worker employed by the Works Progress Administration labors at a job after 1935. Folk singer Woody Guthrie plays his guitar for a New York City crowd in the 1940s, performing songs written about the Dust Bowl. Stories and songs about the Dust Bowl are shared.

pages.text: Pawnee National Grasslands, Colorado, is just one of several areas protected by the government to help prevent another Dust Bowl. Conclusion As the Dirty Thirties drew to a close, rain clouds began to replace dust clouds. The drought was finally over for much of the Great Plains and the Canadian Prairie in the early 1940s. Farmers went back to planting wheat. Familiar golden fields waved across the plains once again; however, farming methods had changed and thousands of acres of grasslands had been set aside by governments to try to prevent another Dust Bowl. By 1939, World War II had started in Europe, and by 1941, North America was in the war. With the coming of the war, much of the world pulled out of the Great Depression. The two clouds of the Dirty Thirties had lifted.
pages.brief: Rain clouds replace dust clouds over the Great Plains. Farmers return to planting wheat, and familiar golden fields wave across the plains. In Colorado, the protected Pawnee National Grasslands stretch under the sky, set aside to help prevent another Dust Bowl.
